-Zifikkir- FOLLY.
One morn in every sumnaertide, The sparrow's early twitterings chide Miss Polly'slateness; She sighs and turns' and wakes at last To sense of rapture deep and vast, And sudden greatness.

• • With conscious, coy, yet stately air, She comes (two feet on every stair), - A radiant Folly; And, marching through the breakfast room The birthday salvoes round -her boom In straggling volley. To her, the day's unchallenged queen, Each subject, be he grent. or mean, Due tribute renders; She cuts the string, unfurls the wraps, And bares, 'mid deep drawn "Oh's and claps, Successive splendours. What's done or set aside to-day Depends, it hardly boots to say, On Folly's high word; ' Who speaks of copies, scales or sums, The malapert thenceforth becomes, A scoff and bywotd. What shall the festal pudding be? It hangs on Folly's sole decree— Cook waits direction; Her Highness speaks the word of power, And naught in raisins, eggs, or flour Can raise objection. Through all the grohlling year beside A fork and spoon (to humble pride) Lift meat or bone up; One day of rich and throbbing life She wields, in awful joy, a knife— Divinely grown up. To her pertains that royal round The birthday cake, its summit crowned With brave devices; • She sits, in queenly state aloof, And deals, sans comment or reproof, Capricious slices. One day she wears her birthday crown, Then, all-unsceptred, topples down To common earth-day ; " Three hundred days and sixty-four Must crawl their sordid course before Another birthday.
—Good Words.

div.head: Earittits.
div.p: Earittits.
• Malice drinketh up the greatest part of its own poison. He who says what he likes may hear what he does not

like. Those who trust in their neighbours' help will wait aiohile for their harvest. Christian graces are like perfumes—the more they are pressed, the sweeter they smell.—Scott. He knows much who knows when to speak; he knows more who knows when to hold his tongue. Mine honour is my life; both grow in one; Take honour from me, and my life is done. The two most precious things on this side the grave are our reputation and our life.—Kemble. As we must render an account of every idle wind, so must we, likewise, of our idle silence.—Cranmer. fie who puts a bird construction on a good act reveals his own wickedness of heart —Livingstone. The telephone girls mnsy fairly boast of being con- ected with the best peopre in the city—by wire. "And so you hays been disappointed in Henry?" " Yes ; bitterlyglisappointed." "And he has proved re- creant to the trust you placed in him ?"' "He has, in- deed." "And yet you trusted him implicitly ?" "Yes; I placed every confidence in him." "But he scorned your love ?" "My love! Who said anything about love? It was a letter I gave him tcrpost, and he carried it in his pocket for a fortnight. I shall never, never trust , another man. I shall post my own letters in the future. THE DANGERS FROM COLOUR BLINDNESS.—No man who has this defect should be a physician. He cannot tell whether his patient is flushed or pale. ,As was said of one such, "How should,he know whether this is scar-. let fever? He never saw scarlet in his life." Next to the physician, the chemist is a dangerouS man; he must trust entirely to the labels on his drugs; if they change colour, and this often indicates that they are deteriorat- ing, he does not know, but still sends them out with a cheerful mind. • The sick nurse is alike disqualified, and for the same reason. After these comes the railway signal man, who reads.the red danger signal to stop as if it was the green, commanding him to dash on. Then there is the sailor who mistakes the starboard for the port light of a vessel sighted in the night and reads into it a directly opposite meaning from that it was meant to convey. It is a crime in the colour-blind to itirsue any of these callings when their defect has been brought home to them, and there are other trades which it is foolish in them to follow, because they can never com- pete with those who have perfect vision. The tailor, the milliner, the house painter, the dyer, are instances of these.---Jean Inglow, in Good Words. THE DUKE OF ALBANY. The Duke of Albany once said, "I do not um:Tea-stand why people should always be so kind to me." The reason was not far to seek... He was a young man with an interesting:and amiable iaer- sonality. He had a pensive turn that recalled his father, but with a dash of gaiety of heart which rendered him more acceptable to society than the Prince Consort ever managed to become. His long life of suffering and pain secured for him the sympathies of the people. Despite his ill-hehlth he was even in childhood a bright and pro- mising boy. Professor Tyndall has spoken highly of his capacity at this period, and Dean Stanley, one of his early mentors, so deeply influenced him that at one time the Prince indicated a desire to take Orders in the Anglican Church. At Oxford he was prohibited by the physicians from reading for honours and after he be- came a member of the House of honours, the Queen, 'noticing his eager interest in politics, had „some trouble in dissuading him from plunging into the debates, as a free lance who loved to "drink delight of battle with his peers.". When he was thwarted in this design, the Prince suggested that his services might be utilised in another direction. At the time Lord Normanby resigned the Governorship of Victoria Prince Leopold applied to Mr. Gladstone for the post, and the Tory newspapers and orators of the period heaped the most extraVagant abuse 'on Mr. Gladstone for refusing the offer. Mr. Gladstone was even challenged in the House of Commons on the subject, but his lips being sealed by the Queen. he was unable to defend himself, or do more than make an evasive and ambiguous statement. The truth, however, was that Mr. Gladstone did not refuse the Prince's offer. He referred it to Mr. Murray Smith, Agent-General for Victoria in London, with a request for his opinion. Mr. Smith replied that the appointment would give great satisfaction in Australia, but when the matter was laid before the Queen she peremptorily vetoed the project, assigning as a reason her fear that the Prince's ill-health unfitted him for the duties of the position to which he aspired. Obvious reasons of State have, however, always made the Sovereigns of the Hanoverian dynasty reluct- ant to permit Princes of the Blood-Royal to serve as satraps In distant colonies where asperations to independ- ence are not always dormant. —The Life and Times of Queen Victoria - A LIFE DRAMA OF A LODGING-HOUSE.—It is difficult to imagine any professional man raising himself again after drifting so low as the common lodging-house; yet lam acquainted with many instances in which the teat hap been accomplished. One of the most dramatic cases that occurs to me at the moment happened with regard to a man who was formerly an inmate of the very lodging-house in which we have discovered Mr. Frank Burke. In this house, some years ago, one of the best- known characters was called "The Doctor." It was no nickname. James Arnold seas a doctor. He was a physician who formerly hrd a sp'endid practice in a well-known town in the West of England. He married a very beautiful girl, the daughter of one of his princi- pal patients, and everything promised fairly for a long, happy, and honourable career for him in a noble prcfes- sion. Unfortunately, after a year of happy married life, his young wife died suddenly under very tragic circum- stances. Distracted with grief, Dr. Arnold rushed for re- lief to that fatal remedy for care and anxiety—alcohol. The inevitable ruin came, and, like most of the wreckage of provincial towns and country places, Arnold, de- graded and ruined in his profession, drifted at last to London to swell the ranks of the great city's misery. He came to this lodging-house, and he earned the nightly: fee for shelter by selling fusees in the street. One night,l while running after an omnibus to throw a box of fusees up to a gentleman on the knifeboard, he slipped and fell in the road. A hansom cab was coming along behind. The man turned his horse's head to pass the bus, and before he could pull up the cab had gone over the poor fusee-seller. The unfortunate man wig picked up, found to be badly injured, and taken to the nearest hos- pital. While there he was recognised by one of the doctors who had been a fellow-student. He was shocked to see a brother professional in such a pitiable condition. When Arnold was convalescent and fit to be discharged, the hospital doctor gave him clothes and money, and persuaded him to take the pledge. Dr. Arnold only returned to the lodging-house once to shake hands with the deputy and bid him "good-bye." To-day he is back again In the old town, and has recovered his old prac- tice. When last I heard of him he had come into £4,000 a year, had married again, and was doing well. This is a life-drama of a common lodging-house, which has 'ended happily. Alas, that such an ending should be . rare !—George R. Sims, in Casselrs Saturday Journal. ABOUT. DIFFERENT ?TATTERS.

I wonder if there iS any truth' iii the statement one has heard so repeatedly during the past few years, that "the seasons are gradually changing." Since our arrival in this wonderful city, we have been strangely perplexed at the conflicting state- ments coming to us from all sides as to.the climate of San Francisco. At one time we are told Vat " snew was once seen here, and the people went vvild,over it, and, wasn't it a time for the poor Chiffese, who became a target for evefyone, young and old alike." Again, we are told that "'snow has ilsited the city each winter for several years past." llovvever this may be we, at all events, arrived just in time to participate in all: benefits arising out of 'loth frost and snows I am inclined to think that there is reason in the statement, that "climatic changes are going on," and that England, whiltre- joking in having her good old-fashioued winters—l had almost said Tory winters—has the .consordion of knowing that she is not by herself, other nations having to bear as best they can the privations at- tending severe and prolonged frost. . The papers here contain 'farrowing descriptions of the weather `thank east ;" of trains snow bound, 'awl passengers. suffering unheard of , horrors, blizzards destroying all before them, in fact, almost depopulating whole districts. Accounts are published daily, wherein eastern capitalists' are described as having made their minds up about it, and have de- termined to clear out, bag and baggage, making tracks for the golden west. Well, as I have said, we have had some frost and snow here, sufficient' of the former to burst water pipes, and destroy a good numiher of plants, and enough of the latter to amuse the youngsters. But - these interesting phenomena visit us only when the sun hides her head behind the mountains which surround the city. Here, in this city of the west the sun plays an important part. Houses are built and let subject to the sun's rays. Rents rise and fall according es the sun dic- tates, and woe be to the owner of the tenement alma which the sun never shines, for that habita- tion will never be worth to its owner more than a paltry twelve or fourteen shillings a week. It is almost as desirable that the sun should shine upon ' your sitting-room as that you, the head of the family, should have no family. land my family have trudged somewhat wearily over the whole of the north beach district of this city looking for a house of four rooms and decent-sized kitchen. For this we are willing to pay 15s or 16s per week, but in every case in which we meet with a house that might suit, we are questioned as to the family. Our answer either causes the door to be shut upon us or adds a couple of dollars to the rent. You may, in England, persecute the Malthusian ; here, if you ,dare to be guilty of such wickedness as replenishing the eaoll, you are thrust into holes into which no son of man ought to lay his head. I have come to the conclusion that it requires a Lord Dundreary to-understand the situation here. All the papers agree in painting the country in the brightest colours—that is to induce emigrants to come here; I came with a boat load nearly, and I am• told I have too many—l give the puzzle up. A very happy incident has occurred in consequence of My address being added to one of the letters. A copy of the "Examiner" containing my views on Mrs Parker's "lady help "work was sent out here to Oakland, a town just across the bay. It pleased the gentleman receiving it so much that he at once wrote me, seeking an interview. This was at once arranged, and last Sunday 1,11,1r.110pe, and my son Charley set out to visit•our newly-found friend. Paying our quarter each we steamed across the bay, about six miles; a train in waiting for us took us some miles up country towards the mountains. ' And,' by the way, it is surprising what a distance five cents will carry you out hero. I udderstand that in Oakland city one may ride about all day for simply nothing at aIL In the railway company's4harter lan told it is dis- tinctly stated that for certain privileges out:side the city the inhabitants shall have free carriage within the city's • limits. Well, after a most beautif4 and, as I was in- clined to think, or compare/ it to an English summer's walk, we reached our new-friend. What a reception we had to be sure!, We were soon at home; our host and his good wife strove with each other which should make us most welcome, and we were soon sat at a table, not quitegroaning under, but all the same, covered with pre- served apricots and tomatoes. The good dame seemed thoroughly besides herself with pleasure to s..e how hear- tily we put on one side the good things placed before us. Out in their own orchard these fruits were grown last

summer, and the good lady was pleased, and Ead a right to be pleased, in saying no better fruit was canned in California than the fruit before us, and all her own do- ing. After attending to nature's wants, we adjourned to the verandah, the sun blazing down upon us as i f it was July . Mr. Matthews, our host, served his apprenticeship as a blacksmith at the Vulcan Works, Earlestown, near War- rington. Being of an adventurous spirit, he turned his trade to account in the Crimean War. Passing safely through that, he soon after went to seek his fortune in Canada. Meeeting with a fair Canadian Willing to help in the quest together, they took part in the great Cali- fornia gold e• a. From that to owning and managing as a large cattle ranch, was an eg.sy step. Didn't we sit and listen to the tales of mining camp life; to the tale of hard experience gained on a cattle ran ch,of the awful blizzards, during which the owner, helpless himself, knew his cattle were falling by the hundred, choked and smothered by the clouds of frozen sleet, and snow. Well, I guess we did, and right well we enjoyed ourselves. It was the happimt day we had passed since we left the old sod. A pressing and hearty invitation to go over whenever we liked, will ,all being well, find us in this district again, more especially as a little information will be required as to preserving the fruit we are promised if we only take baskets along with us. Oakland city is built on what seems to have been flat and marshy land, hence while the rainy weeks are on it is apt to be rather slushy. Otherwise it seems to be just the place for a man to retire to, who, having made his pile, like our friend Mr. Matthews,* wishes to leave the madding crowd behind him. Lots, innumerable, are to be had for very little, and workmen having a taste for orchard and garden work are purchasing them, crossing the bay in the mighty steamers, night and morning. We have one little trouble to surmount ere we can say we are fixed, that is the finding a house suitable for us. We are all keeping well. Especially is this the case with the youngsters, each one looking considerably better and. fleshier than wken in England. Living on the edge of the bay, the children are away fer hours together plag- ing near the rolling tide. I hope, as a newly enrollgi son of St. George, to say a few words respecting this band of Englishmen in my next. March 16th; 1888. 2,305, Taylor-street, San Francisco.

Richard Cobden once asked, speakin,- in his noble, up- right fashion, and thinking of a famous, successful, and unscrupulous statesman, "How will it be with him when all is retrospect ?" This is the great touchstone of life— how it looks when regarded through all its long perspec- tive, at a time when its chief actor has little or no power to add to or improve the picture. . _ ._ •

THE EXAMINER, SAT URD MARRIAGE 01? THE REV.; G. D. WRAY AND 'aIISS WILKINSON. A wedding that attracted much public notice was solemnised at St. Paul's 'Church, Bewsey-road, War- rington, on Wednesday afternoon. The contractiN parties were the Rev. George Daniel Wray, M.XO'.. vicar of St Peter's Warring,on, son el the _Rev. n. Wray, late vicar of Crawley Down, Sussex, and nit+ Blanche Wilkinson, only Oughter of the S.. Wilkinson, M.A., vicar of St., Paul's, Warrington. the date fixed for the ceremony to take place had been known for some time, and ai both Mr. Wray and Miss Wilkinson were not only well known, but widely respected, especially in the parishes of St. Paul's and St. Peter's, it was not to be wondered at that such a large.number of people gathered at the church to. witness it. Two o'clock in the afternoon was the time fixed for the commencement of the rafrriage service, but as early, as, one o'clock people began to arrive at the church, with a view of securing a" good seat." Only, a limited ritimber of ' the general public, however,, were admitted, the invited , guests being so numerous as to require most of ' the accommodation. A large crowd collected in the•viei- nity of the church, and as the darriages drovenpthereWas a good deal of uncomfortable crushing. Almost precisely J at two o'clock the bridal party entered the sacred edifice, ' the choir and clergy meeting theni at the west door, and the procession then marched to the choir stalls. At the 'close of the procession were a number of little girls, Sun- ' Aay school scholars, appropriately dressed, and carrying., flowers, and as the bridal party proceeded up the aisle the choir, and manylif those composing the vast congre- gation,, sang the well known hymn commencing "The voice that breathed o'er Eden." The marriage ceremony was performed by the Rev. Canon Sharp, of Downham, diocese of, Ely, brother of Mr. William Sharp,of Sankey- street. who officiated in the unavoidable absence of Mr. Wray's former vicar, the Rev. R. B. Hull, of Nortimnp- tort: The service was choral. Mr. Louis Cobbett, df Waybridge Heath, Surrey, one of the former school- fellows of the bridegroom, was best man, and the brides- maids were Miss Powys, Miss Greenall, Miss Bertha ' Oreenall, and Miss Emily Powys. They each wore beautiful cream-colored dresses, arid carried a bouquet of primroses. The bride was attired hi white corded silk, and wore a tulle veil, with a wreath of white heather, myrtle.; and orange blossoms. She also carried a handsome bouquet of choice white flowers. The bride was given away by her father. During the service, Mr. J. J. L3rthgoe, the organist of the churcH, played a triumphal march by Robinson "Marcheaux Flambeaux" by Scottson-Clarke, and " Marche Romaine" by Rimbault. At the conclusion he played Mendebeobn's "Wedding March." It . should be mentioned that the church was tastefully decorated for the occasion, and that carpeting was laid from ,the principal entrance door, and up the central aisle. Almost immediately after the/ceremony the parents of the bride, Mr. and Mrs.-Wilkinson, gave an " At,Home ''' in the schoolroom, near Heath-side, at which most of the 300 persons hi whom invitations had been accorded were present, and at which suitable refreshment-s were dis- pensed, This pleasant gathering was in the' evening followed by a very successful ball. The newly-married coupleleft Warrington in the afternoon for Clifton, there to 'spend the honeymoon. The wedding cake was supplied by Mr. Rolland. of Chester. The following is a list of

WRAY. On Monday evening the Rev. G. D. Wray, vicar of St. Peter's, was presented with a very handsome timepiece, subscribed for by the members of the congregation. The presentation took place in the School-room, John-street. Mr. John Roberts took the chair, and amongst others present were the Rev. G. D. Wray, Miss Wray, Rev. S.,' Mrs., and Miss Wilkinson, Mrs. Cox, Mrs. Edgar, Mr. Jos. Blease, Mr. S. Rudd, Mr. J. Hands, Mr. W. J. Roberts, Miss Jones Miss Pollitt, Mr. Home, Mr. Rat- cliffe, Mrs. Home, Jones, Rudd, Mr. Henry Dagnall, and Mrs. Green.—The CIKAIRMAN mid he had been deputed by the congregation of St. Peter's to perform the very pleasing duty of presenting to Mr. Wray a beautiful marble timepiece on the occasion of his marriage. The subscriptions had come from very humble people, and he had no doubt that on that account Mr. Wray would the more highly appreciate, the present. Mr. • Wray had not been amongst them many months as their vicar, but he had made himself respected, and he hoped the future life of him- self and his intended wife would lw a happy one. (Applause.) Mr. EDGAR, Mr. BLEASE, and the Rev. S. WIIZINtiON also made a few remarks.— The Rev. G. D. WRAY, in acknowledging the present, said the happiness of being married was very great, but it was increased ten-fold by the many expressions of good will which Miss Wilkinson and himself had re- ceived on their approaching marriage. He had never received anything but the greatest kindness from the parishiOners of St. Peter's, and his only grief was that he had not been able to see as much of the parishioners as he wished, because nearly the whole of his time in a large parish like this was taken up in visiting the sick. He was glad to think that he was not the only person in the par- ish who looked forward to a future for the parish of St. Peter's. He had heard other people say that in time they would have a church, which would the better en- able them to carry on the work they were anxious to do for the glory of Pod. He had every reason to, believe that his future 'wife would be most happy amongst the people of St. Peter's, and if she received the same ,kind- ness and help he had received she would have every reason to be happy. (Applause.) The . brass candle- sticks and the letter rack which they sa,sv on the table before them were an expression of kindness from the "mother's meeting." MANCHESTER AND LIVERPDOL ASSIZES.—On Thursday morning the assize circular was issued setting 'forth the arrangements for the ensuing Manchester and Liverpool Asstes. Special jury causes are taken at Manchester on the 25th of April, and at Liverpool oh the 7th of May.

MR. GLADSTONE AND THE NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDER- ATION.—Mr. Gladstone was the principal guest at a din- ner given on Wednesday evening by Sir W. Foster, the President of the National Liberal Federation. In respon- ding to the toast of his health, he said that although he , could not feel Certain about the further prolongation of his health for any considerable time, he rejoiced to know that the contest in which they were engaged did not de- pend upon the health or strength of any intlividual. Re- ferring to the business in Parliament, he said there was work cut out for the present session in the Local Government Bill and the Budget alone. Nothing but public mischief could result if they attempted to slur over a measure so weighty as the Local Government Bin. There must be a thorough sifting of proposals so large and so important and so complicated. They must see that no vexatious imposts were placed upon locomo- tion or any particular implements of commerce in order to bring about a small political result. With regard to local government for Ireland, Sir E. Watkin had asked the-Government if they were prepared to state what were the proposals. The reply of Mr. Smith was of a very serious nature. It was to the effect that until the Irish people had sunk their political opinions they were not to be placed upon an equality with England and Wales and Scotland in regard to local government, though Ireland was crippled by want of kcal govern- ment in her counties and boroughs. Such a reply on be- half of the Government was dishonouring and scanda- lous, and was a breach of Tory and Dissentient pledges made at the general election.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOtTSE OF COMMONS.—Mobrear.

The Speaker took the chair at 3 0 p.m. Mr. Drumror gave notice that he would move his motion, in regard to the disestablishmentpf the Wel& Church, on May Ist. Some discussion was caused when the succeeding question was addressed to the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer. Thf query had reference to the wheel tax, and Mr. H. A. WRIGHT sought to know whether Mr. Goschen would reconsider the proposed tax on all vehiclefr over lOcwt. by raising the limit of weight to such a figure as would n, "nclnde ordinary one-horse carts used for carrying and other goods.—Some subsidiary ques- tions followed, involving a suggestion that traction en- gines should bear a higher tax than lighter vehicles.— Before the Chancellor of the Exchequer replied, Mr. W. Causrmi, the member for Southwark, rose hastily from his seat, and demanded to know whether Mr. Goschen did not entirely withdraw his proposals in reference to the wheel tax.—Mr. GOSCEIRN replied in a most decisive negative, and he added that the present time was net the proper one for discussing the details of the proposed tax. Traction engines, it appeared, will escape with a little payment, as heretofore. The claims of medical men and ministers of religion to exemption from the horse tax were again submitted to the Chancellor of the Exchequer. who gave no further information than that the matter is still receiving the attention of the Government. 'COI.. KENO-HARMAN'S' SALARY.—The first business on the paper was the report of the resolution agreed to in Committee before the holidays in reference to the pro- posed salary to the Under-Secretary to the Lord Lieu- tenant —Mr. Mal-Wilily on behalf of the Irish mem- bers, objected to taking the stage at this time, and moved the adjournment of the debate; but this was negatived by 169 to 104, and the resolution was carried by 184 te 109, after which a bill founded 011 it was introduced and read a first time. , THE BUDGET RESOLUTIONS.

Oa the consideration of the Budget resolutions being resumed in Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. GLanwromr, premising that he did not on this occasion intend to pronounce any definite opinion or' the Budget as a whole, said there were some points of it of which .he approved, while he disapproved of others. For instance, he attached great value to the principle of substituting taxes for grants in aid as a method of re-adjusting Imperial and local taxation, and he thought the reduction of a penny in the income tax a point on which there could be no difference of opinion. Of the new taxes he had:little M say that would be encouraging, and he thought it required a great deal of 'boldness to propose to revive taxes on locomotion, which ho foretold would give Mr. (A °schen considerable difficulty. Of ,the general scheme, he remarked that this was the first time that a surplus of two and a quarter millions had been disposed of without any relief being given to the general consumer—for the relief to the rates, he con. tended, would go to the owners .of property. Calling on the Government to state whether they intended now "to make a clean job" of remedying the inequali- ties in the rating of realty and personalty, he insisted that the opportunity should also be taken to equalisr the Imperial burdens on real and personal property, and this he argued at some length would not be achieved by Mr. Goschen's-proposal to increase the succession duty, which he regarded as illusory. At the proper time hr intimated that the Opposition would submit a proposi- tion to do fustice :between realty and personalty by in- creasing the death duties on the former. The Cnflarcisixon a the EXCREQMSR commenced his reply by thanking Mr. Gladstone for the general tone of Ills criticisms on the Budget, and pointed out, in regard to the complaint that no relief had been given to the consumer, that Parliament and the Ctivernrneut were committed over and over again to do justice to the ratepayers. He denied Joe, that the relief proposed in the Budget would go solely to the owners of property. The consumers would be largely benefited, and especially those whq were interested in that general com- modity—a house. As to the finality of the scheme, he said emphatically that the Government believed that they had adequately met the demands of those who were interested in local taxation. Thor had shOwn their whole hand, and had no further plans; but they main- tained • that their proposals for the readjustment of local and Imperial taxation must be regarded as a whole. As to the inequality between the Imperial taxation of realty and personalty, he thought Mr. Glad- stone had not made sufficient allowance for the great Fall in the value of land of late years, while personalty liad largely increased; and when the Opposition made its proposal for increasing the taxation of realty he should be prepared to argue that his plan was fair and adequate. The debate was continued by Mr. Jeffries; Mr. ffnatcll- - till-Flugessen, Lord Weimer, and Sir Stafford Islorthcote. —Mr. SRAW-LRFICVRE thought there was a glaring in. in the treatment of leasehold and freehold +•roperty.—Mr. Lartommut suggested that the agri• niturist in England should do as the agriculturist in •eland had done—combine and get a reduction of rent: A. present the farmers in England were the slaves of the '.indlords.
Mr. Gosenmepmksted against theluggle that it vcm" rich ntan's Budget, and contended that the land repre• ,ented the farmers as well agothe landlords. The Budget resolutions were then agreed tx!.

Mr. GOSCUFST, in answer to Mr. CausiOn, said a separato ',l would be introduced for the horse, wheel, and van t XPR which affect,ql lewCal tacntion. The House adinurnsd at 12 20 am. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuEsnay. •

The Speaker took the chair -at three o'clock. FaonATE Durr.—ln answer to Mr. Hoyle, the CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER stated that the total probate , duty Amounted to about £4,000,000. . THE BUDGET PaOPosAIS.—A number of questions were again put to Mr. Goschen respecting the Budget pro- p-dsals, and the right hon. _gentleman, while deprecating the attempts to induce hint to interpret a Bill which had not yet been finally 'drawn, said if carts were let out solely for agricultural purposes they would be exempt from taxation, and that the duty on, Yeomanry horses would 'be returned. It was estimated that there were one million horses used for agricultural purposes which would be exempt. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.—Mr. RITCHIE ex- plained that the Local Government Bill would make no alteration in the law respecting the abaterdent in the licence duties, new allowed to those publicans who vol- untarily closed their houses on Sundays or on other days an hour earlier than the law required. The Government would regard with favour any amendment for repealing that part of the Municipal Corporation Act that referred to the disqualification of clergymen and dissenting mini- sters from sittinem councils. , Tun FISHERY DEPARTMENT.—Sir E. BIRICRECIE, in call- ing attention to the present constitution of the fishery departmeat of the Board of Trade, proposed that the de- partment should be placed under an authority compris- ing, in addition to, the officials of the Board of Trade, persons with a practical knowledge of the sea and inland fisheries. He urged the appointment of local councils at all the fishing ports with statutory powers relative to the fisheries within defined limits.—The motion was sup- ported by Sir E. Gray, Major Rasch, Mr. Heneage, and others, Mr. Majoribanks advocating the appointment of fishery boards similar th those which existed in Scotland. —Sir E. BIRERECK withdrew his motion conditionally upon a clause being inserted in the proposed Bill carrying out the proasal for local councils. MiscEttextous.—Mr. Goschen brought in the Budget Bill, and it was read a first time. The Musical Comp:pi- tion Copyright Bill was read a third time. The House Adjourned' at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock. HOUSE OF COMIONS.—NVEDNEstay. The Speaker took the chair at twenty miriute,s after 'twelve o'clock.' FAIR RENT AND ARREARS IN IRELAND.—The greater portion of the sitting was occupied with the considera- tion of the Agricultural 'Tenants' Relief Bill for Ireland, of which Mr. BLAINE moved the wend reading. The bill, which deals with the Question of arrears, and also seeks to get a fair rent fixed, met with opposition—Mr. MAcanrixr, the Conservative member for Antrim, moved that it be read that day six months.—Mr. Gill. Mr. J. Ellis, and Mr. T. Healy spoke earnestly in favour of the bill, the latter hon. member pointing out that there was a constant confiscation of, tenants improve- ments, especially with regard to leaseholders, and that the law on this point ought to be amended.—The SoriCiToß GENERAL for IRELaND could not admit that there was any injustice in the law as to tenants' improvements, and with regard to arrears, they had, he said, already been the subject of legislation of an eminently fair and reasonable kind.—Mr. T. W. RUSSELL did not know how long the question would be before the House; but he was perfectly sure that the substance of the bill would have.to be.cArried; and until that was done the peace of Ireland would not be secure.—Mr. JOHN Molt- LEY, referring to the extraordinary position of the Solici- tor General for Ireland, said he had apparently forgotten that the Government had induced the House three weeks ago tq pass an'a'mendment and accept aproposition which virtually committed themto an admission Of the fact that there was a case for dealing with arrears.—Mr. Betrotra endeavoured to show that thebill, so far as one of its im- portant provisions was concerned, was somewhat stale; but Mr. PARNELL, interrupting him, said the arrears clauses had never been brought forward before.—Sir George TreVelyan and Mr. Sinclair spoke on the bill, the latter amid cries of "Divide." The House then divided, and there were—for the second reading, 190; against, 247; majority against, sg. The announcement was re- ceived with Opposition cheers. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAT. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. _ _

QuxsvioNs.—Questions upon all sorts of subjects, from the betrayal of the War Office secrets to the encourage- ment of gambling among children and the new tax on carts, were asked, and Mr. Goschen particularly had a lively time of it. The clause, he said, imposing a race- horse,cluty would be so framed as to exclude hunters occasionally run in local races, and the duty would be expressly confined to horses regularly used for racing and trained for races in train- ing PARNELL pressed Mr. Balfour for father information as to the attack on the people at Ennis' especially with regard to the stone-throwing of which the Chief Secretary had becu o conticlent ; but

the reply was so framed that it led one to believe the police and military had focussed their attack entirely upon one newspaper reporter.—Mr. GOSCHEN stated that Thursday was the last day on which assent% could be given to the conversion of Consols into the new stock, and the conversion did not fall far short of £280,000,000, exclusive of the assents that would be given later on by trustees. Taking these together with the conversion of the New Threes, he said, amid cheers, the total conver- sion amounted to about. £450,000,000. ' TEE ATTACK ON THE POLICE AT ENNIS. Mr. SMITH having intimated that he should ask for precedence for the Local Government Bill next day, Mr. PARNELL moved the adjournment for.the purpose of discussing Senday's attack at Ennis. Not only Mr. Parnell indignant If pro- tested against the cruel policy. of the Irish Executive in attacking the people, but Mt. GLADSTONE, Mr. JOHN Monurr, Sir GEORGE TREVELTAN and many others spoke earnestly in deprecation of such conduct, Mr. GLAD- STONE saying that the public authority at Ennis showed a want of humanity., a lack of prudent policy, and had indulged in gross illegality. Mr. BALvoun, who was twitted by Mr. John Morley with staying in London to attend banquets instead of in- stituting a proper inquiry, made a feeble ex- explanation; but he was in no doubt from the tone of the speeches that a thorough investigation will be insisted upon. The House divided, when there were—for the motion, 179; against, 249; majority, 70. LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL, &C.—The debate VD the motion for the second reading of the Local Government Bill—which Mr. Stansfeld urged was too important to push hurriedly through the House—stood adjourned at midnight. Report of Supply was agreed to after Mr. Buchanan had urged that measures should be taken to protect our mission and pommercial interests on Lake Nyassa, and several bills baying been brought in and read a first time, the House adjourned at 25 minutes past twelve o'clock.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 14,1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 14,1888.
IRELAND.

A caretaker named O'Donnell was brutally beaten ane stabbed by a party ot men, near Newcastle West. or Sunday night. Three arrests have been made. The hearing of the Quirk murder case was resumed at Wicklow, on Saturday. Mr. Justice O'Brien, in summing up the evidence, spoke for five hours and fifty minutes. The jury, after a consultation of three hours and a quarter, found the prisoner. .lames Kirby. guilty, and he was sentenced to be hanged on 7th May. The prisoner maintained his innocence. - - - • - •

At Longhrea, on Monday, several persons arrested on Saturday evening for having exhibited placards in their windows announcing the Nationalist meeting were brought before the resident magistrate, and remand& on bail until the 19th inst. Mr. William O'Brien and Mr. Wilson, M.P.'s, Were in court daring the proceedings. Nationalist band which approached the court-house 'was dispersed by the police, who had followed them a long distance.

A Parliamentary return, issued on Saturday, shows the number of arrests and convictions for agrarian crime in Ireland last rear. The total number ,of such offences reported avas.BB3,including six eases of murder, for two of which offenders wereconvicted, two were awaiting trial. one was tried without a convi6tion being obtained, and one was not detected. In 19 cases of firing at the person only one offender was convicted, and In 35 agrarian crime cases of firing into dwellings none of the offenders were convicted. Only 10 out of 125 cases of incendiary res were detected;and of 192 ens& of threatening letters only three were detected. In 93 cases ot intimidation be other means 71 were not detected; and of 111 cases Of injury to property 99 showed no conviction. Convic- tions were obtained in nine out of eleven cases of assault on the police. A meeting of the National &hoot teachers of county Cork Was held on Satiirdity, the Mayor presiding. Pro- minent citizens of all sheries or religious and political ovinion were present. Resolutions were passed approv- irk of the claims of theTi Naiional school teachers to better pensions, better residences, and better pay for qualified teachers; and Mr. Lne, M.P., in supporting one of the resolutions, expressed an opinion that the' teachers should take Some stens of a practical nature to attract public attention to their, grievances. He sug. rested that the teachers Of Ireland should give notice to the Government that if by a certain date some measure was not, introduced to remedy their wrongs they would :lose their schools simultarfeensly. The mere possibility of the adopition of such a cotii,re would produce such a , powerful effect upon Parliament and unon the public as would result in the remove' of their rrievances.

div.head: CLTIMENT POLITICS.
div.p: CLTIMENT POLITICS.

It is understood that when the Customs and Inland 'Zevenue Bill comes on for second reading an amend- uent will be moved from the front Opposition bench raising the qnestion of eqnplisinir the succession and probate elnties. _ _

Sunday was the second anniversary of the introduction of his famous Home Rule Sill by Mr. Gladstone. At a •neeting of several thousand Irishmen in the Vicar's croft, Leeds, a resolution was passed, thanking Mr. ;ladstone for his labours in the interests of the two ountries, and praying that he might be spared to fulfil •he task he had so ably undertaken. Sir C. Russell, M.P., and Sir J. Lubbock, M.P., were ,resent on Monday at a disorderly meeting convened at ilackney by the Early Closing Association. Sir Charles, who presided, declined to commit himself to support Sir Lubbock's early closing bill. The meeting, which was composed mainly of shopkeepers, would hardly give Sir -Ain a hearing, and rejected a resolution in favour of his bill. _ _

The Rev. J. Ellis. who is well known as taking a sturdy oosition on the subject of Home Rule, and as an earnest Advocate of it, has voluntarily resigned the living of Wiled's; Yorkshire, which is worth £3OO a year. Fie as done so because he is altogether (Int of touch with the political leanings of his Church, not only on many matters of ordinary Church polity, but notably with regard to Disendovrment. He has no other living in view.

THE BUDGET. Mr. GosPnen.has written to Sir E. Birkbeck, M.P., to the effect that'he desired to give the tenant farmers the benefit of any doubt upon some points raised in connec- tion with the Bridget arrusgernents. There would be nn tax of any sort on farm NM=OBS and carts used on a farm, unless the farmer carted goods for other people.

r - A brae meeting of carmen, contractors, van-maker., and wheelwrights was held at the, Cannon-street Hotel, London, on Saturday, to nrotest against the proposed new wheel tax, when a resolution condemning the tax as retrograde measure was passed. A deputation was appointe.d to wait on Mr. Goschen on the subject.

div.head: 'IRE MID-LANARK VACANCY.
div.p: 'IRE MID-LANARK VACANCY.

- -- Mr. J. W. Phitlipps, of London, was .selectecl by the Executive a the Mid-Lanark Liberal Association on Monday night as candidate for the division, and was 4f terwards introduced and accepted the nomination.

Mr. Hardie, the labour candidate for Mid-Lanark, writes that. lie will not resign. It is anticipated, how- ever, that the real fight will be between Messrs. Phillips ind Bonsfield,.the Gladstonian and Unionist candidates. LORD _R. criuncarLL AND THE TORY DEMOCRACY.

-rord Randolph ChUrchin on Monday addressed a' crowded meeting ip the Town pall, Birmingham, in con- nection with the opening, of the Edgbastdn Conservative Association. Referring to the present position of parties; the noble lord' said that the political barometer appeared to stand. at set fair, and this he maintained was due to the fact that the present Government was a good one, ft was not too strong, and therefore 'Was not likely to fall into rciotakes, which experience taught them Go-. vernments of overwhelming strength usually did.. The leading feature of the Government was the support of the Liberal Unionist party, which was a happy mixture nt loyalty and independence. Then the composition of the Tory party differed widely from all former Tory parties in the House of Cotimons,tecause it was Mainly composed of representatives' who represented large and popular centres of the people. He glanced with satis- faction to the improved state of Ireland, but warned the Government not to depend too much on severe ncl• ministration of the law. The Local Government Bill walashuge and comprehensive measure, and he had no doubt vrould pass into law. He congratulated the Char, cellor of the Exchequer on the excellence of the Budget, which would pass without serious ppposition; and hi' felt assured that the realisation of the Tory derdocracy was near at hand.

div.head: JOKE THICII BROUGHT TEARS TO
div.p: A JOKE THICII BROUGHT TEARS TO
HIS E

Three cominercial travellers sat over their wine and cigars one day after dinner, in a comfortable inn in Devonshire. They were "jolly good fellows," knowing each other as Tom, Dick, and Harry. After comparing notes on the state of trade, etc., jokes said stories went around, till, at last, Tom and Dick began chaffing Harry on the shabby condition of his head, for his hair was fast falling out, and the sparse quantity he still retained Was quite gray, and both de- clared he had deceived them concerning hit age, for his scanty gray hairs proved that he had already "fallen into the sear— the yellow leaf.' Dick declared that he knew of a sure remedy. Harry innocently and anxiously inquired what it was. Dick told him: "Cut half a dozen red onions into thick slices; rub your head thoroughly with them, and—leaving the slices on your head—sit in the hot sun for three hours I" "Nonsense I" Harry., objected. "Well, if you don't choose to try it, go bald I Harry secretly revived to try it, and did. The next day his mischievous friends spied him sitting In the sun, in the stable yard, his head plastered With onions, his eyes full of their juice, and streaming with tears. The shout they set up told Harry that he was sold, and but for Tom's interference Dick's head would have stood in need of a plaster. Dick apologised. and made amends by informing Harry of the admirable qualities of Hrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Re- storer, which never fails to restore the hair to its natural colour, prevents it from falling out, and gives it the luxuri- ance and silken glossiness of youth. It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the world. It should always be kept on the toilet table for dressing the hair. RI is delicate and agreeable.

FATAL FIRE.—A fire occurred early on Tuesday morn- ing in a cottage at Rural Vale, Rosherville, Gravesend, by which two boys, named Jenkins, aged 14 and 8, sons of the tenant, were burnt to death. Their charred re- mains were some time afterwards dug out, in one ease only a portion of the trunk being found.

div.head: , THE PREMIER ii NORTH WALES.
div.p: , THE PREMIER ii NORTH WALES.

The Marquis of Salisbury on Tuesday addressed a great Conservative gathering in the Pavilion, Carnarvon. In the afternoon there was a Conference of the Walsh divisions of the National Union of Conservative Associa- tions, which was attended by about 400 members. Mr. P. P. Pennant presided, and resolutions were passed hailing with satisfaction the introduction of the Tithes Bills as. likely to promote the Conservative cause in Wales; approving of the .provisions of the Local Government Bill,, and condemning any attempt to introduce Irish methoda of agitation into Wales. 'The parili 'which is stated to be the largest building of the ki, Wales, was crowded for more than an hour before the advertised hour for the commencement of the proceedings at the evening meeting. The front of the platform was turned into a beautiful bank of natural primroses, relieved with other floral ornaments, while the galleries and walls of the hall were profusely draped with banners, bannerettes, and bunting. The mottoes intertwined were numerous. Outside, on the road from Vaynol Park, several triumphal arches had been erected, while from many houses flags and bunting streamed, most of them bearing words of wel- come to the noble Marquis. The meeting was presided over by Sir Wa.tkin Williams Wynne, and .it was variously estimated that there were from 7,000 to 10,000 persons present. Among others on the platform were the Marquis of Anglesey, Lord Boston, Lord Harlech, Lord Mostyn, Lord Ormathweite, Lord Penrhyn, Lord Kenyon, Lord Aveland, Mr. Stanley Leighton, M.P., Sir John Pnleston, M.P.. Admiral Mayne, M.P., Mr. E. slweatenham, M.P., the Hon. Harold Finch-Hatton, Sir Pryce Jones, Mr. Assheton Smith, the Hon. Douglas Pen- nant, the Hon. G. T. Kenyon, M.l'., and Mr. Geo. Owen, secretary. There was also a large number of ladies present Lord Salisbury, on entering the hall; was received with prolonged cheering, the vast audience rising, cheering end waving hats and handkerchiefs, while a band broke into the triumphant strains of "See the conquering hero tomes." The proceedings were formally opened by the Cnarn- nem, who read an address of welcome on behalf of the Conservative Associations of the six counties of North Wales, and on behalf of the Unionists generally. Lord PENRRYN then moved a vote of confidence in the Government, which was seconded by Mr. W. R. M. t•Vyrorv, and carried with great enthusiasm. Lord SALISBURY, on rising to reply, was again re- eeived with loud cheers. With respect to the policy of the Government, he observed that their opponents were in Ihe-habit of saying that it was a policy which was really heir (the opponents) own, and that the Gcvernmen t were merely continuing it from them: If they were speaking merely of ,Lord Rosebery's six months' policy, ler would not have much fault to find with the observa. "ions, but when he was told that the policy of the 41,oyernment in foreign affairs, was Lord Granville's oolicy continued, he most energetically disclaimed I that observation. (Cheers.) It was not Lord Gran- ville's policy, either in . its metheds or its results, as shown by the condition of South 'Africa, Egypt, and fghanistan in Lord Granville's time and their condition I now. (Cheers.) The Government, no doubt, had had I ;nany adr, cres, and one Of these was the enlistment ef Mv. Gd• . into its ranks. The brilliant measure of conversion Nide!' that gentleman had devised was one which could not have been carried to a successful issue except by his nice and accurate judgment and his pro- found knowledge of financial matfers. (Cheers.) The Government owed him a debt which he could not ex- Press. a debt which the British people would feel they shared when they appreciated both that measure and toe Budget proposals that bad been made. (Cheers.) That vas one feature of the formation of the Govern- ment. Another was the thorny dispute which might luta taken a malignant turn, and threatened to brine into conflict America anfrourselves. The Government, however, were able to entrust the settlement of the dis- pute to Mr. Chamberlain—(cheers)—who, inundertaking ' it, was stepping outside the bounds of a political party. and serving ministers whom upon other qttestions he had opposed, and who could have been actuated by no consideration but the purest patriotism in undertaking -o difficult a mission at so critical a 'time. (Cheers.) I Comingto the Local Government Bill, the noble marquis, d fter complimenting Lord Randolph Churchill on his Birmingham speech, said he disagreed with him in the 6'atereent that the measure had no enemies, but they were biding their time. The Radleals knew that to , oppose it straight might disagreeably embarass them with their constituents, and not improve their political condition, and so they adopted a plan which was not deficient in ingenuity. 'No' knew that they. (the Radicals) were unpopular with the great majority of the eonstituencies, anti therefore if they wished to oppose t-he measure they said that they liked It, and thereby they hoped to attach to the measure sobae of their own unpopularity. (Cheers and laughter.) For himself he ished to deny the imputation that it was a Radical measure: Two and a half years ago, at Newport, Iv had .t.ut in the forepoint of the Conservative programme a teeasure for the reform of Local Government. •ted he then plainly stated that the councils -xercising such government would be popularly elected, od he further stated that many of the questions affect- "g the liquor trade would be referred to those authori• The talk of Radicalism was all nonsense, and had nothing te do with the subject. Parliament had for :k ears been taking away the powers of county magis- trates, and the only bit of genuine independent power which the magistrates still retained over county govern- ',eat was the liberty to repair county bridges. The amount of power which had been transferred from the mirearchy, as it was called, had, been exceedingly .4 real, and he did not believe that more than a eery few magistrates had ever taken any part in constant administration of county affairs. Re admitted here was a great evil in the bill, but it could not be helped, viz., the setting aside oi individual men who o or with great labour and credit to themselves were doing certain county duties. He was very sorry that was the case, but he hoped they would see very much the same class of men find their way into County Coun- cils who now found their way to quarter sessions. But whether or no, it made no difference in the con. tidence with which he asserted that this was nol ft Radical and revolutionary measure. Be did not be- ' eve that the counties as a whole would return Radical • epresentatives, for there would be, precisely the same ranchise for the new bodies as that which at present returned Conservative representatives to Parliament It had been stated that the Coenty Councils ought not to have an unlimited power of incurring loans, and ir that he quite agreed. While it was wise that the Coun- -6ls should have power to spend their annual income, ' was not wise to trust them with the power of spendine the money of their grandchildren. (Cheers.) They had already suffered too much in that direction with regard to School Boards. (Cheers.) One word as to licensing. lie had thought for many years that the sound- • r-st way to deal with that controversy was ti allow each locality to decide for itself whether 4 would ''not close public-houses on Sunday. (Cheers.) But the Acensed victuallers apparently did not agree with this view. He warned them, however, of the great impru- dence of the step they were taking. Public-houses had 1-een- closed by Parliament' in Scotland. Ireland, and Wales, and those who had desired to close them in those countries also desired to close them in England by Act • of Parliament, and if this power were not granted to the local authorities, depend upon it the matter would be taken up again in Parliament Therefore, he earnestly ...titivated the licensed victuallers to reconsider the posi- i.on they had taken, for he was convinced that if they sue- enstriking out of the bill this provision the result would be an interference with theliberty of the people of London and the neighbouring counties, which he, :or one, should very much deplore. Referring to the tithe question, he said the tithe 'was really a . burden upon , the landlord, and if the tenant had been ,made to pay it, it was owing to a blunder of the law. The Government were very anxious to be able to pass measure, which should place the debt on the shoulders' , of the debtor, that was to sty. that thetandoWner, who really owned the tithe, should be the man to pay it. ' Coning to the question of :Ireland, which always over- Fhadowed all others, he believed that in Wales there was a deep feeling in favour of a united Empire—a feeling so rtrong that its powet had been sufficient to overlay the 'sad and pitiable difference of religion. They could con- gratulate themselves on the state of matters now exist- ing in Ireland, and the one thing necessary for her con- tinned peace was prosperity. A vast amount of the dis- content which existed there was due to adversity, and the misery resulting therefrom, rather than to any English misgovernment. Therefore, what the Govern- ment must do was to week to restore at once prosperity end loyalty, by restoring the reign of order and justice and law. Ile contended that to do this they had not re- sorted to the stringent methods of their predecessors, and that although consolidation might be difficult at first, the difficulty would cease when the Irish people recognised the salutory fact of the hopelessness of exacting any change in „their political position by 'disregarding the rights and lives and properties of their neighbopre. (Cheers.? 'Hie lordship commented on the fusion of nationalities which had taken place on the Continent, andaaid that surely the future of divided nationalities was not the future set before those wt.o desired to raise their people and their country in the scale' of human beings. (Cheers.) In the evening the town was illuminated, bonfires were lighted on the surrounding heights, and a torch- light procession perambulated 'the town, his lordship. being accompanied for a considerable part of the journey back to hie host's residence.

IVARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, morning. The Rev. G. Fc Roberts (chairman) presided, and there were also present Messrs. Balharry, Blackhurst, Jolley, Greening, J. Houghton, Bonnell, Derbyshire, Isherwood, Eckersley, Wright, Humphries. Clarke, W. Houghton. Ratcliffe. Harrison, Owen, Mabel, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and e. H. Ward (workhouse master). Mr. Henley, Local Government Board Inspector, was also pre- sent.

div.head: TILE BE-VACCINATION QUESTION,
div.p: TILE BE-VACCINATION QUESTION,

On the minutes of the previous meeting being put to the meeting, Mr. CLARKE said with regard to the matter of re-vaccination he could not find any Act a Parliament which gave the Board of Guardians power to authorise a doctor to re-vaccinate children or even grown-up per- sons. The minutes•having been confirmed, Mr. Clarke again raised the subject at a later stage of the meeting, when the CLEinc pointed out that the Guardians were in the position of guardians of the children, and Mr. JOLLEY also contended that the Guardians were perfectly authorised in doing what they had done.—Mr. CLAnxE said the matter had not been made quite plain to him, and at some future time he should push it forward.—Mr. DARHYSHIRE pointed out that the order to re-vaccinate was only given by a majority of one, and therefore it could not be said that the Guardians had unanimously directed the doctor to re-vaccinate the children at the expense of the ratepayers.—The CHAnntAn said that a majority of one made it the order of the Board.—Mr. CrAnitz said that the question was whether the re-vac- vination was authorised by Act of Parliament.—Mr. JOLLEY arrued that it was, but Mr. DARBYSIHRE replied that they did not regard Mr... Tolley as the authority for laying down an Act of Parliament.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said he did vote, and should vote again, against re-vaccina- tion, althongh he was as loyal to Acts of Parliament as any man on that Boyd. He should support the Board in carrying out the first order for vaccination, but, for reasons best known to himself, he should certainly object to re-vaccination, as he would consider that as a kind of assault upon a child, and especially as small-pox was on the decline.—Mr. HENLEY thought if they looked at the order they would find that it cleared up the vexed ques- tion of vaccination, and yaccination included re-vaccina- tion. It was clearly a duty cast upon medical officers, and the Local Government Board had quite lately, in the case of a workhouse where small-pox got a great hold, called upon the medical officer to explain why he had not attended to the order. That was a medical question, • and it had always been understood that if the medical officer thought re-vaccination was necessary he was to do it. (Hear, hear.)—The matter then dropped.

During the half-year he had collected and paid to the treasurer of the Warrington Union the sum of £704 ls 9d. —The CHAIRMAN thought the latter part of this report was very satisfactory, and was a credit to the Master. div.head: VACCINATION.
div.p: VACCINATION.

The CLZRIC mentioned that he had received a commu- nication from Dr. Page, an officer of the Local G overn- ment Board, to the effect that he intended to investigate with regard to vaccination in the Warrington Union, and asking to be supplied with certain information, which had been sent him.

div.head: BOUNDARIES QUESTION.
div.p: THE BOUNDARIES QUESTION.

The Cissix mentioned that a boundary commissioner had been at Warrington on Monday with regard to the proposed incorporation of the Cheshire townships of the Union with Lancashire. He also remarked that since the previous meeting of the Board he had seen a copy of the Local Government Bill, and it showed most clearly, that the old grants to the Union were to be continued, in addition to the 4d per head per day for indoor paupers. This would have great effect upon the Union, seeing, that they had gone in pretty considerably for indoor relief.— Mr. DARBYSHIRE said, with regard to the boundary ques- tion, that since the meeting with the commissioner he had been taunted by several ratepayers and movers in the opposition to the transfer with being the only one in favour of it, and he had been told that he was making himself obnoxious in the matter, and otherthings of that sort. He wished to say, however, that he had taken his stand in the matter . purely with the view that transfer would be to the advantage of the township. I He had no other interest to try to maintain; he had no magisterial position to uphold, nor any other interest than the welfare of the township. He knew for many years past the advantages that had been derived by Grappen- hall from its connection .with the Warrington Union.— The CHAIRMAN spoke in complimentary terms of the suc- cinct and clear manlier in which the clerk had placed the view of the matter taken by the Board before the com- missioner. They could not help feeling that in some few cases there might be a question of sentiment on the other side, and some of the gentlemen on the opposite side seemed to feel very much being separated from the olti county of Chester. But When everything was considered they must come to the conclusion that the connection with Lancashire would lte of great utility.—Mr. JOLLEY agreed with Mr. Darbysinre that it was of advantage tei the poot that the townships should be linked with that Union.—Mr. HARRISON thought that sentiment should give way to practical utility.—The matter then dropped.

div.head: STATEMENT BY MR. HENLEY
div.p: STATEMENT BY MR. HENLEY

Mr. HENLEY, Local Government Board inspector, then made a statement of some length as regards the affairs of the Union. Alluding to the intended allckwance of 4d per day per head for indoor paupers under the new Local Government Bill, he remarked that that 4d would not be paid unless those who paid it were satisfied that the ac- commodation for irunates of every class was really suffi- cient both in the workhouse and the schools. As regar- ded the schools there could be no doubt about them, but as regarded the workhouse they had at times very great difficulty—and some pressures in connection with certain classes of inmates, especially, the sick. Therefore fie thought it behoved the Guardians to consider whether it would not be desirable to take steps to put the work- house in such a position that they might be able to pass muster and receive the large sum which would be repaid by the County authorities. 'He could not shut his eyes to the fact that, considering the increase in population, it would be absolutely neces- sary to make some provision for certain classes oi their Inmates, and he thought it would be much better to face the question as soon as possible. Referring to the hos- pital, he said he thought they wcaild all agree that it was not the duty of the Guardians to prevent the spread of infectious disease in the town. That duty had, by Act of Parliament, been cast upon the Sanitary Authority; and if the Sanitary Authority neglected their duty, the result must rest on their shoulders. There were, how- ever, cases—such as a person lying in a shed or by a wayside and suffering from infectious disease—in which the Board's officers would have to take action, and pro- vide shelter, and it was desirable, if it could be done, for the Board to enter into arrangement with the Sanitary. Authority to tak6 such cases on the payment of a cer- tain amount out of the pOor rate. If they could not per- suade the Sanitary Authority to take their cases on equit- able terms, then it would be worththeir while to con- siderthe erection of 'a— sniaTer building for infectious cases so that they might 'use their present infectious. wards for the enlargement of the workhouse. If the Sanitary Authority would not take their cases they would find it absolutely necessary to have some place for isolation in the workhouse. Mr. Henley then went on to say that he thought the workhouse staff was rather undermanned, and he suggested that the master should be relieved of some of his present clerical duties by the appointment of a cleric or assistant;rna.ster. He also referred to the decrease in out-door relief that had taken place in Lancashire during the year 1887.—Some discussion ensued upon this statement—Mr. HARRISON mentioned that the Warrington Corporation had a very, complete hospital'. With regard to the reception of paupers, he said that so long as eight years ago, Alder-' man Burgess, the chairman of the Sanitary Committee, said, in answer to a question of his, that "The Sanitary Committee would take very good care, irrespective of anything that might have transpired at the Board of Guardians, that infection, wherever it might be, should not be allowed to have a footing. It would not be al- lowed to remain in the cottage of the pauper, but it would find its way into the hospital,, As long as he had the honour to preside over the Sanitary Committee he would take care that no infectious disease of any des- cription should have a resting place in the borough. If the Board of Guardians had no place he would take care that the patient would have a place in the hospital." Quite lately Alderman Burgess told him that he still ad- hered to the opinions expressed in the above extract.— Mr. HENLEY said he was extremely glad to hear that ex- tract read, but it was almost ,directly opposed to the report of the Board's own medical officer. Dr. Thorn, in his report to the Local Government Board, pointed out that the Warrington Hospital was an exceptionally good one, and he (Mr. Henley) was of Opinion that it was better that infectious cases should be taken to aml ealt with at one central hospital.--4t the conclusion at
I He
• the discussion a cordial ‘;:ote of thanks was passed to Mr Henley.

div.head: BANQUET TO MR. CIIAMBLALAIN.
div.p: BANQUET TO MR. CIIAMBLALAIN.

Mr. Charrberlain was, on Monday, entertained at h ,anquet at the Devonshire Club, St, James's, London,, aarl Granville presided, and nmonest the other peers, ind gentlemen present were Lord Flartington. Mr. Chil- lers, Sir Henry James, Mr. oShorne Morgan, Lord Bur- "on. Mr. Heneage, Mr. li. Chamberlain, Mr. Barclay, Mr. Fr. Fowler. Mr. Barbour, Mr. M'Arthur, Mr. Kenrick, Mr. Powell Williams, Mr. Jesse Collings, Mr. A. H. Browne, dm. Alter the usual loyal toasts, Earl' Gasovrtur proposed the toast of the evening. He said that doubts had suggested themselves as to whether a demonstration might not be premature, and whether such a proceeding might not have an adverse rather than a favourable influence on the exchange of the ratifications of the tresty which had just been signed. He advised the politiral committee that Mr. Chamber- lain was by far the best. judge on both points. Referring to home policy, he said there was a diffemeas•which divided the Liberal party which it would be folly to deny or to minimise, and which attetntos to destroy had . rather aceentuated. His contention had always been that because they were separated on one point, although of vital importance, there Was no reason why they should be separated in regard to matters'upon which they perfectly agreed. (Cheers.) Mr. CITAXBERLATN, on rising to reply, was received with loud cheers. After thanking his hearers for the kindness with which they had honoured the toast, he referred to the presence of some of his political antag,o- nista, notably Lord Granville. The most ordinary diplo- matic discretion precluded him from saying anything of importance about the negotiations or about the treaty which was now under. the consideration of the Legisls. tures of the countries chiefly concerned. (Hear, hear.) I.le believed it to he their duty to yield everything theft 'rood neighbourhood and the comity of nations con* --lairn at our hands, while at the same time they held fib* to the treaty rights which usage, equity, and inter- national law had sanctinued.

RELEASIC OF A Hama RULE DELEGfrE. Mr. Percy Harold Snelling. delegate of the London Anti-Coercion and Home RuleCommittce, was released from Limerick • Gaol on Thursday, after undergoing a month's imprison- • ment for advocating the Plan df Campaign. lie was met lby the High Sheriff and other friends. , • GRRAT FIRE IN SCOTLAND.—Late on Wednesday night fire broke out in a row of houses at Rocksolloch, Airdrie, near Glasgow, and in less ths n two hours the entire row was cdhsumed. Nine families are rendered homeless, and have lost most of their clothing and furniture. The poor people, among whom are 33 children. are for the present lodged in a shed. Tun Budget came up for further consideration, in the House of Commons, on Monday evening, 'At the resolution continuing the tea duty; and it i 8 likely to be much further discusscil before it is •,‘ brought into full operation. Mr. GLADSTONE made • an important speech, and intimated that, although ll*Me features of the financial proposals met with his approval, there were others to which he took atrong exception. Ho made no objection to a re, illation of a penny in the pound in the income • tax, for, as he dryly remarked, he was not aware of a single case of successful opposition to a dimi- nution of the tax. He exPressed his doubts as to the wisdom of the new wheel tax; and-paid what GosmiEN will doubtless look upon as a left- ilfM.ded compliment, 'when he said—" I mustiay that f think it requires a good deal of courage at present time of day, unless we are driven to it 3' great necessity, to revive and extend the taxes On locomotion." - But is there such "great neces- aitY," ? That remains to be seen. It is true the rn cellor of the Exchequer wants money; but , Ine question is whether, assuming the money is re- Viired, it could not be obtained in a less objection- able way. The strong point against the Budget aa a whole is that, while new taxes are being im- 11"ted, and while a surplus is being created of two and a quarter millions, nothing, as Mr. GLAD,TONE ' Pate it, is being done "in relief of the general', .• ‘e,°ll3llmer." Whatever Mr. GOSCHEN may say to the contrary, there is no disabusing the public ntirld of the fact that, as Chancellor of the Ex- chequer, he has, in preparing the Budget, been thinking too much about the interests of property, ,411 d too little of ,the interests of the people: 'MS shown in a striking degree by the way in which has dealt with the inequality between succes- lien and probate duty. It is to the standing dis- tledit of the landlord class, who have for so many Atenerations dominated both the House of Corn- ' • ratnno and the House of Lords, that in the matter '3 ,4,..._3.zes they have spared land, or realty, at the 174:4),e of personal property. If a man comes 13ossession of landed property by succession, &hat. taxed at the rate of 1; per cent. only; while -'°ther• and probably a poorer man, having Pets° 1, flat property left him, has to pay 3 ;It cent, in the way of probate duty. -" common sense question which at once P4:84), /AS itself is—Why should there be' a • ...Lsinction in favour of land? And there is no Bfaetory answer to that question. Mr. Gosensw to' °Poses, in certain cases, to add a half per cent. succession duty, and spread the payment of. :1•11 tax ovek eight years instead of four as at pre- -4. But, as Mr. GLADSTONE says—" it is one thin g to offer me a sum down, and another to offer of 'tie in sixteen instalments payable in the course %eight years." The broad issue which the•Chan- h,,'"°r of the Exchequer has raised is really one of • treatment of various classes of property. 1;ellat Reformers demand is that the land shall not telieved of its share of the burden of taxation the cost of other property. The cry is for 4(l,tiality, but Mr. GOSCHEN, whilst recognising the Only half satisfies it. Mr. GLADSTONE esti-. 2tes. that, under the new proposal, the amount 'anied from the succession duty would rise from teen £BOO,OOO and £900,000 to something over ; but the injustice is-that personal pro- , • („T„Y "'mild at the same time be taxed to the tune 4400,000. Apart from the proposed relief to , 1:4411 taxation, "3,250,000 in round numbers 1314 d remain as the inequality between the ray- of the two kinds of roperty:' What is re- -7,1,_411ttd is that, while the Chancellor of the • elt eq. uer is about it, he should go the whole lentti; . •of remedying the wrong-which he recognises Ru.,.ekviting. Let him adept Mr. GnsreroNE's Bug- and raise the slaty upon realty to that tiraim;sonalty. "The effect-of such a proposal" 11-tensromei words, "would not be, as thit'llnionly the case with proposals coming from tll,;()PPo.si tion, to impoverish the .Chancellor of ah.'4ahequer but to peurtressurointo his hands, raina enable him to dispense with some of the tinsosovirich he asks for, in .case those taxes • the-441 be found unacceptable to the House and °f the°4x4iy.
