div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 14, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 14, 1888.

two constables, P.C. MONAGHAN ai P.C. Roan:- sorr, were deputed to watch the premises during prohibited hours on the Sunday forenoon in ques- tion. They saw two women enter the side door, remain in a few minutes, and then retire; but net before Mrs. LOCKER'S daughter had on each occa- sion looked up and down the road, presumably to see if the coast was clear. A third woman paid a visit; this was the second defendant, ELLEN LOCKER, the daughter-in-law of SARAH LOCKER. She went away as the others did; but 'returned in half an hour or so. After staying a short time, the watchful daughter of the house looked out as usual, and then ELLEN stepped forth; but this time she was intercepted by the police. The story told at the Polioe Court was that the beer which was found in her possession was for her husband; it was given by the mother for assistance he ren- dered in stillag,ing beer on a Sunday morning. Now, if this tale had been told from the first, it ' might have been believable; but, as it happened, ' it was one amongst other and, admittedly, false statements. When stopped by the police and asked why she had been on licensed premises, ELLEN LOCKER at first denied that she had been there at all. This was story number one. Her next statement was that she had been there for some eggs. But this, story number two, did not shake off the wide-awake constable, who, tap- ping the woman's dress improver, struck a hard substance, and said "That's not eggs, missis." But Ellen kept on as she had begun; she persisted in asserting that she had no beer with her, until, going inside the house, her husband came upon the scene. The police, determined .not to be baf- fled, were about to take hardened Ellen into cus- tody, when—Oh! "Frailty thy name is woman !" —"the husband took from under her dress tho quart bottle of beer produced." The ease, ordinary mortals will say, was complete; but magistrates are not, ordinary mortals; they are not as other men are; they see with other eyes, and hear with other ears; and so, after listening to the evidence, they came to the conclusion that the woman who told so many lies when in the hands of the police was telling the truth, in court, when she affirmed that the beer which was found on her was given her for her husband, for services rendered. She might, to be sure, have carried the beer • away openly in such a case; but she pre- ferred to utilise it as a dress improver; not that she had any idea of smuggling it off the premises: it was a way she had. And the bench accepted this new version of the old, old story, and dismis- sed the case, the MAYOR remarking, in stereotyped phrase, that the police were perfectly justified in summoning the defendants. Just so; there is no question that the police did their duty, but the public are asking whether the magistrates were "perfectly justified" in dismissing the case; whether it would not be a good thing to dismiss "the great unpaid " ; and whether justice would not be better administered by a stipendiary magis- trate?

LORD SALISBURY'S policy would seem- to be a ,policy of drifting, and so, in harmony with the hour tnd the mood, he contrived, for he is a clever man, to say a good deal at Camarvon, on Tuesday, with- out really saying anything. It is as iron entering into his very soul to learn that there is an opinion abroad that both as to foreign and home affairs the present Ministry exist in order to carry out, more or less fully, the policy of their predecessors. Ire- land is, of course, always excepted from the broad statement.. The PRIME MINISTER meekly admits that he has no fault to find with the assertion that he is continuing the foreign policy of Lord ROSEBERY ; but denies that it has anything in common with the action taken when Lord GB.AN- VILLE was the Foreign Secretary. Cotisideting thlt it was Lord GRANVILLE'S' business to restore order to the chaos produced by a previous Tory Government, the statement may be said to be charaderistically audacious. It is worth remem- bering, too, that both Lord HARTINGTON and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN were in the Cabinet with Lord GRANVILLE, and that, as the foreign policy was the policy of the Government, Lord SALISBURY cannot reflect on Lord GRANVILLE without also- condemning the two men through wham at the present time he lives, moves, and has his political being. Perhaps he had an eye to the corner in which he was getting himself when he turned aside to praise the "purest patriotism" of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN in undertaking.. a difficult mission at a very critical time. The member for West Birmingham Must either smile grimly, or feel very mieasy, at being thus buttered by thp PRIME IMINISTER. Not more than four years have elapsed since Lord SALISBURY and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN took no pains to conceal the fact that they detested each other most cordially. But perhaps Lord SALISBURY has been Using honied words with his tongue in his cheek all the while? Com- ing to the question of the Local Govern- ment Bill, it is pretty clear that his lord- ship is by no means in love with it. If he swal- lows the draught, it will be as a bitter potion r and he will not be at-all distressed if there is a slip, at the last moment, between the cup and the lip. He frankly asserts that it is a "great evil in the bill" that it sets aside ",individual 'men who, with great credit to themselves, are now doing county duties." What hes probably means, but 'he cannot bring himself to put it in words, is that he much prefers the old Toryism that has existed so long to the new Liberalism that is taking its place. Tory democracy may be all very well as a phrase, but Lord SALISBURY can see as well as another man that, when it comes to practice, the danger is that, While the 'Tory disappears, the democracy will remain. The Partin MINISTER, by the way, is al- together too ingenious when he suggests that the Radicals profess to like the Local Government Bill beeause they knout they' are unpopular with their constituencies; "and, therefore, if they wish to oppose the measure they saY they like it, and thereby they hope to attach to the measure sorhe of their own unpopularity." Subtle reasoning of this kind may raise .a laugh, but it will not carry conviction with it. It is many months since Lord SAUSBURY showed himself so much afraid of these unpopular Radicals that, rather than face a dissolution„ where they would work their will, he gulped down principles in an Irish Land Bill which he had, only a short time before, vigorously denounced. But he would have it believed that he always stands firm; and that it is a libel oil him tO say he is a reed, painted to look like iron. He does stahel pretty firmly by his policy of Coercion, but the odd thing is that he would try to "make believe" that it is likely to lead to "prosperity and loyalty by restoring order." Governments have been trying for hundreds of years to oonjure Conciliation out of Coercion. They have failed, lamentably failed, and Lord SAmsauxv will fail too; for it is an attempt to make ropes out of sand.

t Don't forget that—Every time you borrow money you lose a friond. Every time you borrow money, eNcept for strictly busineEs purposes, you lose your independence. Every time you speak without thinking will hare to be atoned for by a that of thinking without speaking.
' " TOUCH A.4D GO." Y. L. Sullivan, the American pugilist, left Liverpool for Boston on Thursday. He ,can be spared.

Folly must have an outlet ; it escapes in France just now by crazy admiration of General Boulan- ger; he is the new St. Jing6 ; and .great is his worship in the music halls. There are people in France who fear it may end in a revolntion ; but surely the majority of the French are not "touched." And, besides, the fit may not last long.

Two deaths have resulted from football matches played on Saturday, and, in another case, a player was seriously injured. Risk is inevitable where there are trials of strength and skill, but when lives are lost it is time to considibr whether regula- tions cannot be made for ensuring that, while the game loses none of its interest, the danger shall be minimised.

Speaking at Wisbeach, on Thursday evening, Lord Cross, after posing as an authority, on Irelind, proceeded to refer to foreign affairs, and remarked that "tie present Government had raised the feelings towards England incre- dibly . during the last eighteen months." For once we can agree with Lord Cross; it is in- credible.

The Home Secretary stated, on Tuesday, that since February 12th the Public Prosecutor had interfered in twelve cases of illegal lotteries. •He added that it was the duty of local authorities, to interfere in such cases. LA the Primrose Leaguers .who like lotteries beware; they may find when preaching "England expects every man to do his duty that that duty is being done—in the Police Court.

A shunter named William Davies lost his life, poor fellow, at Widnes, on Saturday morn- ing, through a ,most remarksble accident. One of his clogs, whilst he was at work, got jammed in a check rail. Before he •could extricate it, a goods train came along, and inflicted such injuries that he died the same day. It must have been terrible to be held fast while a train was approaching; that foot covering was indeed a clog.

Lord Salisbury took care not to crack up the Burmah annexation when spaaking of the foreign policy of the Government. It has been a bai business from the beginning . The British Chief Commissionas recently came to the conclusion that it was desirable to disarm the natives; and the result is that peaceable inhabitants are being massacred by the dacoits—the prowling pltinderers of the country. We have not yet heardthe last of Burmah.

Mr. Henley, Local Government Board Inspector, made an interesting statement at the Warrington Board of Guardians,, on Wednesday, as to the aftiti,-s of the Union. Amongst ether things, he remarked that, in his opinion, "it was better that infectious cases should be taken to and dealt with at one central hospital." This is a hint to outside authorities to make arrangements for availing themselves of the excellent central- hospital pro- vided by the borough of Warrington. A word to the wise is said to be sufficient.

Mr. G. W. Smalley, writing to ho "Nineteenth Century," pays a remarkable compliment to Mr. John Morley.. He says :—" I once sat with half-a- slozen others at a dinner-table in a country house when someone started this question—' If yon had to be shut up in a dungeon or on a desert island with but one man for company, who ,would you choose ? ' Five out of the seven men—whose names I should like to give—answered, John Morley. If that be not a proof of charm, both of character and conversaticn, I know not what is."

The Sunday opening of Free Libraries has proved so attractive at St. ildens, Wigan, Man- chester, Birmingham, and other places, that Sal- ford and Hindley have just decided in favour of taking the same step. There is no fear, however, of anything of the kind being done in Warrington just yet; the authorities are so enlightened that thy will not provide a Free Library for grdinary days—to say nothing of Sunday. Their noble practice is to break the la uk by chdrging a penny to ratepayers for the loan of their own books!

Quite an imposing deputation was sent from Warrinkton to London to express opinion and hear opinion upon the features of the Local Government Bill, and it is not unreasonable to in- fer that in due course there will be quite an impos- ing bill to pay. It is very desirable that the "city fathers" should make themselves acquainted with the measure—say, by reading it carefully by their own firesides. But if anything has to be done officially, would it not be as well to call the rate- payers together lind ascertain what they think of it?

There has been a further hearing of the appeal case vfhicli has arisen out of the winding up of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, and the issue is not yet determined: The question raised is as to the proportion to be paid to ordinary and prefer- ence shareholders of the surplus which remains after each shareholder has received back his origi- nal capital. It is a knotty point, and when it is decided it may be that, like the famous case of "Jarndyce v. Jarndyce" there may be no surplus left. However, the lawyers will not be empty- handed.

James Jolley, of St. Helens,-has a mastiff which he describes as very affectionate and quite harm- less. It is playful, too, and, as it has at various times attacked no fewer than four • constables, biting one on the wrist till blood flowed copiously, it is not unlikely that the animal will be known m "the force" as vicious and dangerous. It all de- pends on the point of view. The magistrates have ordered the owner to keep his pet under proper control.. If he is wise, he will control it with a dose of prussic acid; it is altogether too good for world which will not allow it to feed on policemen. It will be seen from our report of the proceed- ings of the Daresbury Highway Board that the question of the encroachment on Grappenhall-lane was discussed. The Board seem to be entering into a give-and-take arrangement which, it is ad, flitted, is not legally binding. Seeing that both sides of the lane are being encroached upon, it is not very clear how anybody in Latchford is to be benefited, except the landowner. Then as to the original enclosure, it seems to be assumed that the Board have no power to interfere. But they have; time is not an element in the matter; for the law is—once a trespass, always a trespass.

Answering a question the other day the Secre- tary of the Local Government Board has made it known that, so far as the Government are con- corned," grocers' licenses will be controlled by the new licensing authority, and in the event of any license being withdrawn no compensation is to be awarded." This means that there is to be compen- sation for on-licenses, but none for off-licenses— that is if the bill be passed as it stands. But the public are having a say in the matter; and there is a growing feeling that it is simply monstrous to talk of compensation in any case when it is a privilege, not a right, which is being withdrawn.

. Mr. Chamberlain is making himself look ridi- culous by the way in which he squirms, and runs . off to form a new association, when he finds him- self out-voted in the organisation he has helped to build up. "Punch" troth him out nicely in the following lines WaS it for this I moulded " the Machine," Boiler and shafting, cylinder and piston, • That it shouki dare, out of pure party spleen, .Not to do any work that I insist on? "A tatur stand on end at being biled ?" Bigelow, that's nothing to the Caucus kicking , At its creator—me! really riled, And ganiebody will hate to take a licking. Is the Caucusian indeed played out Nay, boys of Brummagem, they shall not baulk us, 1 I'll boss a axe, machine, Unionists shout "The Caucus (then) is dead : long live—the Caucus !"

Sir William Harcourt, speaking at York, on Thursday night, contended that by-elections were a means of test- ing the opinion of the pdblic, and said that in 23 dec.- tons which had been decided since 1886 the Home Rulers' position had been i•aproved in 15, and the Unionist posi- tionin eight. The loaner had gained five seats and the latter only one.
LOCAL NEWS.

.—HUNCORN PETTY SESVONAL DIVISION.—A special meet- ing of the magistrates of this division was held at the Court-house, Runcorn on Monday morning. Mr. J., Brundrit presided, and .there was a good attendance. The business of the meeting was to appoint a, chairman in succession to the late Sir Richard Brooke, Batt., and on the proposition pf Mr. C. Reynolds, seconded. by Mr: James Handley, Mr. J. Brundrit was unanimously elected to the position. • . ' LACEY-STREET WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE, WIDNES.—, The members of this society held the last meeting of the( season on Monday evening, when there WaS a capital at- tendance. The Rev. R. Bowdon presided, and delivered an appropriate address., , A programme of miscellaneous items was gone throu,gh in god(' style.' The choir, con- ducted by Mr. E. Shepherd, rendered several pieces in a creditable manner. Miss J. Sadler and Miss H. Tunna- cliffe officiated as accompanists. BAPTIST MUTUAL iMPROVEXENT SOCIETY, WIDNES.—A tea meeting in connection with this society was held on Thursday evening at. the Nelson-street CliaPel: There was only a moderate attendance. Subsequently, Mr, E. Carey, the president of the society, delivered a most in- teresting lecture, entitled "Some notes of a short isit to Amenea.',' Some splendid lime-light illustrations webe presented, j3elng,supplied by Mr. R.H. Davis. The usual vdtes of thanks were accorded: The proceeds are to go 1 in Aid of the new chapel funds. RUNCORN STAIIR-BOWICETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—In con- , ngction with the society No. 406 an appropriation took !Race at /he office,. on Monday evening. Mr. ,John Faulkner was appointed chairman, and Messrs. R. Cot- tinge and G. Riley scrutineers, and John W. Gleave the balloter. The ballot resulted in Mr. Wm. Cooper, fitter, Bridge-street, being entitled to £2OO for 12i years free of interest. No less than seven ballots had lobe taken, owing to the number vf members who are in arrear, and who have previously had an appropriation, being drawn. ,

SINGULAR ASSAULT AT RUNCORN.-At Run Corn Petty Sessions, en.Moz?.day, John Simpson a respectable look- M.o. elderly man, was charged with assaulting P.C. Fryer whilst in the execution of hi,s duty. About half-past eight on Monday night, the 2nd inst., the constable was Struggling on the ground with a violent prisoner at Hal- ton, when the defendant came up, and after striking the prisoner, gave the constable a blew on the head. The prrisoner said heavvas drunk, ana did not know what he was doing. Mr. Brundrit said drunkenness was no ex- cuse, and 6rted the defendant 1N and costs, 13s 6d.

A MIDNIG—IIT ADVENTURE AT WIDNES.---A young man named John Bartlett, was brought before Mr. Gossage, it Widnes Police Court, on TueAday, charged with sleep- ing gut. P.C. Houghton stated that about two o'clock that morning he was called iiitc; the chemical works of Messrs. Hutchinson, where he found the prisoner in a nude stat'e. The prisoner, in his defence, said he was the mate of a coasting vessel nained "Colonel Gamble," and in trying to find his vessel" pn Monday night he fell into the canal, and had simply gone into the Works for the purpose of drying his clothes. The prisoner was dis- charged on the payment of costs. , MILTON-ROAD CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, WIDNES.— At the last meeting of the members of the. Mutual Im- provement Society in .connection with this chapel, Mr. Georgeßae read an essay on "Sir Walter Scott. Mr. Rae gave an interesting account of the life of the great Scotch poet and novelist, and in an able manner read portions of the "Lady of the Lake." Dissolving views of the scenes described were shown, and, altogether a' pleasant and instructive evening was spent. % A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Rae, on the rnetion of Mr. F. .7. Poole, seconded by Mr. Lathom. The llev. R. G. Ilughes presided over ' the proceedings. MISSIONARY SERVICES AT WIDNES.—The annual ser- vices in connection with the United! Methodist Free Church Home and Foreign Missions were heiddit Zion ' Chapel, Widnes, on Sunday. Sermons were preached morning and evening by the Rev. T. Naylor, of Liver- pool. There Were good congregations. • On Monday evening the anntial missionary meeting was held under the pgesidency of Mr. E. Carey. Addresses were de- literet by the Revs. T. Naylor, J. Bryant, R. Yeatman, and E. JAIL and the usual votes of thanks were accor- ded. The collections realised a substantial sum. On each occasion the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. J. Betney, rendered specially-selected music,. 'Tim EDUCATION, ACT AND BOAT PEOPLE.—Dinah Leather, a boatwoman, appeared before the • Runcorn Magistrates on Monday-, to answer the summons of tne Runcorn School Board for not sending her son, aged eleven' years, regularly to school. The defendant said the bov had to go with her to help in working tlfe boat. She sent him to school when she had the chance.—Mr. Brun- drit : The law is that the child* napt go to school, whether you are a boatwoman or not—The defendant: Yes, but It wants something to send him to school.—Mr. 13rundrit : You must pay the usual fine of ss.—The defendant: I must work two months for that money.— The woman paid the line and left the court talking loudly of the injustice of the matter. ROBBING A PnoToonsenen.—On Thursday, at the St. Helens Police Court, before Alderman Harrison and Councillor C. J. Bishop, a young man named Jos.Tinsley. Who lodged at 66, Fenton-street, St. Helens, was charged with stealing an overcoat, value 20s, the property of Max Bernstein, a Russian Jew. who car- ries- on thi business of a photographer at 16, Kent-street, Widnes. , Prosecutor stated( that on the .Bth inst he was in Crab-street, St. Helens, taking photographs. He threw his coat over his machine and drew a cloth over his head to arrange the apparatus. On taking his head again from undar the .cloth he missed his coat. When prisoner was apprehended by Police-con- stable Henebery he said, "I was drunk when I took it." —A fine of 40s was imposed or fourteen days' imprison- melt. MDNES Scuom, BOARD FINANCES.—At a special meet- ing of Widnes School Board, on Tuesday, Mr. Danby, the clerk, submitted a statement of receipts and expenditure for the half-year ended the 25th March. The receipts amounted to £3,580 Us 2d, and included grants from Education Department £2,616 3s 3d, and school fees £BB7 us. The total expenditure amounted to £3,354 153 Bd. The principal items were--Salaries of officers of the Board £233 3s 4d, salaries of teachers £2,021 16s 10d, Neal and other expenses ef administration £ll3 12s 6d, books, apparatus, and stationery, £ll2 8s Bd, 'furniture and repairs to buildings and furniture £154 8s 9d, fepayment of principal of loans £162 8s 7d, in- terest on loans £416 16s Id. There was a balance in hand of £225 15s 6d. The outstanding liabilities of the Board were—Loans from Public Works Commissioners £31,662 9s 3d, other liabilities £470 14s lid. The state- ment was adopted. CHANGE RINGING AT RUNCORN.—At the Runcorn Par- ish Church, on Sunday, the bellringers rang for evening service a peal of six scores (grandsire doubles) in vari- ous methods. The changes were rung upon the last six of the eight bells, which were all muffled at the hand- stroke as a tribute of respect to the memory of the late Mr. William Elvidge, watchmaker, of Runcorn, who had been a ringer at the church for upwards Of ten years, and who at the time of his death was a member of the Chester Diocesan-Guild of Change Ringers. The peal commenced at ten minutes to six, and terminated at 28 minutes past, thus-lasting 38 minutes. The first bell was rung by George R. Joynson, Whilst the'secona being the bell the deceased fornwly rang was allowed to re- main at rest, and the remainder were rung by the fol- lowing :—Samuel Hoxworth, treble and conductor; Robert Linaker, Thos. Williamson, Thomas Brown, James Dykes, and (tenor) Faithful Woodward.

, ROBBING A FATHER AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Charles Tipping, a young man, was charged with having stolen an overcoat, a blanket, and a sheet, value 255, the property of his !other, Thomas Tipping, gardener, Ditton.—The prisoner had not lived at home for some tithe, but on the 29th March he went to the house and was allowed to stop. —On thA night of the Ist April the father went to bed, leaving the prisoner on the sofa, the articles being safe in the front part of the house, but next morning they had disappeared, and the prisoner was not to be found. It was afterwards ascertained that the prisoner had attempte4 to sell the goods to Michael McConville, a second-hand clothes I dealer, stating that,he would'not have troubled him had the pawnbrokers b&ri open, but he wanted food for his wife. He sold the.overcoat to Joseph Miller, beerhouse ' keeper, Brook-street, St. Helens.—The prisoner was com- mitted to take his Itnal at the County Quarter Ses- sions. THE MURDEROUS ASSAULT BY A SOLDIER AT WIDNES.- 6aniel Gilmour, a discharged soldier, was again brought before the magistrates, on Monday, charged with feloni- ously wounding Joseph Donovan, with intent to murder him, on the 24th March. Mr. Knowles appeared for the prisoner. Superintendent JolinAon said he intended to call seVeral witnesses, and then ask for a further re- mand, as Donovan was still unable to appear. Michael I Conway, labourer; of 53, Moss Baok-road, stated that on the night of the assault he was drunk. He was in Ryan's house, in Barn-street, where Donovan lodged. During the night the prisoner came into the house, and said he would give Donovan a "Clout." The priioner 'was, drunk, and appeared to be in a "rage." Afterwards a bottle was thrown at Donovan, and smashed on the wall about two feet from where he (witness) was standing. He thought tbe bottle was thrown by the prisoner. 118 did not think Donovan was drunk; but they were all having beer at the time. The prisoner was again re- manded. ' NEW POOR RATES FOR WIDNES DlSTRlCt.—irci Goff, assistant overseer of Widnes op Thursday appli to the Widnes magistrates for sanction to pay a poor rate of 2.8 44 for the townshiplf Widnes estimated to realise £15.000.—1n answer to questions from the Bench, Mr. Goff said there was £l2 5s 6d of the old rate not collec- ted, but the amount was recoverable. A portion of the arrears was owing by the Rev. George Bond. The rate for the previous year was only 2s in the £, and realised £13,000. The rate was this year higher through the in- creazed demands of the Widnes School Board.—Mr. H. Wade Deacon said the , increase of 4d was not accounted for by the demands of the Sehoo/,,Board.—Mr. Goff said the overseers bad no funds to Meet the. School Board demands .until the rates came in.—The Bench sanctioned the laying of the rate.—On the;, application of Mr. Houghton, assistant overseer for tho various townships, " the magistrates arse sanctioned the laying of the follow- ing rates :—Bold Is in the 2, to. realise £791 18s 3d; Cronton is in the £, to realise £232 17s 9d: Ditton Is in the 2, to realise £O4B 4s 9d. These rates were fpr six months only. , '

CONFIRMATION SERVICE AT RUNCORN.—In the presence of a large congregation, the Bishop of Liverpool per- formed the annual service of consecration at Runcorn Parish Church on Wednesday night. The candidates, who numbered over 70, were from Runcorn, Halton, Weston, and Weston Point. The clergy present were the Revs A. Maitland Wqod, G. A. Tindall, J. D. Ozanne, W. ellrys„nt, J. Lockwood, J. H.- Wilcockson, and G. ' Fisher. The Bithop !addressed the customary warning' and admonition to the confirmee.s. RUNCORN GUARDIANS ELitcnox.—ln the Run Corn Union there were only contests at Ituncorn and Appleton: In the former plaek thbre were six candidates for five seats, and the votint was as follows :—Mr P. Speakman 808; Mr S. Taylor 805 Mr J. W. Lightburn 715, Mr H. J. Orrice 622, Mr D. H. Jones 519, Mr P. Smith 387. The four retiring Guardians find Mr Jones are therefore elected. The interest in the contest was not of a very ardent description. At Aupleton the voting was as fol- lows i—Mr W. Hewitt 252, Mr J. Knowles 252, Mr Wm. Rostock 77. Mr Hewitt and Mr Knowles were therefore elected. '

PRESENTAT,IONS AT WIDNES.—At the quarterly meeting of the members of the Parish Church Young Men's Select Class, the Rev J. R. Jones, BA., the teacher of the class, who is about to leave the town, was presented wltli an elaborate secretaire with electro-plated fittings. Mr Jones sifitably • acknowledged the gift. On the same evening there was a meeting of the Ladies' Bible Class, the mem- bers of which presented Mrs Williams; the wife of 'the vicar, with a handsome breakfastservice, in reeognition of her Services' R... 3 teacher to the class. Mrs Williams, in acknowledging the gift, expressed regret that her con- nection with th&elass would Foon have to terminate, as 3lr Williams had accepted the living of Rainford. A QuEsremes_nr..v.Cmutos AGAINST A POLICEMAN.—AIice Hatton, of 53, James-street, was brought before Mi. George Pilkington, atWidnes Police Court. on Thursday, to answer a charge Of being drunk. P.C. Holbrookstated that On the night of the 31st March the defendant was helplessly drunk in Bridge-street She was making her way towards the river, but she fell down in the mud, and he raised her up arid took her to he, home.—The de- fendant denied that she was drunk, and stated that she was going with a "gentleman "to a fiat. She .alleged that the constable had made improper overtures to her. —The constable denied this statement, and said a school- master who was with him at the time could prove( its untruthfulness.---The case was adjourned for a week, so that alditional Witnesses might be called. DEMI LURING iltig RAILWAY COMPANY AT RUNCORN:. Ye.steriay. at Ruticorn Police Court, Samuel Jones. who stated that he lived at 95, Premier-street, Liverpool, was charged with attempting to defraud the London and North-Western Railway ympany by travelling frdm Lime-street to Runcorn without having paid his fare. On the previous afternoon Inspector Stamford saw the prisoner acting in a suspicious manner, on the platform at Lime-street just before the departure of the 5-20 train for London. He saw the prisoner "dodge" into a third- class carriage altersthe ticket collector had examined tickets there, and the Inspector accordingly travelled in the same train. At Runcorn a ticket was demanded from the prisoner, but becould not produce one, and stated that he held only got 2iel and wanted to goto London. In default orpaying a fine of 20s and-costs,the prisoner went to gaol for a month. • Rescoax Benuat BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the cemeteryson Wednesalay. Mr. W. H. Roger- son presided, and there were also present—Messrs. H. Coleburn and R. Morris, with W. Jones (assistant secre- tary.)—The Secretary reported that the interments for the twelve months ended March 25th numbered 363, last year 316, increase 47. The fees received duringthesame_ period amounted to £375,8s 4d, last year £3l2s 2d, in- crease £63 3s 2d. *The total number of interments since the cemetery was opened March Ist, 1860, were : Church 3,150, Dissenters 4,007, Roman Catholic 630, total 7,789.—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £7 us 5d and in- terest falling due, amounting to £23 6s. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Coleburn, seconded by Mr. R. Morris. . . .

DEATH OF A RUNCORN, TRADESMAN.—It is with regret that we announce the death of Mr. George Joseph King, draper, of Bridge-street, Runcorn. For some time past Mr. King had suffered severely trom bronchitis, but on Easter Monday ho was able to go to Frodsham, and to walk thence to Hdlsby. On returning home his malady became much worse, and in spite of the medical skill a Dr. Mangan, death occurred on Saturday afternoon. The I uneral took place on Wednesday afternoon, at Runcorn cemetery. The mourneTs were Messrs. William King (brother), J. 'H. Booth (brother-ip-law), J. R. Booth (brother-In-law), and S. Crosby (brother-in-law), W. B. Booth (nephew), --- Williams, H. J. Grice, and W. H. Rogerson. The Rev. G. Fisher, curate of Holy Trinity 'Church, conducted the funeral service. The hearse and coaches were supplied by Mr. Peck. MILL BROW MILITARY BAND CONCERTS, RUNCORI4. The best concert of the season took place in Runcorn, Public Hall, and the good audience present testified to the popularity the concerts have „attained under the management of Mr. R. Pierpeint. . The vrograrnme opened with the fantasia "Pirates of Penzance " by the band, who at another part of the evening performed a grand selection, "Reminiscences of England," in a man- ner that earned them the hearty applause of those pre- sent. Miss Florence Dick, of the Liverpool Operatic Society, sang "The Nightingale's,Trill," When the heart is young," and, " Ora Pro Nobis." Possessed oj a sop- rano voice of good quality and range, she created a most favourable impression, and was, heartily encoredr, Mr. Saxmar, who has a mellow bass voice, gavg "The Diver," "Rocked in the cradle of the deep," and "To- morrow will be Friday," i good style. Mr. Harry Col- lins was most successful in his humorous songs, and he was twice recalled. His clever banjo performances and imitation of various musical instruments by the mere sounds of the mouth were very diverting. Mr. William Goode performed the clarionette solo "Coming thro' the rye," in clever style. Mr. Tom Outhwaite ably officia- ted as conductor, and Mrs. W. B. Kay fulfilled the duties of accompanist , FOOTBALL.— Widnes v. Llanelly : ' After having visited Hull and Wakefield the celebrated Welsh football team Llanelly, visited Widnes on Tuesday, and in the evening played a match with the local auto in the presence of about 2,000 spectators. Widnes had to draft into their ranks three men from their second team, and Llanelly were unable ,to play their usual three-quarter backs. During the first half ,the visitors played with a strong wind to their backs, But they were seldom dangerous, tha Widnes forwards more than holding their own. Plumpton made a splendid attempt to drop a goal, and following up well scrimmages took place on the visitors' line. Again Plumpton got hold, and passing to Wilkin- son that player scored a try. Plumpton failed at the place kick. This infused some life into the visitors who shortly afterwards compelled Owens to touchdown, and a few minutes later L. B. Williams making his mark near the half-way flag, Morgan kicked a magiuficent'goal. At half-time the score was Lltmelly 1 goal 1 minor to Wid- nes 1 try 1 minor. In the second half Widnes had the advantage of the wind, and severely pressed their op- ponents, but their efforts to score a major point were rendered futile through the splendid defence of the visi- tors'.backs, and they could only add four minors to their former score. Llanelly retired the winners by 1 goal 1 niftier to 1 try and '5 Minors, • WHTTLEY DISTRICT SCHOOL BOARD: ELECTION OF MEMBERS.—Thefolldwing have been duly nomi- nated and elected members of the above Board, which comprises tbe parishes of Whitley Inferior and Whitley Superior :—Messrs. Henry eild. Wil- liam Fletcher, and George Priestner, Whitley Superior; and Messrs. William Moreton Clarke and, Charles Mounfleld, Whitley Inferior. The following were elected at the previous election in 1885 : Messrs. Robert Fairhurst, Charles Winnfield, Henry Neil& Philip N. Rutter, and James J. Smith. THE ROME IRON TRADE.—The second quarter of the year has opened more hopefully, there being now every probability that for the next few months values of iron will rise from the low level to which they have recently sunk. This has had an encour- aging effect upon the iron markm, and' prices have atiffened during the week. This reaction has made itself felt More particularly in the pig-iron trade. Whilst in the Scotch warrant market prices show little change, and quotations for makers' iron•are remarkably irregular—due, undoubtedly, to the heavy stocks of iron--the pig-iron trade of the north of England ,and in other districts is getting firmer from week to week.—lron. -

_ A RIVER PHENOMENON.—The river Mersey in the vicinity of Warrington Bridge has presented a start- ling appearance on several recent evenings. Bubbles of spontaneously inflaniniable gas have been rising in patches on its surface, bursting into brilliant flame on contact with the air, with an effect so weird as to lead to tolich speculation and wonder:. ment amongst the numerous spectators who 'hive gathered to witness the phenomenon. At times the flashes of light have corruscated on the river in large tracts, emitting a bright light accompanied by a noise like Miniature artillery. The cause is vari- ously assigned to some experiments which are being made for .the purpose of devising a signal light' for use at sea, or the natural formation in the muddy bed ,of the river of phosphuretted hydrogen or "marsh gas," which,,as'is well known, bursts into flame on contact with air.

div.head: FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

A. -shoeltang accident occurred at, Widnes, on Satur- day morning, to.a young man named Wm. Davies, who resided in Church-street. Davies was employed as a shunter by the London and North-Western Rail- way Company, and about ten o'clock on the day named he was engaged shunting a goods train at the siding of the Lancashire Metal Company, when one of his clogs became fastened in the check rail of the siding. While he u`as endeavouring; to extricate his foot, the goods train came along, and Severed one leg completely from the body, 'and the either was so terribly crushed that amputation was neces- sary. Dr. Saul, who was at once summoned, ordered the unfortunate man's inamediato removal td the Royar Infirmary at Liverpool, and he was accord- ingly taken down by special train. lie,. however,
expired at three o'clock the same afternoon. On Tuesday Mr. Clarke Aspinall, the city coroner. held an inquest on ths body, and a verdict of accidental death was returned.
THEFT OF•DUCKS AT RUNCORN.

At Rnncorn Petty. Sessions, on Monday, Martin, Gilligan, farm labourer, was charged with having On the sth inst stolen three ducks, the property of .Charles Ball, fruiterer, High-street, Runcorn.—The evidence showed that the prisoner was employed by Mr. Rutter, of Halton Lodge Farm, but on the day in question he was not at work, but was drinking with a tanner's iabourer named J. Dunbebin. In the afternoon the prisoner left the Half-Way House, Halton- road, stating that he was going for some cheese I and bread, but he did not return, and that afternoon the ducks were Missed by Richard Billington, by whom they were kept. In the field where the prisoner had been employed for three weeks Inspector Millington, P.S. Jones, and P.C. Fryer found traces of a fire and some charred bones and feathers, and hidden in a heap of soil they found one of the missing ducks. Footmarks that corresponded with the prisoner's qlogs, which were nailed in a peculiar fashion, were traced along the side of the brook into a concealed hollow where Some bread crumbs and some feathers were found. A coat and cap which the prisoner claimed were also four@ in the Viein- ity.—The prisoner, *ho strongly declared his innocence, was sentenced to a month's imprisonment.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this authority was held at Dutton., Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton (chairman), the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Aaron, Hadfield, Brandreth, W. Whitlow. Parr, Hewitt, and Linaker (Clerk).' ' PAMOCIIAL AUTKORITIES.—Mr. Hadfield gave notice that at the next meeting of the Authority he would nom- inate gentlemen for the townships of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship.—Mr. Aaron gave a similar notice with regard to Weston Parochial Committee.

THE -COUNTY GOVERNMENT Bur..--In the course of some'conversatioa with regard to the',County 'Govern- ment Bill, the Clerk remarked that if the Bill passed that Authority together with the Daresbury Highway Board, would be abolished. District Councils would tal their place and to these Councils 'various additional powers would be given, including those under the Burials Act, so that Halton Burial Board would also disappear. The Connell would likewise have the power of abolishing ot fixing the days of fairs, but this power would not affect , this district much, as he j)elieved there was only one fair at Frodsham. He also mentioned that 4d per head per day for each indoor pauper would be allowed the Guardians from the County, ansl 4s per week for each pauper lunatic. Ile calculated tha,t the. alkutance to the Union on account of indoor paupers would be about £2OO a year.—Me. Whitlow remarked that he hoped men would be returned to the new Authorities who had to earn their money and would know how to spend it.— The Clerk said that would depend on the electors.—Mr. Parr thought the proposed wheel tax 'was a very fair one, and in fact he did not rind math fault with the new Budget.—The Clerk said the only thing he objected to was tha,t traction engines which did so much damage to roads were not taxed. (Hear, hear).—Mr. parr: And bicycles • these bicycles cannot keep their .own side. (Laught.t.—The matter then dropped)-This was all the business of public interest before the Allithority. • RUNCORN BOARD OF' GUARDIAN'S. - -

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Wotkhouse on Tuesday afternoon. There were'present Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton (chairman), the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Aaron, Taylor, Bran- dreth, Hadfield, Parr, W. Whitlo Hewitt, Speak- mom, Lightburn, Lewis, Cimpkira, Hall, and H. Linaker (clerk). _ • . _ _

. INCREASE OF tkoikxcr.—The Clerk mentioned that the, workhou.se master's return showed that during the last week no fewirthan 102 vagrants had been relieved as compared with 19 inthe corresponding week oL last year.—A Guardian remarked that this was probablf due to the ship canal works bringing unemployed persons into the neighbourhood. • • • RESIGNATION OF THE ASSISTANT CLERK.—The Chair- man said he was sorry he had received, and he was sure the members would be sorry to hear read, a letter from Mr. W. H. Linaker tendering his resignation of the office oi assistant clerk to the . Union. Mr. Linaker wrote that he/could not but express his deep regret in severing an association which had been so pleasant, and lasted so many years.—Mr. Taylor said he was sorry to hear the letter read.—Mr. Hadfield: It is probably on account of his ill-health.—Mr. Taylor: He gives no reason.—The Rev. J. Lockwood: Perhaps it is in conse- quence of our treatment of him.—Mr. Hadfield: Oh,' don't say that.—The Rev. J. Lockwood: Well, I hope not.—Mr. Taylor: Pintist say I am not surprised to hear 'it.—Mr. Parr (referring to Mr. Lockwood's remarks) They do not get that badly treated here I have not seen it since I came on the Board.—Mr. Hadfield said it was not fair for Mr. Lockwood to put that view on-the mat- ter" lie did not think it was a money matter at all.— Mr. Speakman pointed out that no reason was given for the resignatien, and added, that probably in his present state of health it was Mr. Linaker's conscientious con- viction that he should resign. He (Mr. Speakman) thought it would be better if the resignation was not , accepted by the Board, and if a letter was sent to Mr. ' Linaker asking him to reconsider his decision. He moved to that effect.-The Clerk said they' might depend upon it the matter of remuneration had nothing to do with it. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Taylor seconded Mr. Speak- man's proposal, which was agreed to. it THE DUTIES OF OvEasExas.—Mr. Hadfield asked if, when calls were not paid, it was the overseers of assis- tant overseer who had to be summoned.—The Chairman: The overseers.—Mr. Hadfield said that at a meeting held inProdshain one of the overseers actually aikeß if the calls had been paid. He did not seem to know whether the call had been paid or not, mid he (Mr. Hadfield) thought that a man who was ignorant of that sort of thing ought not to be an overseer at all. (Laughter.) Yet the same man had been appointed by the magis- trates for another twelve Months. He had always had some sympathy for Frodshim when it was back with its call, but heshould have no sympathy as long as they had an overseer who did not know whether the calls were paid or not. (Latighter.)—The matter then dropped.. This was the'principal business;

WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, yesterday. 'Sir. 11. Wade Deacon, J.P., presided, and there were present—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. Robin- son, E. Carey. J. Morrison, W. Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk), and Miss Proctor (librarian).. '

div.head: ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: THE ANNUAL REPORT.

Mr. Allen read a report of the work of the committee for the period commencing with its appoinment on the 4th, October, 1886, and ending with the financial year a the Local Board on the 25th March, 1888. At the out- set the thanks of the committee were tendered 'to Mr. Lancaster, the librarian of the St. Helens committee, and also to that committee for the aid given in selecting furniture and books, and the general ar- rangement of the library. After interviewing many candi- dates for the post of librarian the committee decided to appoint a lady-librarian. There was some doubt as to the wisdom of this at the time, but events had fully justiaed the decision of the sommittee. The reading-room was informally opened on March 19th, 1887, and the library was formally opened by Professor Benda'', Principal of the University College, Liverpool, on the 16th May, 1887. The committee had much pleasure in stating that both the lending and reading departments had been tho- roughly appreciated by the ratepayers. groin the 19th March, 1887. to the 25th March, 1688, there was a total attendance of 151,515 persons, or a daily average of 480. The number of books issued was 48.797, or a daily average of 180. The number of borrowers' tickets issued was 1,752. , The number of volumes purchased was 2,421, and the number presented 636, being a total of 3,057 volumes. The committee also desired to lbecord its thanks to Mr. Allen. clerk to the Local Board, for the very valuable services which he had rendered in connec- tiod with the work of the committee.—The last para- graph in the report was inserted by the chairman, at the unanimous wish of the members.

div.head: MONTHLY REPORT.
div.p: THE MONTHLY REPORT.

Miss Procter reported that during March the books borrowed from the Lending Departmerc and consulted in the Reference Department was 5,586, being an in- crease in the Lending Department of 221 over last month and in the Reference Departtpent n incrgase of 4. The average was 215 per day.
FINANCE, Accounts amounting too £l5 14s 10 were passed for payment. • ,
VOTES' OF THANKS TO SIR. _DEACON.

Dr. O'Keeffe-Tm;ved a vote of thanks to Mr. -Deacon for the excellent manner in which he had presided over the meetings of the committee, and conducted its busi- ness. The credit of getting up the four lectures was en- tirely due to Mr. Deacon—(hear, hear),—and that they were appreciated, and a source of interest,was proved by the-fact that they were so well attended by the public. Re hoped similar lectures would be 'given in the future- (Hear,.hear.) Alluding to the "At Home" which Mr. Deacon held, Dr. O'Keeffe said it was an intellectual' "free and easy " of that high exalted kind which en- nobled the mind and elevated human nature. It was the first of its kind, and he hoped it would not be the last.—Mr. S. Robinson seconded the motion with great pleasure, and spoke in high terms of eulog,v of Mr. Deacon's services for the welfare a the town.—The motion was carried unaniniously.7 The Chairman said he was very, much obliged to the members for their thanks. The duties of the chainnan had peen light, and they had been a source of great pleasure to him, and a great matter of interest. The committee had very sensibly spent most of the money under their control upon books whichowere chiefly read, and although they had made one or two slight mistakes in selecting books which were not taken out as much as they might be, the Committee had, on the whole, acted wisely. With regard tothe personal matter, the soiree was an 'extremely pleasant event to him; it gave him great sagsfaction that so many of his blends accepted the invitations sent cut to them, and it was pleasant
to hear the feelings generated had been pleasant one, and that it would he remembered as a success. (Ap, Dlause.)
WIDNES LOCAL BOARD:

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. P. H. Gossage presided, and there were also present Messrs. E. Carey, D. Wright, T. Handley. J. Midwood, R. Cook, H. Gaskell, junr.. J. Houghton, J. Taylor, J. T. Allen (clerk), T. Higgin- son (surveyor), I. Carr (engineer), and J. Dickson. (nuisance mspectok).

div.head: QUALITY OF. THE GAS.
div.p: THE QUALITY OF. THE GAS.

The following certificate was read from Dr, Norman. Tate, of Liverpool :—ln accordance with instructions re- ceived I visited the gas works at Widnes on the 6th April, and there made a test of the gas supplied on that day between twelve and one p.m., and I now certify that I found the illuminating power to be equal to 17.2.5 candles. I also tested the gas in the ordinary manner for sulphuretted hydrogen, but failed to find the presence of that gas. I may add I examined the apparatus used in testing, and found it all in satisfactory order.

div.head: WIDNES AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. . _
div.p: WIDNES AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. . _

The Chair Man said by th-e-iii;ria-tiZsa.LoWi"Boards a meeting of the ittpresentatives of sanitary authorities was held at the Town Hall, Leeds, on Friday, the 6th April. " He (the chairman) was unable to attend, and Mr. Handley went, and would, no doubt, explain what took place —Mr. Handley stated that the meeting dis- cussed the Billy and passed a resolution generally approv- ing of the Bill, and a committee was appointed, consisting ,of members of the Council of the Association and ten other members, to consider the clauses of the Bill, and draw up any amendments that might be necessary. Wid- nes was entitled to two members on that .committee.—On the motion of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. Wright, the Chairman and Mr. Handley were appointed the repre- sentativa of the Board on that committee.—The Clerk ' explained that the Local Government Bill- would leave Widnes as it was, except that the Local Board would be changed into a District Council. The Rural Sanitary Authority would also be a District Corn- ell, and several. District Vouncils would be joinedtogether to make mkt electoral.division, to return one member to the County Council. The District Council would take over the debts and liabilities of the Local Board, and would also undertake the present duties of the Board, and certain other duties provided for by Section 47 of the Bill. The County Council world have power, after in- quiry, to diminish the district of a Council, but if that was done the debts and liabilities of the town would be transferred in proportion. The District Council would consist of the same number of menfbers as consti- tuted the Local Board at present, but the Council would have the right to elect certain selected Councillors. (Mr. Heyes : Aldermen.) The present system of voting would be abolished, and the principle of one man one vote \ would be adopted. If the Bill was passed in its present condition the County Council would come into force in January, 1889, and the District Council in January, 1890.

div.head: TBE ELEcTIONS,
div.p: TBE ELEcTIONS,

• The Chairman-reported that through the retirement of Horrabin, the eNpense of a contest had been avoided, and he thought their thanks were due to thatkentlernan. The Chairman asked the Board to pass accounts amount- ing to £22 18s for preparing the voters list and other necessary work.—The accounts were passed'. The Chairman then declared Messrs. B. Brown, D. Wright, J. Taylor, F. Heyes, and F. C. Liddell duly eleoted.

HIGHWAY COILHITIIIE. - On the proposition of the Highway Committe:, various tenders were accepted, plans, sections, and estimates for th makibg of Bold-street, submitted and approved. Re- commended that Bold-streene made under section 150 of P. H. Act, 1875—that the vsual notices be served upon property owners to do the work—and that upon their failing to comply:the work be done by the Board under the aforesaid section.—Mr. James White, oil and tallow.merchant. wrote protesting against the making of the passage behind Parr's Bank if he shad to pay any proportiOn of the cost. His works were partitioned off from the passage, and those persons who wished the passage to be made should bear the cost.

div.head: HEALTH OF TEE TOWN.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF TEE TOWN.

The Medleal Officer reported to the Health Committee that during March there wiere 101 births and 40 deaths, being at the rate of 40.4 and 16.0 per 1,000 respectively. .—Thejsluisance Inspector reported that there had been three fatal cases of measles and one of typhoid fever. Scarlet fever had again broken out at ileaconsfield-road ; a child had been removed to the Fever Hoseital and was now convalescent. The committee recommended that the charge for the admission of patients to the Fever Hospital be 3s per day, patients to provide their own medical attendant ; and instructions were given to the Clerk and the Inspector to arrange for the admission of patients. There was also submitted to the members the annual report of the Medical Officer of Health, a sum- mary of which has appeared in this journal. 4Mr. Hayes moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Gaskell, referring to the remark of the Medical Officer in his annual-report that the scavenging "had not been done Satisfactorily," said the typhoid fever and dysen- tery that pvailed lathe summer months might be at- tributed to the fact. The diseases from which all these people died were all of the tholera type, which were not caused by thc dry weather alone, but also by the action of hot weather upon filth.—Mr. Carey suggested that it be an instruction to the " New " Health Committee to re- port what steps they intended to take with reference to the matter.—After some discussion, Mr. Gaskell moved a resolution to that effect.—Mr. Heyes seconded the motion. Ile was sure that the scavenging would never be done properly until the Board took it into their own hands.—The motion was carried unanimously.

div.head: FINANCE.-AN INCREASED RATE.
div.p: FINANCE.-AN INCREASED RATE.

In inoving the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee, who recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £3,063 lOs Bd, Mr. flandley stated that during: the past year the estimated expenditure was £11,549, an& the actual expenditure was £11,154, show- ing a saving on the estimate of £395. The expenditure was equal to a rate of 2s 2id in the pound, but the Board only laid a rate of as in the pound, because they had a 'balance in hand from the previous year of £1,355, which had been provided for twelve months' interest and re- payment of principal on the public offices and the main 'sewer, which became due a few weeks after the financial year. For theicoming half-year ended the 29th Septem- ber next, thq total estimated expenditure was .£6,333 9s, 'being an increase over last half year of over £5OO. This increase was caused by the interest and repayment of principal of the extension of the sewer, upon which about £lO,OOO was being spent, and also of the Infectious Diseases Hospital. A rate of Is 2d in the pound for the half-year would produce £8,034, and ae,corcling to the estimates and the balance in hand, would leave them with a surplus of £23 at the end of the six months. The committee had tried to keep the rate as low as possible, but they were obliged to lay a higher rate than last half- year. He proposed that a rate of Is 2d in the pound be laid for the next half-year.—The motion was seconded 11 and carried. 1 PAUPERS AND Tiffi FEVER 110SPIT,,AL. It a meeting of the General Purposes Committee held lon the 26th March, a deputation from the Guardians at- tended.—After a lengthy discussion, the following was I agreed to as a definition of a pauper :—All tramps and all in receipt of:relief (money or kind) immediately prior to the removal to the hospital. It was recommended that sor the year ending March 25th; 1889, Widnes cases under the foregoing detinition be received upon the Guar- dians tindertaking to pay 3s. per day for each case and to provide medical attendance.—The minutes were passed. THANKS TO TIIE CHAIRMAN. _ _

Mr. Carey proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman for the courtesy and ability with which he had condueted the business of the Board during the past year.—Mr. Houghton seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. The Chairman acknowledged the compliment and the meeting concluded.
SENTENCE ON THE REV. GEORGE BOND.

An Ecclesiastical 'court of Inquiry into charges of drunkenness preferred , against the Rev. George Bond, vicar of the Parish Church, Farxivrorth, was held on Friday, March 23rd, at the Law, Association Rooms, Liverpool: The evidence then taken before the court, over which the Yen. 'Archdeacon Iffroy presided, was laid before the Bishop of Liverpool, and the vicar having expressed his willingness to submit himself to the bishop's decision, his lordship on Tuesday pronounced sentence at the Diocesan !Moms, Lord-street. The sentence was that the Rev. George Bond should be suspendesl for the space of three years from the discharge and execu- tion of all the functions of his clerical office—(that. is to say) from preaching or administering .the sacraments add performing all other duties of such clerical office in the church and new parish of Fornworth or elsewhere in.the diocese of Liverpool, and frota receiving any of the profits and benefits of the said vicarage and benefice —(that is to say) from receiving and taking the fruits, tithe rents, rent charges, profits. salaries, stipends, &c., and other emoluments whatsoever belonging and apper- taining to the said vicarage. The sentence con- cluded with the customary explanation of the cer- tificate of _good behaviour and morals, signed by three clergymen, to bq shown by the suspended vicar before he be allowed to take up his clerical duties again. A full copy of the sentence will be affixed. to the principal door of the Parish Church of Farnworth to-morrow (Sunday). At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, the Rev. George Bond was summoned by the Widnes Local Board for the sum of 1:9 8s Sd for rates due as -follow :—Gas rate, L 5 15s M; water rate, lis 6d• general. aistrict rate,' U 15s GI Mr C. Whitfield asked for an order for the payment of the money in, six days, and. the Bench agreed to do so. / .

div.p: FOOTBALL.

*„* Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the bead office, Bew sey-street, Warrington. not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning

RUGBY RULES. SANKEY Exexision V. BANK QUAY Fraz Werincexas.— ' ,The above match was played at Arpley on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the Sankey Excelsior by 1 goal 4 minors to 1 minor. Manalsorcei v. MANCRESTER AND DISTRICT.—This match, whieh had been set aside for the benefit of J. Rigby, was unavoidably postponed owing to the death of Mr. H. J. Fletcher, who was unfortunately killed in the football match, on Saturday last? Past and kpresent of the Manchester Football Club. Mr. Fletcher had consented to assist in the above benefit. WYCLIFFE V. WARRINGTON WANDKEIERS (IST TEAMS). —This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, in splendid weather, before a fair number of spectators. The Wanderers were strongly represen- ted, whilst Wycliffe were minus the services of Hamer, W. Lowe, and Alf. Jones. Wycliffe won the toss and the Wanderers kicked off. During the first half the play was very even, only four minors accruing to the home team. In the second half Wycliffe non-plussed their opponents at every point of the game. A good rush of the home forwards resulted in Healey getting a try, but it was not improved upon. Wycliffe finally on a pleasant game by 1 try and 12 minors to nil. For The winners Arthur - Jones, Knowles, Teare, and Rowe were the pick, whilst Dawber, Astill, Lawton, and Graham were the best for the visitors. RUNCORN " A " TEAM V. WALTON IST.—This match - • was played on the Irwell-lane enclosure on Saturday. ' The game was very one-sided, the visitors • being out. played at all points, and Runcorn ran out easy winners by 3 goals, 2 tries, and 8 minors to nil. For Runcorn, -Gatley, Abrams, WarcPson, and Crompton were very ,conspicuous, whilst the passing and saving of the halves greatly accounted for the severe defeat of the Waltonians. The visitors were best represented by Barry, Legge, and Ridgway. Teams :—Runcorn: Full back, S. Booth; threequarters, Lunt, Crompton and Bowyer; halves, Hollingsworth and Evans; forwards, Gatley, Ford, Cox, • Abrams, Hampson, Whinyates, Grounds, Raffe, and Higgins. Walton: Full back, Barry; threequarters, W. H. Legge, Millar, and Ridgwrsi ; halves, P. Hamill and A. Whitehead; forwards, F. Muir, E. Kent, A. Laing, E. Hickman, H. barker, Spenser, S. Cooman, .Hughes, and Waterson. • KENDAL HORNETS V. RUNCORN. Perhaps the fastest inatch seen in Westmorland this season was the one played at Kendal on Saturday between these well-known exponents. For forty minutes the Hornets had the best of the play, but in the last twenty minutes the wearers of the green pressed hard, and eventually won on the mark. W. Hughes put the ball in motion, and for some time his men pressed. Allen, Armstrong, and Walker, by short runs and kicks invaded the Runcorn 25, Brazen' dale having to concede a minor. The kick-out brought no relief. Hine and Wilkinson', with a quick dribble, again invaded the visitors' ground. Cookson here got a free kick, and the ball went to Cross, who dropped a beautiful goal. This roused the wearers of the green, who, with accurate passing, worked the ball to the home line. Walker and Battersby caused them to beat a hasty retreat, but Hughes ran back in good style. Par- sons and Ellwood dribbled so well that Brazendale con- ceded another minor. Some fine kicking amongst th,e backs and a magnificent run by Wainwright brought about half-time. Walker started the second period with a short kick, his forwards rushing in a body to the Runcorn line, where a strong attack was kept up by Cross, Battersby, Walker, and Armstrong for fully fifteen mintites, each having hard lines in not scoring. Armstrong got 'over the line, but in picking up sent the ball dead. The Run- eorn defence was superb from now, and a complete change came over the scene. Runcorn, through the in- strumentality of Broady, Cookson, Wainwright, and Davies, whose passing was a treat, pressed the Hornets, who touched down. Walker's kick-out was charged. • Shortly afterwards Hughes passed to Davies, who drop- ped a clever goal. Again Walker's kick-out was charged and play raged furiously on the Hornet's line, when, just before call of time, Whitby dodged over from a scrim- mage on the line. Score—'Runcorn, one goal and one try; Hornets, one goal. Wrnmzs v. WMMDEN.—This return match was played on the ground of the former deb, on Saturday. There -was a large company round the ropes, and the ground was in splendid condition. Widnes played with the wind and slope in their favour in the first half, and at once assumed the aggressive. Parkinson, from the quar- ter, made an attempt at goal, but the ball falling short, he dashed afteg it, and collared the visitors' back before he could get away, and the ball was scrimmaged on the line. Farrell then got hold and made a splendid drop, missing the goal by an ace. The Widnesians again as- sumed the aggressive, Gandy showing to advantage, and Plumpton kicking dead when he had a fine look in. Another dead ball having been scored by the home team, the Widnesians renewed the attack, and after fine play. by Hardman and Barber. Wilkinson secured a try near to touch-in-goal, from which Plumpton placed a magnifi- cent goal. Give-and-take play followed in the home half, Parkinson, Plumpton, and Wilkinson showing to advantage; then Barker, when at the visitors' quarter, dropped at goal, but failed to add anything beyond a Ininor. Another minor having been scored by the home team, Kiddie ran to the line and appealed for a try, but the point was not allowed, the referee ruling that he went in touch before he grounded the leather. Widne4; still continued to press hard, registering three minors in quick succession, and then Farrell, who secured-the ball in the visitors' quarter, rushed in and grounded the oval over the line. The place was a difficult one, and -Plump- ton failed to record the major point. On the change of ends the visitors maintained their position much-more efficiently than before, but they were unable to make an impression, and Widnes were only able to add a minor and then a try, the latter point being secured by Hughes in fine style, Plumpton failing to place the major point. Teams :—Widnes: S. Bingham, back; Plumpton, Parkin- son, and Barker, three-quarter backs: Farrell and Wil- kinson, halfbacks; J. H. Smith (captaip), W. Kiddie, -Hughes, J. Bingham, W. Barber, G. Woods, J. Gandy, . Pennington, and Hardman, forwards. Walkden :T. Price, back; S. Grundy, J. Martinscroft, and P. Yates, three- quarter backs; J. Grundy and A. Jones, half backs; Hirst, T. Barnes, D. Wilcock, J. Ridvard, Isherwood, Kennedy, Goodwin, Reeves, and Hughes, forwards. WARRINGTON " Train V. NEW BRIGHTON Oase- etc IST.—The Warrington "A ". team had a most en- joyable iourney to New Brighton on Saturday, to play their return fixture with the Olvmpic first team the weather being all that could be desired. The home cap- tain won the toss, and Whittle kicked off at 3-45 against the wind. Dawson returned to Evans, who made a short run and kick, the first scrimmage being formed in neu- tral ground. Dawsoa got the ball away with a kick to Samson, a minor point being registered for the visitors from the latter player's return. Dawson dropped out, Evans passing nicely to Bibby, who ran to near the line, another minor point accruing to Warrington. Dawson again dropped out, Bibby obtaining a free kick, which H Higson returned, From a free kick by Titterington, the home forwards followed up well, and forced Warrington to save by touching down. Bate next passed nicely to Evans, who dribbled to near the home line, Kent getting the ball away with a long punt. Warburton returned well, and Isherwood and Adamson gained a lot of ground with a dribble. Whittle passed to Samson, who was brought down near the line by Kent. Whittle again got possession, and running round the scrimmage, passed neatly to J . Bate, who succeeded in dodging past his op- ponents, and grounding the.ball over the line, Isherwood kicking a goal. Dawson restarted from centre, Evans returning into touch. Splendid passing on the part of the Warrington backs again forced the home team on the defensive, Bibby being collared near the line by Higson, New_ Brighton touching down. Shortly after the drop-out Holmes came away with a dribble, and picking up, made a grand run to the line, and when tackled passed SO Bate, who threw to Sanson, the latter player taking a drop at goal, Kent returning into touch. Half-time was called with the score standing—Warrington, 1 goal and 4 minor points to New Brighton 1 minor. On change of ends Dawson restarted, and Warrington, having• the advan- tage of the wind, soon invaded thehome territory. Evans and Bibby dribbled to the line, where Whittle secured from a scrimmage and passed to Evans, this player dropping a grand goal. The Warrington forwards, who • dribbled splendidly, again worked the oval into the New Brighton quarters, and Isherwood getting possession from a line-out, dashed over the line' the same player landing a goal from the place kick. Dawson re-started, and no return being made, play rested in tho visitor? i half, hut a dribble, n which Donohue, F. Bate, and Thorley took part, transferred operations to the other end of the field. Whittle passed to Evans, who ran well, and passed to Isherwood when near the line, the latter player gaining his second try, no goal resulting. After a period of even play in midfield, Holmes, Donohue, Ac- ton, and Lawless dashed off with a dribble from a line- out, the last-named player, after a strong run, gaining a try, Isherwood kicking another goal. H. Higson kicked off, Bibby returning to centre, and Gardner sent the ball into touch from a free kick. By the frequent passing of the ••Warrington players, the oval was taken into the home quarters, Sanson running the ball to the line, and the home team touching down. Evans returned the drop out, arid from a scrimmage in the New Brigh- ton 25, Whittle passed to J. Bate, who, after !flaking a short run, transferred to Evans, this player dropping another goal. On call of time the score stood :—War- rington, five goals, one try, six minor points ; New Brighton Olympic, one minor point. Teams :—War- rington: Full back, D. Warburton •, three-quarter-backs, Sanson, Evans and Bibby; half-backs, Whittle (cap- tain) and J. Bate; forwards, Donohue, Thornley, Adam- son, Isherwood, F. Bate, Holmes, Acton, Lawless, and A. Barlow. New Brighton Olympic: Full back, R. Hi... son ; three-quarter-backs, H. fligson, Dawson, aral Kent; half-backs, Edwards and W. Higson ; forwards, E. Gardner, A. Gardner, Bull, Titterington, Hockey, Por- ter, Stoneman, Broad, and Smallman. WARRINGTON V. LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT. Owing to Halifax being engaged in the final round of the Yorkshire Cup oh Saturday, the Warrington team were left with an open date. Mr. R. Wilcock, however, was invited to muster a district team of Liverpool, and a satisfactory fifteen having been got together, the match

came off on the Wilderspool enclosure. Only a fair at tendance witnessed the encounter, although the weather was beautifully fine. The home club were rather weakly represented, several of their usual team being absent.

• Warrington having lost the toss, Wilcock, as captain of the ?craWi team, commenced hostilities from centre, a return being effected to half-way flag. Massey, by judi- cious kicking, took the game to the Liverpool 2.5, and after Fair. Turner, Massey, and Antrobus had each in- effectually tried to get in, the home forwarlis rushed the , ball over the line, E. Dillon having the best of a maul with Howden. The place, which was an easy one, struck the upright. No reply was made to the drop out; but splendid passing by Speakman, Barnes, and Massey was now witnessed, and a tall kick by the latter was followed up by Randlas, which again placed the scratch team on the ;defensive. However, they kept their opponents from scoring; but Massey very nearly did the trick by a splendid run along the touch line, latig,ue overcoming him when scoring was a foregone conclusion. Barnes and Jolley rtext played a prominent part, and Fair. Tur- ner ran to the line. Howden was here awarded a free kick, which temporarily relieved, and Summer took the game to the Warrington quarter flag. Their invasion was only of short duration, and exchange kicks by Mas- sey and Williams ended with a decided 'advantage to the home club. Rhndles and Ashton now took play to the Liverpool goal, the visiting team conceding a minor to save further disaster. Following the drop out the home team went away with a rush, and Ashton coming through the pack, forced the game on the opposing line. A drop at goal by Massey just missed by the merest ' shave. Wilcock prevented a return being made to the drop out, but splendid runs by Speakman again placed Warrington on the aggressive. Littlewood next became prominent, but an effort by Summer was easily frustrated by a dodgy run on the part of Barnes, who transferred the game to the Liverpool quarter flag. Speakman passed' neatly to Massey, who, in turn, handed to Jolley, and again the visiting goal was threatened. Antrobus, Ban- dies, and Jolley now passed to each other, the latter get- ting over near the corner flag; but on appeal this was disallowed. Mulling by the home backs served as relief to Liverpool; but pressure was brought to bear on the Liverpool citadel after a good run by Boardman. The visitors played up in a plucky style, and invaded War- rington ground. A kick by Wilcock over the line forced Barnes to coneede a minor. Frank Turner re-started, but off-side play ruled a scrimmage at War- rington quarter flag. Jolley prevented Williams becoming dangerous, and after Roberts had tried to force an opening in the Warrington back division, Jolley had a shot at goal, and half-time was called with the score—Warrington 1 try and ,3 minors to Liver- pool 1 minor. The home team now had theassistance of the breeze, and by superior combination forced the scratch team to defend their lines. The second half was only a few minutes old before Barnes put in a use- ful kick, and Jolley, gaining possession, outpaced his opponents, and gained a try at corner flag. No goal re- sulted. Barnes passed to Fair. Turner, who was now playing three-quarter, the latter transferring to Massey, .who dropped at goal, a minor resulting. Antrobus showed up after the re-starting, but a rush by the home team forced Howden to save. Summer changed the venue by smart tactics, and Webster raised the hopes of I his side 'by plucky runs. Try as they would the District could not keep the Warringtonians from invading their lines, and Littlewood and W. Dillon took the game to the line, Frank Turner rushing over. No goal resulted. Fair. Turner passed wide to Massey, the latter running to the line from half way, and splendid kicks by Barnes and Jolley again found the visitors saving. The game now was morceof a farce, the home team doing Whatever they pleased, with their opponents, and the tactics that the Warringtonians indulged in evoked much laughter from the spectators who witnessed the encounter. Frank Tur- ner scored another minor by a huge pwat,and afterwards Povey and Ashton got near the line, Bowden saving again'. Ashton next got over after a sharp sprint, but Massey jut missed scoring after a splendid run from half way. His efforts were rewarded shortly afterwards, for receiving a neat pass from Fair. Turner he had the satisfaction of seeing the leather go safely over the bar. The play from now to the call of time created great amusement, but the climax was reached when Antro- bus dodged over after a brilliant run. A squabble en- sued as to who should kick the goal, each individual wanting to place the premier point. However, Povey came to the rescue, and took the kick, and scored the only: goal from any of the places that had teen tried during the afternoon. Time was then called after 70 minutes of a comical game, Warrington winning by two goals, three tries, nine minors, to Liverpool one minor. • ,

The game was a most enjoyable one, both for specta- tors and players alike, and though it was one-sided the passing at times was brilliant._ During the second half the home team held the upper hand all through, and each time the. pressure was put on the Warring- tonians scored. It would be impossible to individualize any single player of the home team, but on the opposing side Wilcock, Summer, Williams, and Webster were the

pick. The following were the teams :—Warrington: Full back, H. Boardman; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey; half backs, Speakman and An- trobus : forwards, Ashton, Fair. Turner, Frank Tur- ner, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, Povey, Hayes, Bandies, and Littlewood. Liverpool and District: Full back, How- den; three-quarter backs, Roberts, Webster, and Wil- liams ; half backs, Summer and Pugh ; forwards,Willcock, Jones, Fawning, Walker, Dewdney, Rol:efts, Toole, Cur- ran, and Burke.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATU,RDAY, APRIL 14, 1888. THE SHIP .CANAL 'WORKS,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATU,RDAY, APRIL 14, 1888. THE SHIP .CANAL 'WORKS,
AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.

• NO. 13.—THELWALL AND STATHAM. In the absence of anything of the nature of a bridge, there is at present a means of crossing from one bank of the Mersey to the other at Thelwall in the manor ferry, which is the property of Mr. Jas Nicholson, who is lord of the manor. This ferry the Canal Company are to purchase at a price to be come to by agreement or by arbitration, and in its place there will be a ferry across the canal suitable for the conveyance of foot passengers at or near the point where the canal intersects the .road which runs northward from the centre of Thelwall. There is likewise to be a permanent footbridge placed across the diversion of the Mersey at or near the point where the diversion cuts across the present pathway leading from the manor ferry to the village of Martinscroft for the use, but .not the exclusive use, 'free of all dues and charges, of Mr. Nicholson ' and those acting on his behalf, and to this foot- bridge there is to be, on both sides of the river, pro- per and convenient approaches provided. We find, in addition, that the Warrington Highway Board have obtained provisions in the Canal Company's Act with regard to the rights and means of crossing those parts of the canal and diverted river which lie between the Cheshire township of Thelwall and the Lancashire townships of Wooleton-with-Martins- croft and Rixton-cum-Glazebrook. In these provi- sions it is stated that the public shall be entitled to cross the canal in boats .free of tolls payable to the company at two such places, between a mile and two miles apart, as shall be agreed on between the engineer to the company and the Highway Board's surveyor or an umpire to be appointed, on the appli- cation of either party, by the Board of Trade, and the Company are to construct and maintain at the places agreed upon convenient steps on each bank of the canal with a handrail on either side of the steps for the use and protection of the persons cross- ing the canal. The public are also to be entitled to cross the diverted river in the township of Woolston in their own boats free of the Company's tolls, and here again proper approaches to the river with steps and handrails are to be Kovided.s

Chairman of ihe!Chester Quarter • Soisioies and in fixing the amount he shall have regard to all the circumstances of the case, including the advan- tage afforded to the district by the construction of such wharf.
