MbORE AD LOWER WAI.TON,

Considerable progress is being made on this section, and activity is great. At the wharf on the side ofethe canal near Waltod Arches materials continue to arrive in considerable quantities, and they are taken thence on the line of rails that connects with the works. Work has commenced on the Cheshire side of Walton Arches, where rails have been laid, and locomotives may be seen dragging trains of waggons for some distance. Surface earth is also being removed here, and preparations are being ntade for more advanced work. On this part of the works half-a-dozen large wooden erections have been put up by the joiners to be used as hying places by the navvies, and they have a comfortable appearance. Other building operations make rapid progress, and store-rooms are being japidly put up. The American steam navvy makes otfrious headway in the cutting, which begins to assume large proportions. It is now both wide and deep. Of late the bottom of the cutting has been partially flooded with water, and a number of men are engaged clearing it away in order that the work of removing the excavated soil may not•be impeded. Blasting operations are also carried on. Many visitors continue to go from Warring- ton to inspect the cutting, and watch the leviathan dig- ger at work. To guard against accidents, notice boards i .a.ring the words, Beware of the engine," have been placed n the vicinity of the railway lines.. Beyond the cutting proper on this section, and further on towards Moore, a large number of navvies are taking off the sur- face earth, and making other preparations. The erec- tion of buildings connected with the works goes on in the neighrourhood of the village, and on the side of the road leading from the scene of operations to Moore and Dares- bury the erection of a large wooden, warehouse-looking, building is nearing completion. It is intimated, by means of large letters painted on the building, that it is to be used as a refreshment-room. The influx of labour into the neighbourhood is having a beneficial effect, and en- terprising persons take advantage of the opportunity to supply the labourers with tea and coffee. It is stated that within the last few days a number of men have left work on this section, in consequence of not receiving a demanded increase in the rate of pay. THE DEMAND FOR LODGINGS. , At a meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority on Tuesday, the inspector, Mr. Farrington, reported a case of overcrowding near to , Daresbury station at Moore. in a house which was occupied by :a ganger em- ployed on the Ship Canal. The house contained two sleeping rooms and two living rooms, and on his (the in- spectAw's) visit the occupier's wife pwned to having four male lodgers—navvies employed on the Ship Canal— besides herself and her husband and three children and a servant. Mr. Farrington added that on making private inquiries in the village he was told that there had been eight lodgers. This was the house in which a man had died lately, and four men had slept in the same room that the dead man was in. The woman contended that it was not a case of overcrowding, as she seemed to hold that as long as there was room to get into bed there was no overcrowding. (Laughter).—The inspector was directed to take the steps nere,tsary to put an end to the alleged overcrowding. THE BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION COMPANY,

The appeal of Mr. T. H. Birch from the order of Mr. Justice North, of the 16th of January-of the present year, on a stunmons taken out in the winding up of their company, came on for hearing on Tuesday, before Lords Justices Cotton, fry, and Lopes. The effect of the order was to determine between the preference shareholders and the ordinary shareholders the principle of distribution of a large sum which had been paid to the cpmpanyas the purchase money of the whole tinder- taking of the Bridgewater Navigation by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and the appellanti was a gen- tleman who had been appointed n the winding up to represent the interests of the ordinary.,shares. Mr. Justice North construed that resolution as gleaning that the holders of the new shares were to have 5 per cent, and no more, so that any protlts in excess of that WOTIId be divisible among the holders of the ordinary flares. Jo 180 the Manchester Ship Canal had, after many vicissitudes in Parliament, become law, and inthe exercise of its power the Ship Canal Company purchased the .Navigation Company's undertaking for £1,710,000. On the 26th of August, 1887, the Navigation Co. passed a resolution for winding up voluntarily, and four gentle- men were ajp-Anted liquidators. The question then arose upon which the Order appealed from was made.— Sir Horace Davey, Q.C. (with whom were Mr. cozens Hardy, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. 0. Leigh Clare), ap- peared for Mr. Birch, and submitted that Mr. Justice North, intending to follow the decision in the .case of Sheppard v. The Scinde and Pun jaub Railway Company, 'had followed it in the letter, but had departed from it in the spirit. Both on principle and authority the surplus assets, after repaying the capital, should be divided be- tween the shareholders in the proportion in which they were entitled to share in the profits of the undertaking while it was a going concern. In this case every share- holder had received back the capital he had paid, and the question was how the sum remaining, in the hands of the liquidators was to be divided. The future bearing of the case was adjourned.

, • thenqe paksing down the mid-channel. That it will al- ways remain one of the towns of most importance on the line is evident from the conditions of its trade. It deals largely with the Midlands, and is the chief place through which the Staffordshire Potteries obtain their necessary supplies of China clay and stone from Cornwall and other districts. Large quantities of salt and bones are also passed through. At present the largest sea-going vessels getting up to Runcorn only average about eighty- eight tons; but when the canal is finished and the great ocean-going steamers can get up to its wharves, matters will be changed altoee. ther. As an example of the ad- vantages which would accrue from the construction of our great waterway it was stated in Parliament that iron ore which comes to Runcorn by sea from Scotland—say from the coast of Ayrshlrn or Lanarkshire—costs three shillings for the sea passage and six and threepence addi- tional Mr the railway rate onto Manchester; total nine shillings and threepence. When the canal is fmished the cost will be, in addition to that for the sea passage, toll charges three shillings and a penny, wharfage fourpence, total six shillings and fivepence ; being a saving of thirty per cent. A At Runcorn thl works have rjoe as yet begun to inter- fere with the town itself, and we found it a tolerably long walk to head-quarters. After tramping across the town for a considerable distance, we anxiously inquired if we were in the right direction,' and received for answer—accompanied by a grin of seemingly malicious satisfaction—" Yes; but it's quite two miles and a half to the works." However, we found a somewhat nearer way to the scene of operations by turning down to the water-side, and so along a lot of dirty by-ways until we at last emerged upon the open fields. ,Presently we came upon the first sign of work, in the person of a sort of pioneer of the great army of six or seven hundred men engaged further back, and along the couple of miles or so of cutting already begun. He was a stal- wart giant working alone, far in advance of the rest, cutting out a little trench to mark the direction of the canal for those who are following after. Then we came upon two or three others, and -then a whole crowd of navvies clearing off the top crust of the earth, in pre- paration for the steam monsters which will very shortly be travelling in that direction and eating out the • whole mass bodily. As we walk up towards the headquarters and offices and workshops at the other end of the works, we cannot help stopping Mew moments to admire the scenery on each side. Runcorn itself is eminently unpicturesque, except in the neighbourhood of the docks and upon the water's edge generally ; but here it is quite the contrary. To the right lies Halton Hill with Halton village lying along its side, and crowned by the remains of the ancient Halton Castle, with its far-ranging walls. On the left we are Sialking close to the old canal, beyond which lies a great stretch of perfectly flat low-lying land extending to the bank of the Mersey, and the broad estuary lies in the sun, backed up by the rising ground on the Lancashire side. We are accompanied on our walk for a great part of the distance by a cheerful and communicative Runcorhite, who has come out for a pleasure tramp through the mud and clay, to see how the works are progressing. He tells us it is becoming a favourite walk with the townspeople, but that there is fierce dissension among certain of them concerning the capabilities of the steam navvies. Some of- them are absolutely certain that they will digout solid rock, which their opponents derisively deny; the consequence being that the quarrels are at times so energetic as to lead to blows, which he considers a lame and impotent conclu- sion. So do we • but we wisely conclude that the cause ,of fight is just about as reasonable as any of the causes which are urging men on to bigger fights all over Europe just now. There is nothing particularly noteworthy about the excavations in this section except the great depth of earth or rock which, through the conformation of the land, will have to be dug out of certain peations, amounting in one part to sixty feet and in another to ,as much as sixty-seven. We were also struck by the seemingly great width of sonde parts nearly cleared out; but this is accounted for by the fact that for three-quarters of a mile from Runcorn upwards, the bottom width is planned to be two hundred feet instead of one hundred and twenty, the normal width. In this connection we may as well mention here that the top width also varies at certain parts of its course, ranging from two hundred and sixty feet to one hundred and thirty-five according to the material of which the sides are composed. There will be also a very large increase at the locks and sluices, so that vessels can turn without interfering with the fairway • and the canal is also very much widened at ' each end, so that vesrls may discharge and yet allow ' the fairway to remain unimpeded. In some of these places provided for ships to turn round in, the width is' increased to seven or eight hundred feet; and even this space will not appear too great when it is remembered that we expect ships of between three and four hundred feet in length to come up the canal. The great lebel space here, between the canal and the' estuary—as in many other places between Runcorn and Manchester—has been acquired for use as a " tip " for the spoil obtained from the excavations. This process of raising the level of wet low-lying lands to the height of the canal embankmeets will create many a fair acre of good dry land, absolutely free from inundations and all drawbacks of the kind. A noteworthy feature about these great tips is the use made of steam instead of horse- flesh for running the laden waggons to the top'-block at the end of the embankment. Independently of the sav- ing of horse labour e'ffected, the amount of work done is enormous; no less than one thousand wagon loads a day being got rid of by these steam tippers. . .

Wes-ton Point is only about twO'and a half miles from Runcorn, and the docks there, which form the terminus of the 'Weaver Navigation, will be benefited by the same way and to the same extent as those of Runcorn.. That this will be no slight advantage may be seen from the fact that more than a million tons of salt pass annually from the river Weaver for shipment abroad. Vessels will be able to load direct at Weston Point, and so save the large cost of freightage between there and Liver- pool. The works at this place are not as yet sufficiently far advanced to afford much opportunity for descrip- tion.

div.head: MORE EMBANKMENT.
div.p: MORE EMBANKMENT.

After running parallel with the channel of the diverted river, a little to the south of Wildegracve farm-house, the canal will cut through what Li at present part of the Mersey's bed, as it winds up be- hind Thelwall, but which, after the river has been diverted, will be levelled up to the adjoining land. Once past this point the canal is again free from contact with the Mersey for a distance, though only a abort distance, and runs its course through Che- shire ground up to near Statham, where the river, in one of the abruptest of its many windings, again crosses its track. Between the bend of the river at Thelwall and that at Statham the ground—part of i which, it may be mentioned, is n Thelwall, but the greater part in Lymm township—is low-lying ground, and, indeed, its natural level is as nearly as 'possible the Wail as that of the intended level of the Ship Canal waters. It is obvious, therefore, that the canal, through this part of its length, will have to be provided with embankments, and such will be the case. The embankments will be some ten or twelve feet high, except towards the bank of the Mersey at Statham, where the ground rises some- what, but even here embanking will be necessary to give the sides of the canal the requisite height.

div.head: PROVISIONS AS TO LAND.
div.p: PROVISIONS AS TO LAND.

It is obvious that along this part of its route the canal will completely sever the means of communi- cation, from the Statham and Lymm direction, with that portion of land which lies between its north bank and the south bank of the river. In some cases where similar isolation takes place—at Thel- wall for an example—the Canal Company undertake to provide ferries for persons and vehicles as a sub- stitute for the roadways that are closed, but in this case a different method of dealing with the diffi- culty seems to have been agreed upon. Instead of the Company's having to provide some means of crossing the canal, it is laid down in the clauses of the Canal Act "for the' protection of G. C. Dew- hurst and others "—the ()then; "0 being Mr. W. Blinston, and the trustees of the will of Mr. Isaac Ridgway,—that the company shall purchase all the lands of these.owners, situate in the township of Lymm between the northerly bank of the canal and the right, or south, bank of the Mersey so soon as they shall interfere with the present approaches thereto, at Such price as may be agreed upon be- tween the owners respectively, or. failing agree- ment, as shall be settled by arbitration in the man- ner provided by the Land Clauses Acts. Like pro- 'vision is made with regard to the land belonging to Mr. J. V. Fox, which is similarly situated. It would s6em that Lord Winmarleigh is to have a right of pre-emption of all the lands thus purchased by the Canal Company, for in that nobleman's protection the following passage occurs, ;" the owner as to all lands taken or purchased from himself and as to all severed lands in the townships of Lymm and War- burton taken or purchased from other :landowners situate between the boundary of the Rixton estate (so far as the same is co-extensiye with the river Mersey), and the north' bank of the canal, and which shall not be required by the company for the pur- poses of the canal or its incidental works, or to en- able the company to comply with the purposes of this Act, shall have the right of pre-emptipn," &c. It is added, however, "that as to all such severed lands such right of pre-emption shall be subject to any'right claimed by any such landowners." It is further provided that Mr. Dewhurst, !Mr. Fox, Mr. Blinston, and the trustees of Mr. Isaac Ridgway are to have the right of pre-emption over all lands on the south or Lymm side of the canal which was taken or purchased from them, and which will net be required by the company. LYMM SEWAGE FARM. The sewage farm of the Lymm LoCal Board forma part of the land lying between the two bends of the river at Thelwall and Statham, and with regard to

thii farm the Local Board is rasher elaborately pro- tected. As the Local Board and the Canal Com- pany have already come to an amicable agreement with regard to the sale and purchase of the sewage farm or part of it we need only take a brief glance at these propositions. It is provided that the com- pany might, if they choose, purchase the whole or only such part of the farm as they thought fit, but if they purchased only a .part they were, before entering into possession, to convey to the Local Board an equal area of land adjoining the remaining portion of the farm and as nearly as !night be equally suitable and convenient for enabl: . . . .

injthe Loci' &Card to raise, deal with, and dispose of the sewage of and,from theirpresent district. If the company purchased the whole of the sewage farm they were before entering into possession, eithtr to convey to the Local Board an eanal area of land: or they were to pay to the Board such a sum as would enable it to acquire another sewage farm as nearly as might be equally suitable as their present one, and this sum was to be sufficient to enable the

Local Board to erect similar buildings, apparatus., and machinery to those on the old farm, and to make the sewers, drains, and roads as should be reasonably necessary, and over and above all this, if the• Local Board incurred any increased annual cost in the working of the new farm the company were to repay it the increased annual cost. WHARVES, &c. _ -

At Lymm, as at other places, the Canal Company are bound to provide wharvee, and such like con- veniences for adjoining landowners and others. For the benefit of Lymm Local Board, they will, within six months after the completion of the canal, 'pro- vide a quay or landing place within the township ot Imam, at which the Local, Board will be at libertyto embark or land, free from wharfage rates, goods of all ddscriptions required for the sanitary purposes Of the district, and macadam, sand, and other road material for the use of the Board. Mr. G. C. Dewhurst, Mr. Blinston, and the trustees of Mr. J. Ridgway are also entitled to construct a wharf in the township of Lymm, on the south side of the canal, for use, free of wharfage rates and canal tolls, for the conveyance of material to and from land owned by them in the parish, and to be used by them for the cultivation of such land. If the canal be so constructed that any of these owners have no frontage to it on the south side, the Com- pany shall, if so requested, purchase from spch the other owner or owners as shall be willing to sell such land as may be necessary for the construction of a wharf, and shall convey the land to the owner requiring it, the price paid for it by the Company being deducted from any purchase money payable by the Company to this particulaeowner. Another provision obtained by Lymin Local Board is to the effect that, if by reason of any increased traffic to or from any wharf of the Company in the town- ship of Lymm, it shall be found necessary to con- struct a new bridge at Statham Pools, in lieu of the existing bridge there, the Company will contri- bute to the expense thereof such. a sum as the

div.head: ALONG THE SHIPMANAL.
div.p: ALONG THE SHIPMANAL.
AT, IWNCORN. (From the ."14anehester City News.")

It is easy enough to reach Runcorn from London Road Station Manchester, by way of Warrington. You may, it is true, have to kick your heels for half an hour or so at Ditton Junction, where there is absolutely nothing. to see, and you can. do nothing but fret and fume impatiently for the train which is to carry you through Widnes and across the es- tuary to your destination.

. The saints preserve us from Widnes and its filthy smokes and stinks! We made our first acquaigt- ance with.it the other day, and it certainly w6uld not break our hearts if we were assured that we should never see it again. Nevertheless it is a place of great and growing importance, and its trade will be no mean factor in the great aggregate of business which will go o the making of the prosperity of the Ship Canal. And its rapid growth is something wonderful in this old-world country of ours, reminding one more of the mush- room rapidity of development of some new town in the far west of America or Canada than anything else. Less than forty years since it had no popula- tion at all worth mentioning; but sundry alkali and chemical works were established, and by 1870 there had grown up a town of ten thousand inhabi- tants. To-day the population is estimated to be twenty-five or twenty-six thoustwd, The place has thriven too upon-the nastiest of trades, such as the manufacture of railway- grease, bone manures, soaps, chemicals, alkali and the like. Its enthusi- astic admirers say that it ia a healthy town; but on the whole we think we should prefer to run the risk of having good health somewhere else. All tho same, good luck to it if it will help the Canal. We pass over to Runcorn by .the magnificent lattice- girder viaduct thrown across the Mersey by the L. and N.W. Railway Company at that narrow portion of the Mersey estuary—it is only about four hundred yards in width at this point—known as Runcorn Gap. The entire length of this bridge is about fifteen hundred feet, and it is seventy:five feet above the river A high water. More wonderful than this bridge, however, and what has made the town famous, is the marvellous series of locks form- ing the termination of that astonishing work of Brindley, the Bridgewater Canal. It is more than a hundred years since the work was executed, and canal making was little understood in England at the time, therefore the boldness of Brindlev and the inexhaustible resources of his genius are all the more surprising. To bring the waters of the canal over lalleys and rivers, moss and fen, upon a dead level all the way from Manchester tol Runcorn, and than to let the waters down at once by this series of locks to the level of the Mersey, was a feat' which became one of the wonders of the age. The canal, with its lcars and docks and all its belongings, are now. as everyone knows, t 1 property of the Ship Canal Company; but it is nowise intended that the greater canal shall extinguish the lekser. On the contrary, it is still intended that the Bridgewater shallhavea remunera- tiers traffic of its own, and, say the promoters, "we ex, • pect positively that there will be that inter-communica- tion of traffic between the Bridgewater Canal and our- selves, which will make it a feeder to us, and make us a feeder to it." The old canal occupied about five years in its construction, and was opened for traffic in 1767; but the locks were not completed until 1773, when they were opened in the presence of crowds of people from all parts of the country who had come to see the wonderful works; and it is recorded that six hundred of the Duke's viorkmen were entertained upon tha lock banks with "an ox roasted whole and plenty of good liquor." The docks can only be reached by shipping at high tide: but On the completion of the Ship Canal vessels will be able to enter at all thpes. _ -

The stspnger who sees Runcorn for the lirst time is scarcely Ekely to fall in love with it straightway. The town is mean and dingy; but it is certainly not so bad as its opposite neighbour, Widnes ; and it has besides a flavour of antiquity hi its traditions. It is even said to have had a castle and a church before the conquest, and although no traces of either exist at the present time, the name of Castle Rock survives, which is something to swear by and to enable it to look down upon its upstart rival over the Water ; and there is a good solid business air about it also. The rise of its commercial prosperity was due to the completion of the Duke of Bridgewater's great work; but our own still greater work vrifl, it is anticipated, cause it to advance by leaps and bounds. During the hotly-debated early stages of the Ship Canal controversy Runcorn was perhaps the name most com- monly to be heard in everybody's mouth, seeing that, in the scheme of 1883, it was the point marked as that from which the canal was intended to enter the estuary, '

CIIESHIRE. On Monday afternoon the Hon. T. 11. W. Pelham, barrister, One of the assistant commissioners ap- pointed under the Local Government Boundaries Act of 1887,was in attendance at the Council Chem- I her of Warrington Town Hall for the purpose' of hearing observations on the arrangements proposed by the Boundary Commissioners in respect to, a re- adjustment of the boundaries of the Union and Borough -areas of Warrington. The Commissioners • proposed to transfer the parishes of 'Grappenhall, Latchford; and Thelwall, now in the county of Ches- ter, te the county of Lancaster, so that the Union of Warrington and the Borough of Warrington would respectively be wholly within the county of Lan- caster, and invited observations regarding the pro- posal. There were present at the inquiry the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Sutton), Mr. J. C. Parr, Rev. T. Pym Williamson (vicar of Thelwall), Messrs H. Bleckly, J.P., W. Long, J.P., H. Appleton, J. Tinsley, It A. Naylor, H. Greenall, R. Dutton, John White, Aldermen Davies, Holmes, Burgess, and Pickmere ; Councillors F. Dixon, E. Greenall, jun., T. Jolley, W. Pierpoint, J. Taylor, B. W. Francomb, and John Greening; Messrs W. H. Brook (town tlerk), T. Longdin (borough surveyor of Warring- ton), J. C. Sutton (clerk to tbe Warrington Board Of Guardians), Samuel Sutton (clerk to the Warring- ton Rural Sanitary Authority), the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman of the Warrington Board of Guardians); Messrs George Blackhurst, William Derbyshire, John Houghton, William Houghton: G. Clarke (Guardians of the Warrington Union) ; and others. At the commencement of the inquiry thel Assistant Commissioner explained 00.

SCHEME OF THE COMMISSIONERS, who, he said, had had the advantage of consulting with the,justices of the counties of Lancaster and Chester, as well as with the Town Council of Warrington and the Clerk to the Warrington Board of Guardians. It would be observed that there were two overlapping areas which had to be dealt with. There was the Borough of Warrington, which was situated in more than one county, and the Union of Warrington, situated in more than one county, and the question before them that day was—should the three townships which had been named be added to the county of Lancaster, or should part of the area be added to some union in the county of Chester ? It might be taken for granted that, as regarded that part of Cheshire which was in the Borough of Warfington, it must be added to the county of Lancaster. He should like it to be understood that the scheme which had been put forward was not meant I to express any very definite opinion on the matter at I present by the Commissioners, who had not had the advantage of hearing what was the opinion of the in- habitants of the parishes themselves. There was no doubt a great deal to be said on both sides. It was very naturally said by those who were interested in Maintain- ing the Union of Warrington that the parishes for a long time had regarded Warrington as their centre, and used it as such, an'd that the inhabitants were more Lanca- shire than Cheshire men. On the other hand, a matter which required careful consideration was that if the whole of that part was added to Lancashire there became a part of the county cut off from the rest for pblice purposes. It became a quasi-detached part drith I regard to police administration and movement of , cattle. Be thought it might be taken as assumed that it would be necessary for the whole °of Warrington to go in.—Mr. ,J. C. PARR then, on behalf of the residents of Grappen- hall, said that they were much surprised when they found that they were scheduled to be united to Lanca- shire. Since that became known in Grappenhall, a town's meeting had been held, at which fifty persons were present, and at which it was decided with one exception that the inhabitants of ORAPPENHALL SHOULD PROTEST against such a proceeding. A: committee was in conse- quence formed, and Messrs. W. Long, J. Tinsley, H. Ap- pleton, Bradford, Boardman, and Taylor were appointed a deputation to present a memorial at the inquiry. Hav- ing introduced the deputation, Mr. Parr read the memo- rial, which set forth, as a protest against the scheme,

(1) that Grappenhall, cut off by the Mersey and the Ship Canal would be isolated, would form the fag end of the county of Lancaster, and would be at a disadvantage for administrative purposes ; (2) that the distance from the County town, assuming that to be Lancaster, and tile in- frequency of the trains, would render attendance on the County Councils almost prohibitive; (3) that by the al- teration of the Petty Sessional division the magistrates concerned would cease to , be magistrates for the county in which their property is situated, and if they were ad- ded to the Lancashire Bench would only occupy junior positions to magistrates even the most recently appoin- ted ip that county; and (4) that the electoral division must also, sooner or later, undergo the same change, and that it must be contemplated that Grappenhall would be transferred from the Knutsford division of the county of Chester to the Newton division of the cOunty of Lancaster, thus leaving Grappenhall isolated not only by the Mersey and the Ship Canal, but by the whole of the town and suburbs of Warrington, from the electoral division of Newton, to which it would naturally be appended. On the other hand., the memorialists said, if Grappenhall should remain an Integral part of the county of Chester, and be cut off from the Warrinpon Union to form part of the Runcorn Union, .from which it was severed in 1845, • the advantages would be—(l) that its highways, &c., would be within the jurisdiction of its own Union, and highway rates would be collected by the usual Union authorities; and (2) that the township of Grappenhall would be relieved from payment of the Warrington Union rates, which are excessive for a rural and agricultural district. The memorialists also expressed the keen sense of attachment they naturally felt to the county ill which they had been born, and their fathers before them; their love and veneration \. for its institutions and respect for its governing bodies; and their earnest and ardent prayer that they might not be severed from it. Mr. Parr added that out of 192 names on the rate book the memo- rial had been signed by 146.—Alderman PicirmEßE then introduced a

DEPUTATION FROM THELWALL, and stated that at a meeting held at Thelwall a memorial had been almost unanimously signed against the pro- posed changt.—Mr. R. A. NAYLOR, a resident of Thel- wall, then read the memorial, which contained protests similar to those advanced by the residents of Grappen- hall.—Mr. H. BLECKLY, a county magistrate, then pro- ceded to speak on

THE OTHER SIDE OF THE QUESTION, and contended that the interests of the general public should be held in consideration before the interests of a few magistrates; The matter should be looked at in a broad light, and not as a personal matter, and it was only right and proper that public interest should have preference over private interest. The county town of Lancashire, he pointed out, was practically Preston, a place which was easily accessible from this neighbour- hood. The district councils would absorb the whole of the Inca' boards, and in consequence the roads would pass into the control of tliose councils: It would be to the interest of the proper administration of the Poor Law that the three townships in question should be trans- ferred to Lancashire, as Warrington was a convenient centre for the transation of business. The gentlemen of Grappenhall and Thelwall would be placed under no sub- stantial disadvantages; and, on the other hand, it• would be an advantage to them to be transferred to the county of Lancaster. Warrington was the great milch cow which supplied the district around with its wealth and sustenance; and, therefore, he contended that the whole of the population was drawn to it. It avas the town where the people carried on their business, and from which they derived their Wealth. He did not deny that there might be some local advantage in remaining with Cheshire, but he did not believe there was any practical interest as opposed to the interests of the peo- ple of Lancaster.—On behalf of the CORPORATION OF WARRINGTON. ' Alderman DAvnts then called the attention of the As- sistant Commissioner to the fact that the Warrington. .Corporation gas works supplied the three townships in Question with gas, which supported . the opinion that they were in a great measure a part and parcel of the borough of Warrington. With regard to sewerage mat- ters it was very desirable that there should be no sever- ance of Government. The Corporation, for whom he ' appeared, had, through the General Purposes'Committee, resolved that the proposals of the Boundary Commis- sioners met with the approval of the Corporation; and further, that the Commissioners be requested to add to the county of Lancaster those parts of the townships of Appleton and Walton Inferior and parish of Great Bud- worth which lie north of the intended Ship. Canal between the point where the Ship Canal is con- nected witji the river Mersey at Walton and the western boundary of the parish of Latchford.' The grounds .on which the Corporation came to this decision were, in the first place, that inasmuch as it will be necessary at a comparatively early date to apply for an extension of the borough boundary, and aa such extension Would embrace the parishes in question, it is essential that those parishes should be in the county of Lancaster, as the Boundaries Act contemplates that unions and boroughs shall be solely in one county. ' The necessity for such an extension exists from the fact that the large area of Arpley and the lands lying between that portion of Lancashire and the western boundary of the parish of I.Latchford, and the three parishes in connection will, when the Ship Canal has made further progress, become rapidly developed and be covered with houses, ware- houses, and other buildings, and new roads and streets will be laid out, and as such will be in contiguity to the borough. It was most desirable that they should be • under the one central control, and liable to the same rules and regulations as exist in the borough, and for the purposes of sewerge, drainage, and other local man- agement and administration, it was deemed tat they ought to be within the borough. They were at present supplieti with gas and water from the borough, and their sewers were connected with the borough drainage sys- tent. In the next plate, as the three parishes in ques- tion are at the present time within the union of War- rington, it would be most unfair to take (Oiray. from that union the ratable value of those three parishes ans thereby increase the call upon the borough.—The Assi- TANT COMMISSIONER having intimated ,that when the borough was extended the new boundary should be en- tirely 'decided on the merits of the case, and that it ought not to be prejudged by an inquiry, the

VASE TOR •THE WARRINGTON trritoia was submitted by the Clerk to the Board of Guardians, ,Mr. J. C. SUTTON, who, In the course of a long speech, said that the County Council woulcimeet at Preston,, to which place there was direct communication free of delay. Whether or not the ' parishes •in question were separated froin the Wirrington Union that Union would have their poor to maintain even though the rates were• transferred for the aid of the poor of the distant town of Runcorn. Neatly all the magistrates who lived in the three townships were magistrates for Lancashire, and wherein then was there grounds for the contents of the memorial with regard to magistrates. If the purpose of the Boundaries Actvas practical, then surely eVery- thing 'that was really essential to good administration went in support of the Commissioners' proposal._ LA A report that Mr:Sutton then read it was stated that 'the arrangements proposed for the present by the Boundary. Commissioners had the approval of the Guardians, and, it wai believed, of the county and municipal authorities. Long,experience of sanitary and poor-law 'administra- tion, and practical acquaintaaacewith the 'Constantly in- creasing requirements of the district, enabled the Guar- dians to advise theta return to the conditions the Poor. Law Board in 1845 insisted upon reVersing, would be alike unreasonable and impracticable,.andwould be at- tended with hardship to the poor, and injustice to the present Lancashire towns of the Union. The Gunidians were unable to find substantial reasons for opposition to the proposed annexation to Lancashire, and looked upwn the question as being narrowed down to one of shire. Time and events had, however, almost obliterated ' out of mind all consequence that in earlier times might have attached to name of cOunty As Lancashire men had, acquired wealth they had succeeded by purchase to the almost exclusive ownership of Adjacent Cheshire estates. As the worn out and feeble poor had gravitated to the Urban centre, prosperous and well-to-do people had re; I moved to surburban mansions and villa •residences. So general, indeed, were changes ,of occupation and ,resi- delace, that 'nen moved to and fro fr.= one county to the other, probably without the least thought off:idler- ence of shire. Another point raised by Mr. Sutton was, that many of the labourers employed at the Ship Canal works would break down, would require to make use of the hospital, and would also be relieved in the Warring- ton Union. It would be impossible for these people, ex- • cept at great loss and difficulty, to go to Dutton Work- house. Mr. Sutton having spoken further on the sub- ject, sever9l gentlemen present made •

OTHER OBSERVATIONS. Mr. John Winn said he was a resident of one part of Latchford, and could say that, so far as he had canvas- sed, the people who lived on the south-east side of the Ship Canal were' certainly undesirous of being trans- ferred to the county of Lancaster. • It Seemed to him that the Ship Canal would form a, very natural boun- da7.—Mr. W. DARBYSHIja thought that if Thelwall an GraPPenhall were lefrin ' Cheshire, and taken from the Warrington Union, it' would be vety inconvenient for poor-law administration.—After Mr. Penn and Mr. NAY- Lois had again spoken, the inquiry terminated with the passing of ,a vote of thanks to the Assistant CommiS- sioner.

THE SHADY SIDE OF LONDON LIFE.

The Rev. Andrew Mearns. of London, author of "The bitter cry of outcast London," preached te, large congregations. at Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, on behalf of the Congregational Church Aid and Home Missionary Society, on Sun- day moining and evening. There were, he said, over a thousand chapels in connection with the society, which employed 619 men in Home Mission work. In addition, there were a great many preach- ing stations and cottages used for religious services,. and there were hundreds of lay-preachers who supplemented the work of the 619 regularly en' nloyed men. Priestcraft and Ritualism were ram- pant in the rural districts of England,. and if the,' were concerned for the preaching of the pure Gospel they must maintain the efforts of the Rome Missionary Society. In round figures, .£13,090 year watt being raised for this work, but the society had suffered a diminution of the regular income re the extent of £6,000 by the death of two men, and by the closing of the Jubilee Fund of the Congregs- tional Union of England and Wales, from which they had received .£4,000." The income of the society would be doubl-d if all Congregationalists would give a penny per week, and if the school children each gave a rarthing a week it would be trebled. He, therefore, urged his hearers to liberally *support the work. The sermon delivered in the evening by Mr. ifearns was more of the nature of an address, and it was. a very interesting one. His re- marks dealt with the work of the

MISSION IN LONDON. Four years ago, he said, an inquiry was made into the condition of the outcast poor of London, and suceegsful work has been carried on amongst them ever since. 111 TAndon, it was found, there are about half a million of ••ple living in single rooms—one,etwo, and sometime three families oqupying one apariment. As many OS eleven grown-up people were found sleeping in one room, covering the floor from wall to wall. This, he be- lieved, was at the root of very much of the vice pre: valent in London, and it was high time the State stepped in to put a stop to such overcrowding. He could take them to hundreds of Yooms that ar6not fit for habitation at all, but people work in them all day, and sleep 10 them at night. Overcrowding had been prevented bY the State elsewhere, and could be done in London as Niel' There Were. besides:some 30,000 people who livs in

commoN Lonniko-nonsEs.. In most of these religious services are regularly held, and bands of Christian workers go into the thieves' cottage and lodging-houses to hold them. There is no difficulty if the service g are made lively enough. The people who occupy these houses are very fond of readmg, if they have the right kind of stuff to read. It is no use giving them the old four-page tract that looks like a tract. They, will not use it, and will burn it as soon as the back 0, the donor is turned. Give them something with a piC' ture on, and they will keep it and read it. The place 4 can be visited without the slightest danger. The only danger consists in taking a policeman along. , There 14 another class whose condition has been inquired into. They are called the

HAPPY DOSSERS OF LONDON." They are called " happy " because they sleep on the steps, and do not pay anythinglor their accommodation. The street doors-of some of the lodging-houses are never locked, and the "happy dossers" come in at night and sleep on the stairs, and depart early in the morning bO. fore any of the people of the houses are about. These are the lowest of the low people in London. Under such a Condition of.things, how can workmen living in these houses succeed in bringing up a family respectably ? Children, through this, become accustomed to profanity and vice from their earliest yea. Ought not the chil; dreri to be protected ? These "happy\ dossers of London would be far better out on the streets. A fourth dais 0' the outcasts of London comprise the people who are OUT ON THE STREET AT NIGHT without a penny, without a friend, without work, and without a chance of work. These people are found be' tween 12-30 at midnight and 3-30 in the morning. The, plan of the mission is to get as many as possible 0' them to the hall, where they are allowed to steep until six o'clock in the morning, when breakfast is served. There was scarcely i single night when there would not be at least a thousand people on the streets. He had seen the arch at Waterloo Bridge with as many as thirti, people on the ground, Blackfnars Bridge with 120, and London Bridge at two o'clock in the morning with 125, trying to sleep on the granite. In order to,clear the streeti Sir Charles Warren, some thne.ago, adopted the plan 0" giving free tickets to the. people who were out at nigl?!. As soon as this became known, some men went into dn.,' ferent streets and got different tickets, which they sole th others in order to obtain drink. Thus the plan Tailed. After the time when the streets were considered to have been cleared, 159 were found out in one night, and were sent on to have their breakfast. Although the numbers. will decrease as the fine weather conies, there are ye' hundreds out on the streets of London every, night. Take an instance—a man sitting on Trafalgar Square with his wife by his side. Evidently they are strangers; not accustomed to that kind of life. You can tell tki old stagers easily. They usually carry a piece of broo paper, which forms their cushion when they sit dovnl. Those accustomed to be out at night are souncill asleep by two o'clock in the morning, but those who sre, not so accustomed sleep uneasily and restlessly. Y°_," can step amongst the oldsters, and pick out the one, you want without disturbing,: the rest. This, man and woman are evidently strangers, and a conversation ensues. He has-got behind in his rent,(and had to leave his.home, and he remarks, "If 'I could get any otheto place for the Wife to go to I would not mind for myself- .44ls this a genuine story, Or is it a make-up p" iins the reply. "Goon to the. Hall with your wife and be there presently to take down all the particulars you haVe given me,larid will inquire into the truth of the state- ment you have made." The man's story proves correct. He is a carpenter, arid has been out of work for some time; has parted with his tools to get bread, and has been unable to raise the rent. His tools were again phi' cured for him, work obtained, and ma very short time he brought back the money that had been spent on hire* which proved him to be an honest man. He has nmv got a littiChotne,r6und him. In the Mission Halls the people,

SLEEP ON CHAIRS until six o'clock. in the morning, when the gas is turned up,'and the gong, sotmded as an intimation that brealt" fast is about to be served up. At six o'clock each persoli receives a bag, and each bag; contains two thick sand- . wiches, with -one piece of bread buttered and one slrY; Usually one sandwich is taken out, and the bag screwed up again, lest the temptation to eat the lot should •proVe too strong.. A:Me little old l'arlY was 'observed to eat the dry portion of bread first. "Well, old lady; you calf° manage the rest ?" "Can't I though • you wait a bit. Ido not know when I tasted a bit of beef. I am goini to keep that to the last." She finished her dry breaei then ate the piece of bread that was buttered, and thee the beef. "Now, old lady, let me give you another cuP of coffee!' "Not another drAp, sir I would not lose the taste of that bit of beef for anything." ' " What were yriu doing before I took you in ?" "1 used to sell blbaters, sir, but I was took ill, and he'd to go to the Infirmary, and when I came out I could get no Stec_ and had parted with my basket." She • received 3s Oa' with which to get a fresh stock and a basket, and for months afterwards she was seen selling bloatersin UpPer Thames-street, , and never Caine back for further help,* The way to.give charity is to put people in the war ei• earning their own living in an honest manner. During the first year that the Sotety commenced work a large , number of men were sent to Canada, 281 were sent 10 the second-year, and last year over 400 were sent. Nest, week, 200, the first batch for this season, will be sent, and ' there are openings at present for - •

700 NSW iN CANADA. Something, it will be seen, is done by those early break; fiiits, and-by taking tke destitute out of the streets and -giving them a chance of earning their own living. Mr. Mearns, after giving much interesting information,laki that to deal with a question like this was practical Chris- tianity. Ile did not find amonk the Door opposition to religion, but there was a decided objection bo the pro- fessors of religioh, and anything in the shape of priest- craft they would not. have; He had never heard then' . speak„against the Gospel, but they did not think that the Christians of the present day Manifested their- Christianity. To clothe the naked and feed the hungrlf was one effective way of preaching the Gospel. •

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON. THURSDAY .NIGHT. The House of Commons is still on its good beha- viour, and public business is progressing in a man- ner to make the Ministerial heart glad. But during the past week there have been one or two incidents which warn whom it May concern that these halcyon days are always liable to disturbance. One has arisen in connection with Mr. Gladstone's atti- •tude on the ,Budget Bill. On Monday night, the House was crowded in anticipation of finding Mr. Goschen crushed under the wheel of the fiery elo- quence of the great financier. There is no subject upon which Mr. Gladstone, even to this day, is more easily roused than finance. Many members of the -present House can remember how he used to fall upon poor Sir Stafford Northcote when 'he walked delicately amid the paths of finance, and hew him to pieces before the Mace. Mr. Gladstone's views on Mr. Goschen's heresy at the present epoch are pretty well known. In private conversation he is ritt chary in denouncing the Budget in almost every clause. No one can stand before him in a financial debate, and perhaps the most nervous man in the House on Monday night was Mr. Goschen. But Mr. Gladstone, disappointed his followers and delighted the Conservatives by letting Mr. Goschen off with a threat of an amendment on the second reading, a threat which has since been carried out. Having listened attentively to Mr. Gladstone's Budget speeeh, I do not take the view of it which is entertained in some quarters of the Liberal camp. It struck me as being a masterly move, worthy of an old Parliamentary hand. His line of attack is to cenvict Mr. Goschen of letting the land- owners off too cheaply in dealing with the succes- sion duty, and thereby creating n deficiency which must be filled up by the imposition of the cart and wheel tax, not to mention the horse tax and the impost on bottled wine. Monday was not intended by him as the occasion for the general attack on the evening's position. It was rather a reconnaissance in force, designed to open the public eye to the pos- sibility of a re-adjustment of the scheme whereby the cart and wheel tax might be dispensed with, and the saddle of increased taxation placed on the right horse, to wit, the man whose income is de- rived directly from landed property. That is, how- ever, a matter of opinion. The significant fact re- mains that an influential section of the Liberal party ere beginning to grow restive under the con- dition of benevolent neutrality which Mr. Glad- stone has established, and are longing to hear the trumpet sound the fight. One other source of danger to the existing truce is the absence of skilful management on the Treas- ury Bench. On Monday night Mr. Smith effected a little manceuvre which greatly angered the Oppo- sition, and almost led up to the waste of a whole sitting. The night had been solemnly set apart for discussion of the Budget. Everyone was in a state of expectancy of Mr. Gladstone's speech, and the usual order of things was looked for whereby Budget Night is given up entirely to ponsideration of the Budget. But the Government saw a chance of making an'advance with the wretched King Har- man Salary Bill, wl.lich has been hanging like a millstone round their neck since the session open9d. If they put it first on the orders. the Irish members, knowing that Mr. Gladstone was waiting to speak on the Budget, would not sacrifice his opportunity even for the sake of obstructing this obnoxious measure. The calculation proved well founded. There was a shout of indignation when the little trap was discovered, and a coople of divisions were taken. But the Bill, otherwise immovable, was advanced a stage. Whether the petty triumph was worth the stupendous cost is a matter-for the quiet • consideration of her Majesty's Government. It cer- tainly is not a trick to be repeated.,g The publication this morning of Mr. Gladstone's speech at the National Liberal Club last night came as a surprise upon the political world. No prior announcement of the event had been made, and as a matter of fact it was only late yesterday after- noon that Mr. Gladstone made up his mind to utilise the occasion for addressing the party and the public out of doors, and arrangements were hastily made for reporting the speech. The Balfour Banquet was quite another thing, and was looked for in advahce as the principal political event of the night..- I do , not know exactly upon what ground the distinction was based, but the Committee of the National Union did me the honour to invite me to the ban- ' quet, and I found myself' the only Liberal in the crowded hall. Perhaps overcrowded woul4 without suspicion of hypercriticism more accurately describe the situation. Such is the enthusiasm that the Chief Secretary excites in the Conservative mind, that it was found absolutely impossible to meet the demand for tickets, and the stewards in their efforts to please attempted the proverbially impossible feat of getting a quart into a pint bottle. The process of dining was rather a gymnastic performance than a reasonable feast. But nothing daunted the en- thusiasm of the gentlemen present, many of whom had come from. distant parts of the country in order to do honour\to the rising hope of stern unbending autocracy in Ireland. They did not het& Mr. Bal- four at anything like his best. But he was good enough for them, and they separated at a late hour encouraged and delighted. I see the announcement made that Mr. Bancroft. the American historian, in writing his History of _Mexico, has come to the conclusion that the wife of the hapless Emperor Maximilian became insane be- fore she left Mexico. It is to be hoped that this is true, as madness would be a happy release from the torture of knowledge of what was taking place. The story is of course at variance with theimpres- sion hitherto accepted. According to history as it is written, the first trace of insanity on the patt of the T-npress was manifested in her interview With the Pope, which took place shortly after her arriv. in Europe in September, 1866. Whenever' insanity - developed itself, the cloud has never from that day to this been lifted, and the unfortunate Empress, who still lives and waits for the long -deferred coming of her husband, does not know that was shot , ..within a year of her having parted from him in Mexico. I do not know anything in history more pitiful , than this short chapter of the new Mexican Empire which the Emperor Napoleon tried to found. Mr. Bancroft in.his new book tells with simple pathos bow the emperor died. On the night before he was led to execution he wrote to his wife a letter which we may read, though she has never been able to master its purport. "My dear beloved Carlotta," he doomed man wrote, "if God one day permits your recovery, and you read these lines, you will learn the cruelty of the ill fortune which has un- ceasingly pursued me since your departure for Europe. You took with you all chance and all my soul. Why did I not listen to your counsel? So many events, alas! So many sudden blows have broken all my hopes, at death is for me a happy deliverance and not an agony. I fall gloriously as a,soldier; as a king vanquish ed, but not dishonoured. If your sufferings be too great, if God call you speedily to rejoin me, I will bless the Divine Dand which has so heavily pressed upon us. Adieu, adieu! Your poor Max." The Council of the Royal Academy are hard at 4 work all this week rejecting pictures. About two- thirds of what is sent in is sent back, and the poor artists don't know their fate till the end of the month. The Council are a dozen of the menibers, i. e. the full R A.'s, with the president presiding. 'Then there is an army of porters and an easel. Ever, picture is put on the easel in turn, and most remain ' about sixty seconds on it. Thepractised eye is able at once to tell whether the picture is bad enough to be excluded or good enough to be made "Doubt- ful." If it is very bad, the President says "Rejec- ted," and the porter scores an "I on the back with a bit of chalk. Then it goes down totthe sellarage, and a polite letter will by and bye an- pounce the regret of the President and Council that

they could find no room to hang it. Frith, Dobson. Stone, and Fildes are the hangers this year. We hear a good,deal at home and abroad about Lord Loruidile, the Marquis of Ailesbury, and other ornaments of the peerage. But very few people are aware that there is at the present time living in the United States a gentleman known as Dr. Fairfax, whose right to a peerage is even more incontest- ablq than was Little Lord Fauntleroy's. I see from a paragraph in a Maryland paper that "Dr. John Contee Fairfax" has just given up the active prac- tice of his professiop as a family doctor, and has re- tired to his farm, Where he hopes to spend the re- mainder of his life. The gentleman known in Northampton. Maryland, As Dr. Fairfax is the iden- tical personage of whom a description may be found in the sober and solemn pages either of Burke or Debrett, under the title of h Fairfax. Baron.' Nor is Lord Fairfax a baron of recent creation like Lord Brabourne. The Fairfax barony was created in 1627, and the MarYland doctor is the eleventh baron. His father was Clerk of the Supreme Court of Cali- fornia, and what is more, Speaker of the House of Representatives of the State of Alcaldi.„ He died at Baltimore in 1869, and was succeeded bST the pre-1 sent baron, who has lived a useful life earning his own living and unostentatiously doing good. The second Baron Fairfax was Cremwelrs general, who defEated the King at Varston Moor. It was Thomas, the sixth baron, who settled in America, 'sad ever since the family have lived there, in high ppute. filling various offices of citizenship. Several Of them fought in the war, and one was a commodore in the United States Navy. Last year Dr. Fairfax received a command in the Queen's name to assemble with the other peers for the Jubilee festival at Westmin- ster Abbey. But even this did not tempt him. He had his patients to look after, and was busy wind- ing up his affairs previous to settling down on the farm, so he said.

LICENSING PROSECUTION. should like to say, with regard to the licensing case heard bef ore the Borough Bench on Monday, and dismissed, that it is no wonder that the police had some difficulty in getting hold of an offender. The rea- son that I make this remark is because adcess can be had tosthe premises of the defendant by (fivers ways, and, if persons do offend in the way alleged, there is a good chance of their doing it without being found out. An entry in School-street is used by a number of houses. The door of the entry is left unlocked. Besides the means of access from the way that the property is situated, a person can enter from the Old-road, and walk up the passage to the rear of Mrs. Locker's pre- mises, without ever being seen either in Scilool-street or St. James-street. The police deserve more credit than they got for their success on the Sunday in question.— Yours, &c.,

div.head: TEMPERANCE.
div.p: TEMPERANCE.

" BELLEROPHON'S " EXIT. Sir,—lt is clear that "Bellerophon" mistook his voca- tion when he set up as the defender of the liquor trade and a reviler of teetotallers. He made a brave show .t4:l begin with, but his valeur is of the Chinese sort. His guns are wooden dummies, and his fortifications plaster and pasteboard, and they are no sooner withstood and approached than he, feels an irresistible impulse to van- ish into original obscurity, and this he expeditiously does after letting off a squib or two. He appears to be a close student of the minor rets, but he seems to have a curious and, one might say, parasitical preference for the kind of stuff that the real admirers of the writers would like to see forgotten. But then "Bellerophon" goes to books with no higher purpose than that of the elephant in the story which went to a muddy pool to suck up something that it might squirt over somebody. Speaking candidly, however, and laying aside all par- tial and prejudiced feeling which a controversy is apt to raise, I muSt admit that Bellerophon" has his talent. He is not cut out as a whitewasher of publicans and sin- ners, nor as the blackener of temperance people, but nature has given him every qualification necessary for a resurrectionist of literary garbage. It's a mean occupa- tion, but chacun a son yout—every one to his taste.— I am, sir,
CADMUS.

Warring,ton,'April 10th, 1888, THE "OLD TENANTRY" OF WALTON. Sir,—ln your contemporaries there is a flaming ac- count given of the presentation of the loving cup, to Mr. Greenall, on his attaining his majority. lam not going to speak in any disrespectful way of the handsome pre- sent subscribed for, or of the young gentleman who has received it; but of members of the deputation who were entrusted with the honour of being styled the "old ten- antry" of Sir Gilbert Greenall. Why, the fact is, Sir Gil- bert Greenall has but about two old tenants on the es- tate, of e.ny note, one Joseph Ellams, of the Waterworks farm, and old John Wimperly, of Morley Common. Pro- bably there may be on the list a few cottagers ; but you don't call a person old under 20 years' standing, and Sir Gilbert's landed estates have been purchased in these years—and when property has been in the hands of flee present owner so few years, how-can you call them old tenants? It would be something hke to quote the phrase of "old tenantry," when the succession to baronetcy has been handed dotvn to seven or eight gen- erations, similar to the Norton Priory estate, and others too well-known to make any comments upon. But I certainly have an opinion that, judging from many facts, which are stubborn things, that there has been an ex- hibition of newness, not only in the honourable position of landlord, but also with regard to the agents and, the tenants—a thorough want of sound confidence and re- ciprocity of feeling, and what supports these remarks are the changes that have taken place. They may be old occupiers and residents on the estate, and with all due respect to both landlord and those it may concern, I have only to say there is a feel- ing manifest that there should not be made fish of one and flesh of another, but every one be deemed alike —Your'S

div.head: WALTON RESIDENT.
div.p: A WALTON RESIDENT.
THE MARGARINE ACT.

Sir,-1 see in your paper an account of a person named Martha Jackson being fined is and 20s ad costs for selling at Fradsham, margarine, not properly labelled. I may say that on the 2nd February, the date named by the superintendent, I was the person who went into the shop as he came out. Mrs. Jackson called my attention to the matter by stating that the superin- tendent had just been in the shop, and said he should summons her for selling margarinenot properly labelled. Now, sir, this margarine was enclosed in a basket 16 inches long, and 12 inches wide at the top; Much nar- rower at the bottom, and about 8 inches deep. It was wrapped up in a cloth, and the lid closed, so that the superintendent could not have known- what was in the basket had it not been for the labels, of which there were no less than six fastened on the basket. The labels were nearly 10 inches long, and, I believe, over One inch deep, with the word margarine almost covering the whole label. The Act states that the word margarine shall be capital letters 1i inches deep. Well, sir, that Act may be law; but in the above case is that law just? Again, the fine was Is, and the costs 20s 6d, and, as there are many people who, like Mrs. Jackson, believe they are right and acting within the law, it might be of interest to them to know how the amount of 20s 6d in costs was made up. I myself am at a loss to know how such costs could 'be incurred, except the superintend.ent charged so much for the use of his horse and traiT in coming to Frodsham. Or perhaps ehe margarine was sent to be analysed, and the cost put on the seller, in which case I should say the matter was a complete farce, as the superintendent was told it was margarine, and it was wrapped in a paper with the word margarine printed on it. To me there appears to be a case o* straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel.-1 remain • yours, 4c., Frodsham, April 4th, 1888.
OBSERVER.
" PRIMROSING " AT THELWALL.

Sir,—On Easter Monday, being a Bank Holiday, and having half a day to myself, I went for a walk as far' as Thelwall to look at the Ship Canal operations, and corn- 1 ing round by what I am informed is called Oyster Shell I Hall, I came across, in the hedge cop•right opposite the Temperance Hall, a stall with a lottery and some dirty looking ornaments, nuts, pipes, etc., as prizes for the lucky ones. The proprietor of the stall was lounging by the side of his cart in as unconcerned a manner as his donkey; indeed the pair of them seented bent on taking it easy for a time at any ;ate. There was not a soul about and I was much puzzled. as to the man's motive for fixing his stall in a locality, where, as it appeared to me, there was very little prospect opusiness. I don't know if the man's visit had anything to do with the Primrose League, or whdther he thought there was any likelihood of doing business with any of its members. but I see there waa a meeting held there the same evening. In a speech made by Mr. R. A. Naylor, I gather that he has been to Ireland and come back' with the startling announcement that the people of that un- happy country do not sing "God Save the Queen" at the end of entertainments, etc! Why should they? Do the people of England? Do the people of Warrington? I have been to many entertainments of one kidd or an- other in our own town but never do I remember hearing it sung. It is customary, I know, to play a few bars of the so-called National Anthem, but no sooner do the people hearthe first two or three notes than they make their exit as fast as possible—as though the music jarred upon their ears. I attended several of the organ recitals at the Manchester Exhibition last summer, and I can safely say that not one third of the people stood up when "God Save the Queen" was played. I wonder if Mr. Naylor has ever tried to find out the real reason why the Irish prefer to sing "God save Ireland," instead of " God save the Queen:" Mr. Naylor says we are all brothers and sisters, one flesh and blood, and cannot understand why there should exist any ill- feeling. This sounds all very well, but the fact remains, nevertheless, that it is such as Mr. Naylor and the Prim-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 14, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 14, 1888.

rose Lea„aue that are doing all they can to frustrate a policy which would bring about the kindly feeling Mr. Naylor desires so much to see. Does Mr. Naylor really believe he can make a people loyal by treating them as thottgh they were Hottentots? If he believes in the brotherhood of man as he professes to do, let him show his sincerity by trying to heal the breach. But this he can never do by coercion. The olive branch has been offered; the Irish are anxiously waiting to accept it, but this the Tory party, aided by the Liberal Unionists, say they shall not do, and so they Prevent for the present the bin-ding together of the hearts of two peoples in a bond of love which shall never be broken. On this, as well as the temperance question, Mr. Naylor appears to be a little inconsistent.—Yours, &c.,
RAMBLER.,

knew nothing about it. —ln answer to a questiorr, the Clerk said the Board had never assumed any, power to sanction an encroachment; all they could say was that they would not interfere. It was quite open for any ratepayer in Latchford to go and knock down the en- croachment.—Mr.Kenworthy said that had been done in Yorkshire, and would very likely be done in Latchford. —The Chairman thought it was a misfortune that the people of Latchford took the view they did of it. He was convinced tbat the arrangement would lead to a great improvement.—Mr. Kenworthy said he had only met one person in Latchford who approved of it, and he had done something of the same sort himself. Mr. Long asked if the Latch- ford people knew that yard for yard was being got.—Mr Kenworthy said Latchford would get nothing, as Grappenhall would get the benefit.—A Waywarden thought that if the Latchford waywarden had been preseut at the meeting when the thing was first dealt with it would have avoided all that unpleasant- ness.—Mr Long said that that Board had, with the valu- able help of their chairman, always been very strong in resisting encroachments on the roads. The committee, of which he was one, had met Mr Richmond on the spot. Mr Richmond seemed to be under the impression that the land could be enclosed, as unfortunately they had been allowed to do in the first instance in the case of Mr Wallington's garden; but the committee pointed out to him that such was not the case. Mr Richmond then said he should refer to legal opinion on the matter, but afterwards he approached them with a desire to 'know what they wished should be done. The committee said that they were willing not to oppose the proposed alteration, bearing in mind the first enclosure— which was a great objection to the highway, but which he supposed they had no power now to remove— if Mr. Smith Barry would give them yard for yard in other parts of the road so that they could make a really good 33ft. road the whole of the way through. After a good deal of fighting Mr. Richmond agreed to that, and land was to be given them at the entrance to the road from the Grappenhall direction ,which was at present very much choked. He (Mr. Long) did not think the Latchford people would take such a narrow view of the matter as to insist that the whole of the land to be given should be in Latchford. The land to be given was, however, in Latchford, with the exception of the little bit at the mouth of the road: He did not wonder that the ratepayers of Latchford were uneasy after the way the roads had been en- croached upon by landowners in previous years, but he hoped that after the explanation given they would see that in this case the. Highway Board had been looking after their interests.—The Chairman said the arrange- ment come to by the committee was one of the fairest he had ever heard of, and would result in a great improVe- ment. If, however, the ratepayers of Latchford choose to go to law they could do so, but they must do it in- dividually.—lt was then agreed that the arrangement proposed by the committee should be approved by the Board. This was the principal business.

WESTON. Operations on this section are still confined tahe work of preparation. The depot is now the scene of busy ac- tivity, the joiners, blacksmiths, and other handicrafts- men being in full employment. A great quantity of beams of wood are stored on the wharf, and they are being prepared in piles in readinesa for the making of the canal in the river bed. The six huts for the navvies are fast approaching completion, and will no doubt be occupied in a few weeks. Each hut is two stories in height, and the accommodation provided is of the most excellent and commodious kind. The situation in which they are placed—on the Weaver wharf—is very mnch exposed, but the buildings are substantially and strongly constructed to withstand the stormy winds of the Mer- sey.

, RUNCORN. There are now four Amertcan steam navvies in use on this length, and the excavations both at Norton and near the works' of Mesirs Wigg Brothers and Steele are be- coming deeper and larger day by day. At present, about 1,0001 men are employed on the section! During the present high tides an immense quantity of material —sleepers and railway metals principally—has been un- loaded at the Old Quay Docks. In the space of less than a week five steamers arrived at these- docks, each vessel havipg & carrying capacity of about 300 tons, and an idea of the bulk of material that was placed on the quay side may easily be gathered. The observations as to the rise and fall of the tidal water in the river are still being made at Runcorn and it is rumoured that some surpris- ing facts have Leen obtained. It is said that at one portion of the ebb tide the water falls no less than one foot in the brief period of a quarter of an hour, and could a calculation be made of the vast quantity of water • that is thus rolling on to the sea, the result would be surprising. Perhaps when Mr Walker has obtained a minute knowledge of the ebb and flow of the water, and the time when its volume is the least and its force tht weakest, operations will be commenced in the river. TH.ELWALL. During the present week great progress has been made in the construction of the navvies' huts near Morris Brook, and it is evident that before long many of. the workmen will be provided with fairly comfortable resid- ences upon the scene of their labours. Many other erec- tions—offices, sheds, &c.—are either finished or all but finished, and indeed this locality, with its munerousbuild- ings. has something of the appearance of a busy back- woods village. On the intended channel of the canal, two steam navvies of the "American" type are regu- larly at work, and locomotives are kept engaged in shunting the wagons which the 'devils " rapidly fill. The bridge across the river at Thelwall has been com- pleted, and a line of 'metals laid upon it. Across the river work seems to be carried. au with undiminished energy, and the embankment continue -to grow so rapidly that it threatens to very shortly to altogether eclipse the view of Wildegrave farmhouse and out-build- , ings from the south. Yesterday it was to be noticed that the grounds at Cedar Lawn, lately the residence of Alderman Pickmere, had been taken possession of, and that hedges and trees were being cut down, preparatory to the work of excava- tion being begun. Cedar Lawn is one of the houses that will be entirely demolished, as it stands almost on the intended centre of the canal, which will here begin
to open out into Latchford Lock's. At about one luin- dred yards to the west of the site of this residence. the Warrington and Altrincham Railway will be carried over the canal on a large viaduct,_
LYMM.

At Statham, which is part of township 9f Lymm, some effective work is being done. As yet there are no steam navvies in operation here, but lines of metals have been laid, ilnd on these plies a small locomotive, the "Moore," whieh draws the waggons filled by manual labour to the spoil heaps to be emptied. The canal here again comes in contact with the Mersey, and 'piles are being driven into the river's bed for a bridge to connect Statham with Rixton Leys, lying oil the opposite side. It is stated that a misunderstanding has taken place ' between the gangers engaged on Rixton "Leys and the contractor for the canal, and in consequence the hands were stopped on Thursday until. a settlement is arrived at. The Lymm sewage farm at Statham is now in the ' hands of the navvies, and a line of rails has been laid through it. It is understood that when the rails of this section have been connected with those at Thelwallsteam navvies will be brought along. LYDIA!.

LOCAL BOARD am-rim—The following is the result of this election, viz :—Foster 583, Rogers 539, Gibbon 527, Swallow 387, Ardern 382, Thomason 349. The three first-named, who were the retiring members, were ac- cordingly re-elected. ILLESS OF THE Rev. J. H. OUSTON.—We understand that the Rev. J. H. Ouston, Congregational minister, is at present suffering somewhat seriously from illness. On Sunday last the Rev. Hugh Davies occupied the pul- pit of the Congregational Church, and announced that a special service would be held on Wednesday evening, at which earnest prayers would be offered for the restora- tion to health of the pastor of the congregation. • (Lynn) COMPANY 3RD V.B.C.R. The second monthly handicap competition took place on the Lymm Range, on Saturday, with the same 3rd class regula- tions. • The following members gained prizes : •Pts. To- alwd. Score. tal. • Lance-Corporal J. Bell Privets J. Oxton 4 63 67 Private W. G. Driver 5 62 67 Private T. Clare • Private F. Warburton 6 61 67 Private R. Clare Pince-Sergeant S. Jackson Private H. Wilson Private H. Bates Private S. Hiude 8 54 60 The company assembled on Sunday morningfor a church parade at Oufrington Church. The sermon was preached ' by the Rector, the Rev. W. G. Knocker, who gave an in- teresting discourse on Christ's re-appearance after his crucifixion. In conclusion he made a special appeal to the volunteers present to lead-wood and sober life and not to be afraid of the taunts of evil-disposed comrades. After the service the route home was by way of Sandy- lane and Rush Green to the Cross, where, after a f.ew words front Captain Jones, thanking the men for turning up in such good numbers and for their clean appearance' and good behaviour, they were dismissed.
