div.p: FRODSHA3f.

IVlsiremos.—On Wednesday afternorn the annual, visitation took place at the Parish Church: Frodsham, when the charge was delivered by the Ven. the Arch- deacon of Chester, after which the churchwardens 'and sidesmen from the surrounding parishes were admitted to their offices. They afterwards partook of tea together in the schoolroom.

UNION CHURCH, FRODSHAM. In this place of worship a sale of work was opened on Thursday afternoon by Ms. McKennel, wife of Dr. McKennel, of Bowden, near Manchester. The church was built upwards a twelve months ago at a cost of nearly .£2,000, and the object of the bazaar was to clear off the existing debt of .£265. There were eight stalls laden with a charming as- _ sortment of articles; and in the centre wasi a stall containing plants and flowers kindly giveniby Mr T. Rigby, who is desirous of maivating a love of flowers amongst the young, with a view to bolding an exhibition later in the year. The iollowing ladies presided at the stalls :—Mrs. Beck, Mrs. T. A. Rigby, Mrs.Vilkinson, Mrs. Dobson Mrs. rurton; Mrs. Roberts, Miss Gibson, Miss Charlotte Gibson, Miss Ormerod, Miss Rigby, Miss Jane Rigby, Miss Alice Rigby, Miss Entwistle, Miss Bowden, Miss Moores, Miss Wilkinson, and Miss Caldwell. There were present at the opening Mr. T. Rigby, Mrs. McKennal, Mr. A. Rigby, Miss Rigby. Mr. S. Rothwell, Mr. J. W. Roth- well, Mrs. T. A. lßigby, Mrs. J. W. Rothwell, Mrs. F. W. Dunsford, Miss Bibby, and Mr. W..P. Gibson. Mr, T. Rigby, in introducing Mrs. Mackennal,' ex- pressed the gratefulness he felt to those present for at- tending there that afternoon, and for their kind encour- gement which, he would take was represented by their presence. and which he believed would be later on represented in a more practical manner: They had one purpose in their hearts they wanted to accomplish, and that was to see their building freed from debt. (Hear, hear.) They had been very successful so far, and he was grateful to the many friends, who by their gene- rosity had succeeded in reducing the debt of £2,000 which the building cost, td about £265. They hoped to be able to realise that amount by the sale. The ladies who.had provided the articles for sale had shown a desire to help forward .a good cause, and he was grateful to them personally. They were favoured with the presence of Mrs. Mackennal, and were only sorry that Dr. Mac- kennal was not with them that day, as he had manifes- ted a very kind sympathy towards them, and had shown a readiness to help in the work in which they were engaged. .(Hear, hear.) He was very grateful to Mrs. Maskennal for her presence, and he requested that lady to declare the Pazaar open. Mrs Mackenhal said that when she was asked to per- form that ceremony she assented very willingly. (Hear, hear.) She hoped they would realise the money they required by the sales to clear the building from debt

div.head: ALLEGED SUNDAY BEER-SELLING.
div.p: ALLEGED SUNDAY BEER-SELLING.

EXTRAORDINARY CASE. At the Borough Police Court. at Warringt,n, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton) and , other magistrates Sarah Locker, a married woman, who holds an off-license at 48, St. James's-street, Latchford, vas summoned for having sold beer dur- ing prohibited hours on Sunday, the Ist April; and Ellen Locker, her daughter-in-law, was summoned for aiding and abetting her in the offence. Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defence.—The Chief Constable (Mr. „Hunt) was about to open the case by making a statement to the magistrates, when Mr. Davies- protested against a chief constable, superintendent, or other member of the police force making a statement. It was against the law, and therefore he should not be carrying out his duty to the profession to whicluhe belonged if he did not object. He thought the magistrates would agree with his objection when they heard the case. Mr. Justice Hawkins, in a recent caseinthe Law Courts, had gone so far as to state that no solicitor would be doing his duty if he allowed a chief constable or any other °Aker to say one word or cross-examine a witness, because the defendant might not have either the money or the means ei defending him- self, and it would, theretore, be very improper to prejudice a man's position, as it would do.—The Magistrates' Clerk said that Mr. Hunt, as chief con- stable, had no locus* standi to make a speech or examine a witness, but, having laid the informa- tion, he was entitled to give evidence.—The Chief Constable wasthen sworn, and gaysa description of the premises in the occupation of the defendant, and shewed that there were two entrances to the house, one in School-street and the other in St. James's-street.—P.C. Monaghan stated that frominstructions received he went on Sunday, the Ist April, in company i with P.C. Robinson, to watch the premises of the defendant, who held ail off beer license. At 10-30 he saw a woman got to the side door of the premises in School- street, and after remaining inside fonr or five minutes come out and go away. At eleven o'clock:another woman went in and stayed three or four minutes, and then went away. On each occasion Elizabeth Locker, the daugh- ter of the defendant, came outside and looked around as if to see if the coast was clear, before the woman cams out. At ten minutes past eleven the defendant, Ellen Locker, went to the house, and after staying for a short time left again. At 11-35 she came again, and remained at the house until a quarter to twelve. Mrs. Locker's daughter came out as before, and looked to see if the road was clear, and then the defendant Ellen Locker came down School-street. When she reached the place where the officerithad been concealed, witness stopped het, and asked *hat she -had been doing on licensed premises. She said that she had been for some eggs. He tapped her dress improver with his stick, and on feeling a hard substance said "These are not eggs, missis.' (Laughter.) He then took her back to the house and asked her for the bottle of beer she had in her possession. She denied having it. On his threatening to take her to the police station, however, her husband came and took Mom her dress the quart bottle of beer produced. Wit- ness asked to see Mrs. Locker (occupier of the house), but was told that she was ill in bed. On going to the house an hour afterwards, however, with the Chiet Con- stable, he found Mrs. Locker sitting in the kitchen.—P. C. Robinson gave evidence in support of the information. In cross - examination he said that he had understood that Thomas Locker, the husband of Ellen Locker, worked ' for his mother, and received an allowance of beer for it.—ln reply to the Bench, it wag explainpd that the other women who had visited the house wf re not stopped because they were going away 'from the police.—Mr. Davies, addressing the Bench for the defence, said that the present case was one of the most paltry with which he had had to do. The defendant, Sarah Locker, had lived at the house in question for nearly ten years, and would deny that dur- ing the whole or any part of that time she had ever sold beer duringprohibiied hours. Her son, Thomas Locker, the husband of the younger defendant, had been in the habit for the past eight or nine years of assisting his mother. For that service he received an allowance of a quart, sometimes only a pint, of beer every Sunday morning. Up.fo within a few weeks ago, when the elder defendant broke a blood vessel, from the effects of which she was still suffering, her son was in the habit of drink- ing the beer on the premises but during Mrs. Locker's illness his wife had fetched the beer every Sunday morn- ing, and he had drunk it at home.—Evidence in support of this statement was then given by the defendant's daughter, and by Thomas Locker, after which the Mayor said that Bench had considered the case, and there could be no doubt that the police were placed in a very difficult position. Their duty was to report in cases wherever they had reasonable grounds for supposing that the law was being broken, and if they did not act up to their duty in that respect they were considered very culpable. If the police officers in the case were not aware of the circumstances which had been brought out in evidence they were perfectly justified in summoning the defendant, 'because from what they saw there was certainly strong evidence that the law was being broken. Taking all the circumstances of the case into considera- tion, the Bench had decided to dismiss it.

div.head: DARESBIIRY HIGH. WAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBIIRY HIGH. WAY BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held at the Court" Room, Daresbury, on Thursday, afternoon. Mr. E. Greenall (chairman) presided, and there was a large attendance of members; Mr. H. Linaker (clerk), and Mr. Peerman (surveyor.) THE CONVERSION OF CONSOLS. It was stated that a circular had been received by the Clerk with regard to tie conversion of government stock, belonging to the township of Grappenhall, and that the circular had been signed by the Chairman.—The Chair- man explained that this meant that next year they would receive 3 per cent, as usual on the stock, but af- terwards for 15 years they would only receive 21 per cent.

div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AND EXTRA TRAFFIC.

The Clerk stated that £l4 5s 5d had been paid to the Board's treasqrer by Mr. .Walker, ship canal contractor, for extra traffic On,the road at Moore; and near the Stag Inn,,Lovver Walton. The Surveyor had carefully cal- culated the cost likely to be incurred in repairing the damage caused by extra traffic, and had sent-in an ac- count to Mr. Walker, who had returned a cheque for the sum stated.

It Nias stated by the Suryeyor that he had provided for ttfe cost of the repair of this road in his estimate, and consequently the matter was re- ferred to the surveyor. • =

A NEGLECTED ACCOUNT.' An account from the late suryeyor, Mr. John Darby- shire, was submitted amounting to £5, for the storage of pipes. Mr. Darbyshi.re also wrote that the pipes could lie for the next 12 months free of charge.—The Chair- man thought it was too bad. His recommendation was to treat the account in the same way as they treated the last account of £2O sent in by , Mr. Darbyshire.—Mr. Aaron: Let it lie on the table.

The Surveyor's estimate of expenditure for the next 112 months was submitted and amounted in all to £4,640, 'which is an increase. on last year's estimate of £1.085 110 s. • • ITFIE ENCROACHMENT ON GRAPPENHALL ROAD. 1 On the Surveyor's report with regard to Latchford township being read, the Chairman referred to the en- croachments on Grappenhall-road, and said lie under- stood that Mr. Kenworthy, the waywarden for the town- ship, had a memOrial to present on the subject: He re- marked that some time ago, owing to an awkward mis- take of their late surveyor, an encroachment by Mr. Wallington had been allowed to pass.:Mr. Wallington was afterwards taking some more land from Mr. Smith Barry, and taking the same line of wall when; he (the chair- tnan) objected and told him he had no right to do it, and 'after a long discussion a committee of that Board was • formed to deal with tho matter. He (the chairrrian) had seen Mr. Richmond, Mr, Smith Barry's agent, and told him that whatever quantity of land was taken from the highwaythat Board must have an equivalent giventhem, that for every yard taken they must, have a yard given them elsewhere.,—The - Clerk said the upshot- was, after the committee had met several times, that Mr. Richmond agreed to give a piece of land further on the road where there was a very bad corner. The improve- ment to the road would, he thought, be very great.—The Rev. A. Kenworthy said he knew nothing at all about the matter till the recent Latchford town's meeting, at which there was a great deal of ill will expressed against the encroachment. He presented a memorial from this town's meeting stating " that complaint was made that Mr. Wallington and Mr.- Smith Barry were encroaching on the road known as Grappenhall- road, and that it resolved and carried unanimously that as such encroachments on the highway are an un- warrantable appropriation of public property, the way- ' warden be instructed to bring the matter before the Highway Board and express the unanimous opinion of this meeting that such encroachments should be re- moved, and the land restored." This encroachment, Mr. Kenwo4hy added, was not right, and was not legal.' They had had Counsel's opinion about it, and it seemed to be altogether illegal.—The Chairman asked if the persons who objected to the encroachments were rate- payers in the extraMunicipagportion ofiLatchford.—Mr. lienworthy said every one of them was.—The.Chairman asked if they were aware that the Board had Met Mr. Smith Barry's agent, and tried to come to an arrange- ment.—Mr. Benworthy said he was not present at the Board meeting when the matter was dealt with, and

ova OWN CORRESPONDS/CFA. 17, Union Court. Old Broad-street, E.C. The Stock Exchange has been engaged in the fortnightly settlement, for the past thtee days, which came to a termination on Thursday, and instead of the expected renewal of activity on the close of the settle- ment quite the reverse tpok place. For the moment the markets are overcast by the German and French difficulties, which if allowed to ga on may cause a com- plete reaction and a heavy fall in prices. In any event holders of Russians should sell without delay.- There has.been some steady buying a all flist-class securities during the past week, which has naturally causecbmany of these securities to touch a figure they have never before reached. The week will also be asso- ciated with the accomplishraent of the conversion scheme, but the influences direct and indirect upon securities caused by the displacement will be felt for a very long time. While this activity has been maintained in investment ,purchases, speculative dealings for the moment are unknown. Scarcely a bid a day for a share can be recorded, with the result that the mining and speculative markets have become a dead letter. /Even' the gamble in diamonds has exhausted itself for tlfe mo- ment, and prices, although they fluctuate pretty wildly at times, are exhibiting a tendency to break up. Copper shares have again came to the front, and Tin- tos have renewed the position they occupied before De Beers dazzled the market. Tintos have gone over 20, and are likely to go higher, but a purchase would be very risky, as a slight reaction has already set,in. We expect,to see a teturn to life in the miscellaneous gold mining sham; before Icing, and speculative holders might do worse than purchase a few of the low- priced at present quotations, including Consolidated Esmeralda. _

Home rails have been film again. We have been cor- rect in our forecast Of the Brighton A's; which will soon cease to be the pawn of the railway speculative dealer. We think Brighton A's form one of the cheapest Invest- mint stocks to be had at present. The traffic returns of the past week show a decrease of £3,075, compared with the corresponding week of last year, which was Easter week. The returns for Sunday and Monday of this week show a decrease of £6,026. 11 In the miscellaneous market the most noticeable feature is the gradual but steady decline in Pavilion Music Ifall Shares, which ffem over eight have fallen to 51 to 6, and there is every prbbability of their going even below par. Messrs. Rothschilds have the issue of two loans against one by Messrs. Barings, but Barings seem to have made the biggest profit. They secured the Uruguay loan it is said at 73, issue it at 824, and get it sent to a premium of 5, which is not bad business.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Mr. Gilhooly, M.P., waA released from Cork Gaol on. Friday. Mr. W. J. Hill, the well-known comedian, died at noon on Friday. •Mr. VL Saunders has brought an action against Sir Charles Warren for arresting him in Trafalgar-square. ' Mr. Stuart, of Chigwell, was terribly crushed by being 'thrown and rolled upon by his horse on Thursday while hunting with the Essex staghounds. At Wicklow Assizes on Friday, Cornelius Reidy was sentenced to twenty years' penal servitude for shooting at a man named Lane, at Castle Island, County Kerry. Evidence was given before a Select Committee of the House of Lords on Friday that many workmen under the sweating system, in the East-end, were no better paid then coolies. Yesterday, at a special meeting of the Executive Com- mittee of the Liverpool Uathedral, it was resolved to sus- pend all action for the present so far as the building of a cathedral is concerned. _ _ _

At Manchester, on Friday, George Rideal, :aged 33 ; clerk, and Ann Griffiths, 18, servant, were charged with ' attempting to commit suicide, Meal was sentenced to three month's imprisonment, and the girl was liberated on her own recognizances. Suosn BOUNTIES CONFERENCE.—This conference was resumed on Friday at the Foreign Office, Baron H. de Worms presiding. The sitting did not last long, as the members had been invited to visit the Marquis of Salis- bury at Hatfield in the afternoon. Gomm, Goma, GONE !—The handsome premises of the Birmingham Liberal Club which were erected two years ago, at a cost of £84,000 were brought under the aue- tioneerl hammer on Friday, the Club having failed ow- ing to dissensions in the Liberal party in the borough. The property was purchased for £23,000, £B,OOO less than the sum paid for tbe site alone. THE ENNIS DISTURBANCE.—At Ennis, on Frid,y, a num- ber of persons were charged with taking part in an ilk-. gal assembly at that place on Sunday last, and three others were charged with stoning the police and soldiers on the same occasion. The accused objected to both cases being taken together, and after an argument the case of stonethrowing was adjourned for a fortnight. I LIBERALS AND THE COUNTY CrOVERNMENT BILL.—A: meeting of Liberal members "specially interested in the provisions of the Local Government Bill" was held at the National Liberal •qlub on Friday, morning_ The meeting was strictly private. There were about ninety menffiers present altogether. Mr. Stansfield having brieffy opened the Aeeting, ai discussion followed; the prevailing opinion being that the leaders of the Liberal party should be pressed to urge upon the Government the necessity for more time for debate on the second reading of the Bill. Mr. Morley agreed, and a resolution was adopted that the Chairman confer with M. Glad- stone with that object. A committee was appointed to consider the details of the Bill, with a view to concerted actibn. • •

div.head: SERIOUS FIRE AT A COLLIERYv-200 MINERS ENTOMBED.
div.p: SERIOUS FIRE AT A COLLIERYv-200 MINERS ENTOMBED.

The utmost consternation was created in North Wales An Friday afternoon by the report of a disastrous fire at the Vauxhall Collieries, Ruabon, where between 200 and 300 men are employed. It appears that shortly before noon a fire broke out in the engine-room on the surface, where all the winding operations are condiicted. Every effort was made to save the building, but a strona_ wind • was blowing, and the entire struc- ture as speedily enveloped. The, fire ewine from Wynnstay mansion was despatched, and Sir Firakkin Williams Wynn personally superintended the *ork of subduing the flames. The greater portion of the build- ing waS, however, completely gutted, and both winding ropes were-broken, all the miners being thus efitombed. Considerable alarm was felt throughout the neighbour- hood, and thousands of people hurried to the collieries. A later telegram says the fire has been subdued, and the colliers liberated from the mine by means of an adjoin- ing shaft.

div.head: EMPEROR FREDERICK.
div.p: THE EMPEROR FREDERICK.

Exams, Famsy.,—The Emperor Frederick, who passed a good night, rose at halfipast seven this morning, and subsequently received verbal reports. BERLIN, FRIDAY NOON.—The contraction which has led to the insertion of a fresk canula in the Emperor's, throat is believed to indicate that the local complaint has at- tacked the trachea.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. , The House met at 4 o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—EarI Delaware gave notice for an early day to call attention td the hours of employment of railway servants, and to ask the Government whether there were any. 'objections. to periodical reviews being made on the subject.—Lord Denman moved the second reading of the Women's Suffrage Bill. On the motion of Lord Combrook, the second reading was postponed to this day six inooths.—On the motion of Lord Cgmper- down, Lord Coleridge was added to the Select Committee appointed to insuire into the duties of high sheriffs. The House adjourned at ten mfnutes to five_ - HOUSE OF COMMONS. - The Sneaker took the chair at three o'clock. The Milford Docks Bill was read a third time QUESTIONS.—In answer to Mr Caleb Wright, who asked whether the cost of elections, both- for district and- county councils; wquld have to be borne by, the candidates or would be paid by the rates, Mr. RITCHIE said that all proper casts of returning offi- cers would be paid out of the county and district fund. Mr. A. BALFOUR replying to Mr. John Morley, said he could yet state the .ay on. which the Irish Land• Pur- chase bill would be Mtroduced. GOVERNMENT BUSINESS.—Mr. W. &ins moved that on Fridays Government business should take precedence of the motion for Committee of Supply.—Mr. 'Anon= CREME opposed; he insisted that Goverrnment by the present motion was destroying the last right private mem, ben; had for bringing forward grievances. The mo- tion was simply made to rush the second reading of the Local Government Bill through the Houge.—A discus- sion ensued in which Sir J. Pease, Mr. Whltebread, and others objected to the proposal of Mr. Smith, insisting that time ought to be given the country to understand the Local Government Bill during the second reading.— Mr. SMITH sought to,justify his proposal, and Mr. GLAD- STONE et/0k objection to it—For the motion 243, against: 143. • NEW Fativvicx brought in the bill to pro- vide for the weekly payment of wages in Great Britain and Ireland, which was read a first time.—Mr. FIiiTH brought in the bill to abolish the livery franchise of the city of London, which was also read a first time. LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. :The adjourned debate was resumed On Mr. Ritchie's motion oo the second reading of the Local Government Mr. RATHBONE thought the bill as it stood objec- tionable in Many points, more especially as regarded the overlapping of areas and checks against unlimited ex- penditure.—Mr. FOREST Froaox expressed the opinion that the measure would be favourable to the Conserva- tive party, and that it would increase rather than diminish the influence of county gentlemen in local government. He did not see why, publicans ' should be werse treated than brewer § pr distillers ; but he hoped the trade would think twice before they rejected the offer of the Government.— Mr. BROADHURST insisted that the Bill onght to abolish the qualifications for guardianggpf the poor, so that the exclusion of the labouring el corn the administration of the poor laws might no longer txist. The Bill, on the whole, was founded on broad and liberal lines, but • at present it was like a large skeleton without either flesh or blood. (Laughter.)—Mr. Thomas Ems thought that omissions and reservations in the measure seriously detracted from its value.—Mr. TAELING said he believed •the proposals of the Government as regarded relief from local taxation would be gratefully received by the agri- cultural interest. yLEFT SITTING.]

WE, THE UNDERSIGNED, DO HEREBY REQUEST YOU TO SUMMON A PUBLIC MEETING of the inhabitants of the the Borough of Warrington, to consider the proceedings of the "National Association for the Promotion of Technical Educa- tion" and the desirability of forming an Association in War- rington to .--operate therewith. Dated at Warrington, sth April, 1888. (Signed by 52 persons.) In pursuance of the above requisition, I hereby convene a PUBLIC MEETING to be held on TUESDAY NEXT, THE 17TH APRIL, at 2-15, in the TOWN HALL. THOS. H. SUTTON, Mayor. Town Hall, 13th April, 1888.

RUNCORN UNION.—ELECTION OF GUAR- DIANS. TO THE RATEPAYERS OF 'RUNCORN TOWNSHIP. RESPECTED FELLOW RATEPAYERS.—I beg to return my sin- cere thanks for the honour you have conferred, and the oonfl- dence•you have shown in so unitedly returning me as a Guardian to the Runcorn Township. I will endeavour to serve you, and discharge the duties devolving upon me, in an unbiassed and conscientious' manner. I will at all times endeavour to avoid the expenditure of the Ratepayers' ironies In any manner, excepting for real necessary purposes and uses. I will support such measures as may tend to promote the reduction of the rates • and while at all times I shall con- sider the Ratepayers' interests and welfare as my own. I will nevertheless give my sympathy and support to all cases of genuine poverty.—l am, respected Fellow-Ratepayers, yours truly, D. H. 3ONES, Draper, Runcorn, April 12th. 1888.

FOOTBALL "FATALMEs.—A young man named .Toseph Sinith, aged 23, who was seriously injured in a football match at Hexham-on-Tyne, on Saturday, died on Tues- day afternoon from injuries to the spine. Deceased when playing'half back was collared by two opposing players, Lifted from the ground, and he fell heavily on the back part of his head and neck. He was a schoolmaster at Gateshead.—A sad accident occuired at a football match at Whalley Range, Manchester, on Saturday, which re- sulted in the death of one of the players, Mr. H. 1. Fletcher, of Bean Cliffe, Eccles, aged 23, a member of a well-known family, of cricket and football amateurs. Mr. 'Fletcher was taking part in a friendly game under the Rugby rules, between past and present members of the Manchester Football Club, and whilst "tackling" ano- ther player he came into such violent collision with his , opponent that his neck and spine were seriously injured. hn He was it once carried off the ground, and as lie was in a critical condition he was conveyed to• the Manchester Al Infirnyuy, where he received prompt and unremit- tig attention. His injuries, however, were so serious that he died on Sunday morning. = S
